# THE PRINTER
## TO THE READERS
### SENDS HEARTIEST GREETINGS <note>original: "S. P. D.," an abbreviation for the Latin "Salutem Plurimam Dicit," a formal greeting meaning "sends many greetings."</note>

A FEW years ago, dear READER, we published a reasonably substantial volume by various authors treating **the subject of chemistry** <note>original: "περὶ χημείας" (peri chēmeias). In the 16th century, "chemistry" and "alchemy" were often used interchangeably to describe the study of metallic transformation and medicinal elixirs.</note>, collected through the efforts of **GUGLIELMO GRATAROLO** <note>Guglielmo Gratarolo (1516–1568) was an Italian physician who became a prominent editor of scientific and alchemical works in Basel.</note>, the Physician. Since that venture was successful for us, and we perceived that it was welcomed by those devoted to this Philosophy <note>The "Philosophy" mentioned here is the "Hermetic Philosophy," a term for alchemy which sought to understand the hidden laws of nature.</note>, we applied our efforts to further refining and explaining this art to the best of our ability. Therefore, with the assistance of friends—learned men—we have gathered more writings, and from those collected, we have selected what I believe to be the better works. We have distributed them into these two volumes in a more convenient and affordable format; and we are even now considering

# PREFACE

...more excellent works, if God grants us leisure and our friends provide help, to bring them into the light: so that men eager for this most excellent and useful art <term>art: the "Hermetic Art" or alchemy, which aimed at both the transmutation of metals and the creation of life-extending medicines</term> might use and enjoy them. 

But someone will say that through these editions of mine I bring more harm than benefit to the **Commonwealth** <term>Commonwealth: original "Reipubl." (Respublica), referring here to the "Republic of Letters" or the general public good</term>, since the art is empty and the science is non-existent; seeing as it deals not with matters that are entirely certain, but with those that are uncertain and only rarely occurring—indeed, most rarely, or perhaps never—but rather treats the mere opinions of many men. 

For [they say] no one, in our own or the preceding century, has performed those things which the writers of this art so magnificently and diversely promise. Since it therefore lacks its intended purpose <note>original: "fine." In Renaissance logic, a true "art" or "science" had to have a "finis" (an end or goal) that was actually achievable.</note>, and all things are done for the sake of a purpose, it follows that it is neither an art nor a science, and that those who study these things or believe in lazy imposters are ridiculous and foolish. 

To these critics, it has been more than sufficiently answered with certain proofs by excellent and most learned Philosophers, and the truth of this art has been proven (especially indeed by the most celebrated Phi- <note>The text ends mid-word. The catchword "lofopho" at the bottom of the page indicates the word is "Philosopho" (Philosopher).</note>

α 3

[losopher] **Pietro Bono of Ferrara** <note>original: "Petro Bono Ferrariensi." Author of the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella* (The New Precious Pearl), written c. 1330. This is especially true since it is not my role to teach or to defend specific factions, but rather to publish teachers of good literature and the arts for the common benefit, and to bring them together so that the truth might be struck out as if from the collision of flints. 

Meanwhile, however, I will say what seems right to me—unskilled as I am. The art is mostly contradicted by those who (even if they are otherwise most learned) have never been practiced in it. Indeed, no one acts or judges more recklessly than the ignorant and the unskilled. For many things seem impossible to the inexperienced which, nevertheless, are very easily accomplished by art and nature, as is seen everywhere in all...

[in almost every] kind of art, experience teaches. On the contrary, a skilled and experienced investigator of most sagacious nature—and, if I may say so, her helper <note>original: "coadiutor." This reflects the alchemical theory that the "artist" does not create, but assists nature in perfecting itself.</note>—is able, through talent and diligence, to perform and bring about even those things which seem impossible to the unskilled and ignorant, and beyond the grasp of the common people. 

As for me, although I have never touched matters of this kind, nor am I the sort of person who can judge anything concerning such an abstruse mystery, yet I cannot bring myself to believe that so many learned philosophers and men of great name—indeed, even illustrious Kings who were the principal writers of this art, whose writings we are now presenting—were themselves deceived or wished to deceive others. This is especially so since they have otherwise maintained a most excellent reputation among all the learned for so many centuries now: such as **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in early chemistry and alchemy.</note>, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works dominated European universities for centuries.</note>, **Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and chemist known for his systematic laboratory classifications.</note>, **Villanova** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a Catalan physician and theologian to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note>, **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315). # PROPOSITIONS, OR
## MAXIMS OF THE CHEMICAL ART.

### PROPOSITION I.

*EVERY pure and clean extract from its ore <term>Minera: raw mineral source or ore</term>, from stones, as well as from foreign matters, without any preparation, which does not melt like wax, is unsuitable for this work. From this, it is concluded that all metals are excluded, as well as all species of Marcasite <term>Marchasita: a term historically used for various sparkling minerals, often iron pyrites, thought to be immature metals</term>, glass, crystal, coral, and all pearls, which do not liquefy in the fire.*

### Proposition II.

*Every sublimable substance <term>Sublimabile: a material that can be turned into vapor by heat and then solidified again</term> that adheres to the sides of the vessel, preventing the sight of the material inside the vessel, is removed and unsuitable for this business. For this reason, the four principal spirits <term>Spiritus: the volatile elements of alchemy that "flee" the fire</term> are especially excluded: namely quicksilver <note>original Latin: "argentum viuum"</note>, arsenic, sulfur, and every kind of tutty <term>Tutia: a zinc oxide residue collected from smelting furnaces</term> and magnesia <note>In alchemy, "magnesia" refers to various mineral substances or a specific stage of the chemical process, rather than the modern element magnesium.</note>.*

### Proposition III.

*Every mineral, of which there is no earth, is foreign...*

<summary>This page lists the opening fundamental axioms of the alchemical art, defining which substances are unsuitable for the "Great Work." It rejects materials that do not melt easily or those that leave a residue on the glass during heating, including metals and the four volatile spirits.</summary>
<keywords>chemical maxims, alchemical theory, ores, sublimation, four spirits, mercury, sulfur, arsenic, tutty, magnesia</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>continuity: This page continues the list of "Propositions" or alchemical axioms, completing Proposition III regarding mineral origins and moving into further exclusions based on the nature of organic matter and the requirements for the "masculine" principle in the Great Work.</meta>

...is alien and hostile to this work. From this, all things are excluded which proceed from animals, such as hair, blood, flesh, dung, eggs, and the like; and also all animals themselves, such as tortoises, <term>caragdi: likely beetles or snails, frequently cited in alchemical lists of "low" organisms</term>, moles, frogs, bees, and similar creatures.

## Proposition IV.

Any animate thing, or that which proceeds from inanimate things <note>The author likely refers here to substances produced through spontaneous generation or biological processes rather than mineral growth.</note>, is unfit for this greater art. From this proposition, all superfluities <note>In this context, "superfluities" refers to waste products or byproducts.</note> of animals are especially excluded, as well as all vegetables and those things which proceed from them, such as wine, <term>Aqua ardens: "burning water," or distilled alcohol</term>, oil, honey, urine, semen, and things similar to these.

## Proposition V.

Everything that cannot be blackened <term>denigrari: the 'nigredo' or black stage</term>, whitened <term>dealbari: the 'albedo' or white stage</term>, and reddened <term>rubificari: the 'rubedo' or red stage</term> by fire within one hour of a natural day <note>A "natural day" refers to a full 24-hour cycle.</note>, does not enter into the composition of this work in the role of the masculine principle <note>In alchemy, the "masculine" element (often associated with sulfur or the sun) represents the active, fixed, or transformative agent in a reaction.</note>.

## Proposition VI.

Everything that lacks red smoke <note>original Latin: "fumo rubeo"</note> when enclosed in a small vessel over a proper fire, does not enter into the composition of this work, holding...

# PROPOSITIONS.

*...the place of femininity. From the two aforementioned maxims <note>Referring to the previous propositions defining the masculine and feminine principles.</note>, alums and salts are excluded, and every kind of boraxes <note>original: "baurachiorum," referring to various fluxing agents used in metallurgy</note> and <term>gignarum: likely vitriols or mineral-based salts</term>, and all liquids proceeding from them.*

### Proposition VII.

*No single thing can complete a work of a higher order. From this, it is especially gathered that the <term>Philosophers' Stone: the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term> is made from two things: namely, male and female; or from the red and the white <note>The "red" and "white" typically represent Sulfur and Mercury, the two primary principles of the Great Work.</note>.*

### Proposition VIII.

*Whatever cannot be completed in one vessel and as one unit is unsuitable for this work. And from this, a plurality of vessels is especially excluded <note>The author emphasizes the "Unity of the Vessel," a common alchemical tenet suggesting the entire process should happen in a single, sealed container called the "Philosophical Egg."</note>.*

### Proposition IX.

*Whatever is not strong enough to finish such a perfection and make gold and silver within a space of a hundred days at most is hostile to this work. From this, the "nine months" <note>Some alchemists believed the process required nine months to mirror human gestation; this author rejects that timeline.</note> are especially excluded; or rather, it is gathered that the Stone ought to be completed in one hundred days with its final perfection, up to and including the time of <term>multiplication: the final stage where the power and quantity of the Stone are increased</term>.*

<summary>This page lists three alchemical axioms regarding the dual nature of the Stone (male/female), the necessity of using a single vessel, and a strict timeline of 100 days for the completion of the work.</summary>

# P R O P O S I T I O N S .
## Proposition X.

Anything that, in the first six days, having been melted with the required fire in a <term>philosophical vessel: the "vas physicum," often a sealed glass container like the "Philosophical Egg"</term> in its necessary furnace, does not appear saffron-yellow <note>original: "croceum"</note>, and in the other six days red, and in the subsequent days white with a perfect whiteness <note>original: "albedine perfecta," the *albedo* stage of the alchemical work</note>, and in the thirty concluding days most intensely red with a perfect redness <note>original: "rubicundissimum rubedine perfecta," the *rubedo* or final stage</note>, is not within the intention of this work. From this is especially derived the method of operating: namely, that the <term>philosophical stone: "lapis physicus," the goal of alchemy</term> must be placed in a glass vessel, inviolably closed, in a <term>philosophical furnace: "furno physico," often called an Athanor, designed for constant, regulated heat</term>, and it must be melted over a slow fire. In that state of fusion, it must be kept at a uniform fire for the space of eighteen days. In the first six days, the <term>medicine: "medicina," another name for the substance undergoing transmutation</term> will be saffron-yellow; in the next six days, it will be red; and in the other six, it will be black <note>The text here lists "black" (nigra), though the previous sentence mentioned "white" (album). The *nigredo* or blackening usually represents the death and putrefaction of the matter.</note>. Afterwards, it will be red with a most intense redness, which you will maintain for thirty days, during which you must nourish the said stone with two lights <note>original: "luminibus," likely referring to lamps or specific heat sources</note> that are not very thick, day and night, for the duration of the said thirty days. When these things are finished, a saffron-yellow color will appear, which will cover all the red like a cloud. And that saffron-yellow color will cease within the space of eight days:

## Proposition XI.

*Every medicine that cannot multiply itself infinitely is not the intent of the work of the greater order <note>the "Great Work" or "Magnum Opus," the ultimate goal of alchemy</note>. From this it is chiefly gathered that the multiplication of this work is one part of the aforementioned medicine: for the redness, the aforementioned vessel should be placed with twelve parts <note>referring to proportions of the substance or "projections"</note> with the fire of three lights for fifteen days, and it will arrive at the ultimate redness, and it will be a perfect Red <term>Elixir: "Elyxir," the transformative substance that perfects metals</term>, and thus you can multiply it infinitely.*

THE BEGINNING of the Book of THE ASSEMBLY OF PHILOSOPHERS <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a fictional meeting of Greek philosophers.</note>, in which Arisleus <note>Arisleus is a legendary figure in alchemy, often identified as the author or narrator who records the wisdom of the ancients.</note> gathered the sayings of the more prudent disciples, introducing Pythagoras <note>Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BC) was a Greek philosopher; in alchemical tradition, he was viewed as a master of secret, sacred sciences.</note> the philosopher and teacher, and collecting the opinions of the disciples. This book is also called the Third Pythagorean Assembly, titled "Concerning Hidden Wisdom." Now, Pythagoras commands the disciple Eximidius <note>Eximidius is likely a Latinized corruption of a Greek name, possibly Anaximander or Anaximenes.</note> to begin the discussion and to discourse upon the hidden wisdom, and then for the others in their turn to offer their own opinions. Thus, he begins:

EXIMIDIUS says: The beginning of all things is a certain nature, and this nature is perpetual, infinite, nourishing and cooking <term>cooking: from the Latin 'coctio', referring to the alchemical process of maturation or transformation through heat</term> all things. Moreover, the times of corruption <note>the breakdown of matter</note> and generation <note>the birth or creation of new forms</note> are, as it were, the boundaries by which we reach that which universal nature nourishes and cooks. Truly, the stars and the heavenly bodies, since they are fiery, are by their very nature part of the process of cooking and nourishment. So that... <meta>catchword: vt au- (so that...)</meta>

...so that they might remain stable and perform their duty correctly, God established the air between them and the earth, and the things to be nourished and cooked <term>cooked: from the Latin 'coquendas', referring to the alchemical process of maturation or ripening through heat</term>, which would contain the stars and prevent them from—especially the Sun’s blasts, for I say nothing of the others, he says—burning up all existing things. And if the air did not breathe into the spirits by which creatures are generated, the Sun would destroy all existing things with its heat. But also water would destroy all things with its coldness and moisture, unless air intervened. Therefore, since air is hot and dry <note>original: "calidus & siccus"; interestingly, the text here assigns the qualities of fire to air, though air is more traditionally hot and moist in Aristotelian physics.</note>, it so reconciles the heat of the celestial fire and stars with the watery coldness, so that a perpetual friendship might remain between them, and the nourishment and benefit of cooking <term>cooking: 'decoctionis', the process of heating a substance to extract its essence or mature its nature</term> might proceed for all existing things.

THE ASSEMBLY says: You have described fire well; continue then.

He <note>Referring to Eximidius</note> says: I magnify and honor the air, because by it the work is improved, as it thickens and thins, and as it grows hot and cold. Its thickness occurs when [the elements] are distinguished in heaven because of the rising of the Sun. But its thinness occurs when the air is thinned and heated by another Sun <note>This likely refers to the "alchemical sun" or the artificial heat of the philosopher's furnace.</note>. When that air is thinned, the Sun becomes near; when it is near, heat reaches man and creatures.

ANAXAGORAS <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that all things are composed of infinitesimally small particles.</note> says: You have described the air well. But know, O Assembly, that the thickness of the four beginnings <term>beginnings: 'initiorum', referring here to the four basic elements of the universe</term> rests in the earth alone, because the thickness of fire falls into the air, and the thickness of air—together with what is gathered from the thickness of fire—falls into the water.

# PHILOSOPHY

The thickness of water as well, and that which is united from the thickness of fire and air, rests in the earth. Thus the thickness of these four <note>Referring to the four classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> rests in the earth, and they are joined within it. Therefore the earth itself is denser <term>denser: the Latin 'spissior' refers to being thick, compact, or less permeable; the "grossest" form of matter</term> than all the other elements, as is clearly apparent and can be seen. Fire, however, is thinner <term>thinner: Latin 'rarior', or "rare," meaning subtle, light, and spiritual rather than physically dense</term> than the others; and just as the earth, which is denser, is lower, so fire is higher and more worthy. Air, truly, is less thin than fire, and water in turn is less thin than air. For everything cold and moist is of less thinness than that which is hot and moist. And the earth is of less thinness than water, because it is cold and dry; and everything cold and dry is less thin than that which is cold and moist.

**PYTHAGORAS** says: You have well-arranged, O sons of learning <note>original: "filij doctrinae"; a traditional way of addressing students or initiates in alchemical texts</note>, the descriptions of these natures from which God created all things. Proceed, therefore.

To this **LUCAS** says: I make known to you that from these four natures God created all things, and all created things return into them; in these they are generated and die in their own time, just as God has ordained.

**LOCASTES** says: Know that the creation of the world was created from two dense things and two thin things, and nothing of the dense things exists in the sublime creation. For this reason, it is thinner <note>The "sublime creation" refers to the celestial or ethereal realms, which the author argues are even more subtle than the Sun itself.</note> than the Sun and all lower creatures.

**ARISLEUS** <note>Arisleus is a legendary figure in alchemical literature, often acting as the chief disciple or interlocutor in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> said: Master, because you have gathered us together for the benefit of future generations, nothing more useful could have come to our knowledge than this understanding of the elements. And he replied: I have said before that God brought forth all things—that is, the four elements—out of nothing, and then from these He produced all created things: the heavens, the thrones, the angels, the stars, the sea, and everything that is within them. And because we see that those four elements are almost enemies to one another, the creatures formed from them are therefore diverse. For if all things had been created from the same single element, they would be of only one nature, and they would always agree. 

Nevertheless, God has so united and coupled those four that they must observe a perpetual peace: thus the dry is often mixed with the moist, and the hot with the cold, and they come together fittingly; from this union emerge creatures which are even most precious. Of those elements which come together, two are seen and touched <note>The "visible" elements are Earth and Water.</note>, while two are neither seen nor touched <note>The "invisible" elements are Air and Fire, often considered the "spiritual" components of matter.</note>. 

For if only those things which are seen and touched are joined, undoubtedly the remaining elements are also mixed in, for they are present within the first two. For Air, participating in the nature of Fire, also has something in common with Water; similarly, it was said above that the Earth embraces all these things within itself. For when our copper itself is placed with the water of the sea—

**Parmenides** said: Know, wise men, that the envious <note>The "envious" (inuidi) is a standard alchemical term for authors who deliberately obscured their writings to prevent the unworthy from succeeding.</note> have treated the subjects of waters, broths, bodies, and metals in many different ways, in order to deceive you who seek this knowledge. Therefore, dismiss all these things, and cause gold and coins <note>original: "numos"; here meaning the finished, metallic state of the Stone or the perfected matter.</note> to be made from this copper <note>original: "ære"; while literally copper or bronze, in this context it refers to the "Philosopher's Copper," the base material of the work.</note> of ours; and take the copper, or lead for its fattiness or blackness, and tin for its liquefaction. Know that unless you well-fit the natures of truth and their compositions, and join kindred things with their kin, you will achieve nothing; this is because natures meet with their own natures, contain them, and rejoice in them. For they rot and are born, because the nature which rules the substance also destroys it, turning it into dust and nothingness; then, that same nature renews, repeats, and gives birth to it frequently. For the very same thing that brings death also brings life.

Therefore, strive to know what it is that makes a thing rot and renews it, and what its flavor is, and what is its distance and closeness, and how after enmity there comes friendship, and how corruption <note>The breakdown of a substance's current form.</note> and generation <note>The birth or creation of a new, perfected form.</note> occur, and how those natures embrace each other in turn, and how they become harmonious in a slow fire. Once these things are noted and understood, apply your hands to the work. But if you are ignorant of these stated qualities, do not approach the work, since the whole thing is harmful, a misfortune, and a sorrow. Now understand the words of the Sages, and keep this brief saying in mind: namely, that **Nature rejoices in nature** <note>original: "Natura naturâ lætatur"; a foundational axiom of alchemy suggesting that only substances of a similar nature can act upon or transform one another.</note>,

<summary>Parmenides warns against the confusing metaphors of previous alchemists and introduces the central concept of the "natural" cycle of decay and rebirth. He emphasizes that the alchemist must understand the sympathetic relationships between substances, summarized by the famous maxim that nature rejoices in its own kind.</summary>

...and it contains nature, and nature conquers and overcomes nature. In these words, the entire work is understood. ...judged, it receives life and is multiplied and increased like all other things. # PHILOSOPHY

**AGADMON** says: Cook the copper <note>original: *æs*; while literally copper, in alchemy this often refers to the "base" metallic starting material of the Great Work.</note> until it becomes a light and impalpable body, and place it in its own vessel: then sublimate <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: *sublimatio*; the process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor, then allowing it to solidify again. Here, Agadmon suggests repeating this five to seven times.</note> it five or seven times until the water descends, knowing that since the water is powder, it is diligently ground. But if you doubt how water becomes powder, know that the intention of the Philosophers is that the body—which was not water before it fell—becomes water together with the water, and water is mixed with water, and they become one. Furthermore, you must know that unless you turn both into water, you will not arrive at the precious work.

<margin>+</margin>For it is necessary that the body, overcome by the flame of fire, be destroyed and made weak along with the water in which it is, until it becomes entirely water. The ignorant, however, when they hear the name of "water," think it is the water of the clouds; but if they read our books, they would know that it is the **permanent water** <term>permanent water</term> <note>original: *aqua permanens*; a central alchemical concept referring to a specialized solvent, often mercurial, that does not evaporate and can dissolve gold without losing its own nature.</note>, which cannot be permanent without its companion with which it has been made one.

<margin>+</margin>This is the water which the Philosophers called the **water of gold**, the **fiery poison**, the "good thing of many names," and the sand which **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> commanded to be washed many times, so that the **blackness of the Sun** <note>original: *Solis nigredo*; the *nigredo* or "black stage" of the work, representing the initial putrefaction and purification of the material.</note>—which it had received during the dissolution of the body—might be wiped away. And know that unless you take this body of mine which lacks a spirit, you will achieve nothing of what you desire, because nothing foreign enters the work, nor anything that is not sincere <note>original: *syncerum*; meaning pure or unadulterated.</note>. Therefore, cast away all plurality: for nature is content with a single thing, and he who is ignorant of it will perish.

<summary>Agadmon explains the process of turning solid matter into "permanent water" through repeated sublimation, emphasizing that the "water" mentioned is a philosophical solvent rather than common rainwater. He stresses the necessity of purity and the unity of the material, warning that only a single, pure nature can complete the work.</summary>

They have described it [the art] by various names, yet the truth is always found in their writings. For they said: mix, cook, whiten, grind, roast, coagulate, and dissolve the <term>Ethelia</term> <note>original: *Etheliam*; an alchemical term likely derived from Greek, referring to a volatile spirit, a vapor, or the "hidden" nature of the substance</note>, and produce the <term>rust</term> <note>original: *rubiginem*; refers to the transformation of the metal, specifically the achievement of the red stage or "rubedo"</note>. The words are many, but the <term>governance</term> <note>original: *regimẽ* (regimen); the method of controlling the heat and process</note> is one. If, therefore, you wish to find the truth, there is no need for that division of labor; rather, only take care of this: adjust the <term>complexion</term> <note>the balance of the primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>. Then, cook it gently for a long time. Do not grow weary of the boiling and the soaking until you see the <term>Elixir</term> <note>original: *Yxir*</note> adorned in Tyrian and royal clothing <note>Tyrian purple was the most expensive dye in antiquity; here it signifies the successful attainment of the deep purple or red color of the perfected Philosopher's Stone</note>. In these words, although they are "dead" [on the page], there is nonetheless life for those who understand. Therefore, read them frequently and always meditate deeply upon them, and wisdom will come to you.

**HYARGUS** says: The <term>bronze</term> <note>original: *Æs*; in alchemy, this refers not to common hardware bronze, but to the "philosophical" metal or the base matter of the work</note> of which the Philosophers spoke is not the bronze of the common people, nor is it common tin. Rather, it is our "body," which must be mixed with the body of <term>Magnesia</term> <note>original: *Magneſiæ*; not the modern element magnesium, but a name for a mysterious "mother" substance or mineral used as a starting point</note>, so that it may be cooked and ground without weariness until it becomes a stone. Then, that stone must be ground again in its vessel with <term>water of life</term> <note>original: *aqua vitæ*; usually refers to a distilled spirit or a potent solvent</note> and <term>nitre</term> <note>saltpeter</note>, and be completely broken down. 
<margin>NB</margin>
Moreover, you must have water continually available, so that the more you cook, the more you may sprinkle it on, until it acquires the rust <note>the red color</note> which is the foundation of the work. Cook this and grind it with <term>Egyptian vinegar</term> <note>original: *Ægyptiaco aceto*; a symbol for a powerful, sharp solvent or acid used for purification</note>, and you may call either of them—either the bronze itself, or the vinegar and water—the "Bronze."

**CADMON** says: You have said, Hyargus, that both things which come into the mixture are called bronze...

<summary>The text shifts from moral advice to allegorical instructions, emphasizing that despite many names, the alchemical process is a single "regimen." Speakers Hyargus and Cadmon define the "Philosophical Bronze" and describe the repetitive cooking and grinding necessary to reach the "Tyrian" (purple/red) stage.</summary>

...therefore his name is made known, he who inspired the Sages to turn the body into spirit, possessing a power and color that is unchangeable and incorruptible. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It must also be made known to you, investigators of this art, that that sulfur could not whiten the copper until it had been whitened itself in the prior work; for the habit of this sulfur is to "flee." This happens as soon as the quicksilver and the copper itself are joined. For then they often mutually dissolve and "conceive," and they do not allow the spirit to flee, but both become quicksilver. And so this material—which at first was neither copper nor quicksilver—is nonetheless created through the mixing of quicksilver; once added to the quicksilver, it contains that first quicksilver whose habit was to flee. Wherefore the Philosophers have said: **"Sulfurs are contained by sulfurs."** <note>original: *Sulphura sulphuribus continentur*; a fundamental alchemical axiom meaning like substances are used to stabilize one another</note>. Do not think, therefore, that this substance which dyes and then flees is the **coin of the common people** <note>original: *numum... vulgi*; a warning that the "coin" mentioned by alchemists is a metaphorical substance, not actual money</note>; rather, the intention of the Philosophers is...

...most firm, because unless it is mixed with the white or the red (which is **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> of its own kind), it will undoubtedly flee. **EXIMENVS** said: The Philosophers have called our water and our work by many—indeed, almost all—the names of metals; but however they may call it, they always mean the water itself. <margin>124</margin> This water, when placed in its vessel with its own components, prevents the substances from being burned; and the more the substances themselves are seized by the flame, the more they hide in the innermost parts of the water, so that they are not harmed by the heat of the fire. And so, with the substances diligently ground with the water, the **Ethelia** <term>Ethelia; a technical term in alchemy for the volatile spirit or vapor that rises during heating</term> ascends, and thereafter the water leads the work to its true end solely through its own **imbibition** <note>the process of the solid matter "drinking" or absorbing the liquid</note>.

**ANAXAGORAS** spoke again: I notify you that the **Ethelia** is thirsty and fit for drinking, having been cooked by the preceding sulfur. I command you, however, to cook it continually and repeatedly, and let it not weary you. And know that the perfection of this work is the **water of sulfur**, which is cooked with it until it becomes **rust** <note>original: "rubigo"; in alchemy, this refers to the "Red" stage or the Red Lion, the penultimate state before the Great Work is finished</note>. For all the Philosophers have said: He who can turn gold into rust has already found the purpose of the **poison** <note>the "poison" or "venom" often refers to the transformative solvent or the initial base matter</note>; but he who cannot is as nothing.

**AZIRATUS** said: I command those who come after to take the coins which the Philosophers made, mixed with parts of bronze <note>original: "æris"</note>, and place them in a vessel for cooking, ensuring the vessel itself is very well closed. Then, truly, when the bronze is ground with the coins and turned into water, a blackness will appear from **Kuhul** <term>Kuhul; likely referring to kohl or antimony, used here as a metaphor for the "nigredo," the initial black stage of the alchemical work</term>, which arises from the blackness of the coins. When that blackness is consumed, a precious **whiteness** <term>Albedo; the second major stage of the alchemical process, representing purification and spiritualization</term> will appear to them. Then, they should be dried by cooking until they are turned into a stone.

Cook that stone continually with a fire stronger than the first, and it will be broken down and shattered, and turned into ash. O, how precious is this ash to the children of doctrine, and how precious is that which is made from it! Therefore, mixing the ash with water, cook it again until that ash liquefies. Then cook it and imbue it with permanent water <note>A common alchemical term for a stable, non-volatile liquid or "divine water"</note> until the composition becomes sweet, pleasant, and red. Imbue it further until it becomes moist. Then cook it further with a fire stronger than the first, and diligently close the mouth of the vessel; for by this **regimen** <note>the systematic method or sequence of the work</note> the fleeting bodies are made stable, the spirit is turned into bodies, and the body into spirit, and they are joined to one another. Then the bodies become spirits, possessing tingeing souls <note>A "tingeing soul" refers to the substance's power to change the color and nature of other metals</note>, because they germinate together.

**OBSEMEGANUS** said: I say that the envious <note>A term often used by alchemists to describe authors who intentionally hid their secrets from the unworthy</note> have laid waste to this entire art with a multitude of names. ...is given, and beware of increasing the moisture: or rather, set it down dry, and make the dry substance into a strong mass. For by the benefit of the Sun it has been cooked and congealed, and that most excellent whiteness causes it to overcome earthly fire.

And know that the **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur"; the active, masculine principle in alchemy, believed to cause color changes.</note> which blackens the body cannot be dyed, nor can it be handled, but it handles and dyes other things. Likewise, know that the sulfur which blackens is that which opens the door to the non-fleeing, and turns it into the fleeing along with the fleeing ones: which we otherwise call the **Water of Sulfur**, turning **copper** <note>original: "æs"; while literally copper or bronze, in this context it refers to the "body" of the philosophical metal being transformed.</note> into unalterable and indelible colors.

**MANDINUS** says: Unless this **secret** <term>arcanum; a hidden or mysterious power or substance central to the alchemical transformation.</term> contains that which rectifies it, it is of no use. For this reason, the ancients said: That which is perfected is a single thing: because diverse natures do not rectify the thing itself, but only one, and that which is suitable, which you must indeed manage sparingly. For ignorance of management has caused many to err. Do not, therefore, concern yourselves with the plurality of these compositions, nor the varied things which the Masters have placed in their books. For there is one nature of truth, by which the natural is changed, because its secret is hidden in its belly with the natures changed, and it is neither seen, nor known, nor felt except by the Wise. He, therefore, who sparingly manages the **copper** <term>aes; while literally copper or bronze, in this context it refers to the "body" of the base metal being transformed.</term>, and knows its temperament, extracts from it a nature surpassing all natures. Then the words of the masters will be fulfilled, namely: that **Nature rejoices in nature**, and **Nature overcomes nature**, and **Nature contains nature** <note>original: "Natura naturâ lætatur, & Natura naturam superat, & Natura naturam continet"; this is one of the oldest and most famous aphorisms in alchemy, attributed to the Hellenistic author Pseudo-Democritus.</note>: and yet they are not diverse natures, nor many: but only one, differing in form, having its own properties in itself, with various attributes, through which it works what is fitting to its nature. Hence the Master did well, in that he began from one, and finished with one. Then he called those unities **sulfurous water** <term>aqua sulphurea; a symbolic term for the "divine water" or solvent used to dissolve the "body" of the metal.</term>, which overcomes all nature.

<margin>Note well</margin> ...separate its **soul and water**, and afterwards **whiten** <note>original: "dealbate"; the process of *albedo* or whitening, a key stage in the alchemical Great Work where the matter is purified.</note> it, and you will find what you seek. We do not doubt that these things concerning the revelation of our **Stone** are sufficient for the **sons of doctrine** <term>doctrinæ filijs; a traditional term for initiates or students of the "Sacred Art" of alchemy.</term>: its powers cannot be corrupted. If it is placed in the fire, its power increases: if you dissolve it, it is dissolved: if you coagulate it, it is coagulated. No one can be without it, and all people possess it, yet all people are in need of it.

And though it has many names, it is nevertheless called by one name, in which there is no difficulty: that which is the most common of all things is what is most truly signified by it. However, those who name it more precisely and properly only make it obscure and less understandable. And in truth, it has but one name; and where it is useless, it is named magnificently and significantly, but where it is useful, it is strictly concealed.

It is a **stone and not a stone**, it is also spirit, soul, and body: it is white, black, and red, brassy, Tyrian purple <note>original: "tyrius"; a reference to the famous and expensive purple dye of antiquity, signifying the "Royal" color of the final alchemical stage.</note>, and displayed in all the colors of the world. It is heavy, solid, unmoved by fire, unmoved by water, and unmoved by wind; yet it is also very light, hollow, and spongy, moved by fire, moved by water, and moved by wind: it is false, and it is also...

## THE PRINTER
### To the Reader.

*It has pleased us, fair Reader, to look out for your benefit by adding another version <note>original: "exemplar"; a source manuscript or copy.</note> of the **Assembly** <term>Turba; referring to the "Turba Philosophorum" or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</term> which we had in our possession. This is not so much because of a different order of contents, but because of the variety of opinions and names of philosophers. For it happens that in another volume, the same thing is expressed with a different meaning, in different words, and by a different author. We include this so that you do not wander astray in a matter of such great importance, but may follow in your own operations whatever appeals most to you. Farewell, and if you find any use here, give credit to the most famous and excellent Physician, Master **William Rascalon of Worms** <note>original: "Guilielmo Rascalono Vormatiensi"; likely the scholar or patron who provided the manuscripts for this edition.</note>, by whose generosity we obtained these copies.*

O sons of knowledge, [do you not see] the Sun rising in the heaven overcome and warm the air with its fire? When that air is warmed, the heat arrives at a state of subsistence <note>original: "subsistentiam"; a state of standing firm or becoming a physical reality.</note>, thickening and condensing the spirits <term>spiritus; in alchemy, these are the volatile, vaporous essences of substances.</term> from which creatures are generated. For the air is compressed and contained by the water, and thus the air is overcome, because its heat is joined to the heat of the Sun, and its moisture is joined to the moisture of the water. Do you not see thin water ascend into the air by the eminent heat of the Sun, and the Sun delights in it and is aided by it? Because if the water did not aid the air with its thin moisture, without doubt the fire would overcome it. Fire, however, draws moisture from the water, by which the air is tempered, and then it overcomes that very fire. Therefore, fire and water are enemies, between whom there is no kinship: because fire is hot and dry, and water is cold and moist. Air, however, since it is hot and moist, has concord with the moisture of water and the heat of fire, and because of this, a generative friendship <note>original: "amicitia generans"; a central alchemical concept where a middle element acts as a bridge between two opposing forces.</note> occurs. Behold all the fruits, which are made from a thin aerial vapor, because by the heat of the Sun life is revealed from the air; and this is by the ordinance of God.

### OPINION III.

**Anaxagoras.** I say that the principle of all things that God created is piety and reason: because in creation piety appeared, and the density of the earth through hoped-for reason. **LOCUSTOR.** <note>The identity of Locustor is debated; some scholars believe it is a corruption of a Greek name, while others see him as a fictional representative of early Hermetic thought.</note> There are only two natures which Lucas describes, one of which is not known nor described, except by piety and reason; the other is not seen nor felt, and it is the heavens. ## SENTENTIA XI.

**ARISTENES**: The key to this work is the art of coins <note>original: *numorum ars*; likely referring to the metallic transformation or the circular, coin-like shapes the matter takes during the process.</note>. Take, therefore, the body that has been shown to you, and fit it into thin plates; then place it into the water of our sea, which, while it is being governed, is called Permanent Water <term>Aqua permanens: A fundamental alchemical solvent, often symbolized as mercury or a "water that does not wet the hands," used to dissolve and transform metals.</term>. Afterward, place it over a gentle fire until the plates are broken down and become water, and join them to the Ethelia <term>Ethelia: A term derived from the Greek *aithalē* (soot/vapor), referring to a volatile spirit or a refined substance that rises during distillation.</term>, and roast them together over a slow fire until a thick broth <note>original: *brodium faginatum*; literally a "fattened broth" or dense liquid mixture.</note> is formed. Turn this into its own Ethelia until it coagulates and becomes a variegated coin, which we call the Flower of the Sun <note>original: *Solis florem*; a reference to the golden state or the solar stage of the Work.</note>. Then cook it until it is deprived of blackness and whiteness appears. <margin>+</margin> Afterward, govern it and mix in the soul of gold, and cook it until it becomes a red Ethelia; grind this with patience, and do not grow weary of soaking it with the water that came out of it—which is permanent—until it becomes red. For this is the burnt copper <note>original: *æs combuftum*; a technical term for a specific metallic oxide or calcined state.</note>, the flower of gold, and the ferment. Manage this with permanent water, then dry it until it becomes a powder and is deprived of all moisture.

## SEVENTEENTH STATEMENT

> SOCRATES: Know, sons of the doctrine, that without lead <term>plumbum: In alchemy, this rarely refers to common metallic lead, but rather to the 'lead of the Sages'—the raw, heavy, or 'black' starting material of the Great Work.</term> no tincture is made, and that in it resides the power of the work. Do you not see, says Hermes, by the grace of the triple nature, how many times it is immersed in the body, it turns that body into an unchanging color? Therefore, the first power is the vinegar, the second is the lead, of which the Sages have said that it may be immersed into all bodies, and it transforms all things and dyes them with an immutable color. 
> 
> Take, therefore, the lead which is made from the stone, and cook it until it turns black <note>The *nigredo* or 'blackening' stage, representing the initial dissolution and purification of the matter.</note>. Afterwards, grind it with nitre water <term>aqua nitri: A solvent or alkaline solution, likely containing potassium nitrate (saltpeter).</term> until it becomes like a thick fat <note>original: *pinguedo spissa*; a reference to the material reaching a viscous, oily consistency often called 'the oil of the philosophers.'</note>. **MENEBDUS**: Many things have been said: however, I advise those who come after us that they should make bodies into non-bodies, and incorporeal things into true bodies <note>This refers to the alchemical process of "spiritualizing" matter (vaporizing or dissolving solids) and "fixing" spirits (solidifying vapors)</note>. ## DISCOURSE XXVIII.

**ZENO**: I see you have joined two bodies, which should by no means be done; therefore I say to you, sons of wisdom, that it is necessary for you to putrefy the composite for forty days: then to sublimate <note>To heat a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</note> it five times in a vessel: then to join it to the fire of dung <note>original: *stercori ignis*; the gentle, steady heat produced by a fermenting pile of manure, a common laboratory heat source in the Middle Ages</note> and cook it, and the colors which then appear are of this kind. But when composing the Elixir, take care that you do not extract the spirit too hastily, for perhaps it might die: extract however <note>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "au," likely for *autem* (however).</note>

### DISCOURSE XXXI. <note>original: *Sententia*; literally "opinion" or "maxim," used here as a numbered chapter or speech within the assembly</note>

**DIAMEDES** <note>One of the philosopher-speakers in the Turba</note> said: Know, O wise men, that from a human being nothing is born except a human being, and from irrational animals <note>original: *brutis*; referring to animals lacking human reason</note> nothing except their own kind. And for this reason I say that Nature is not improved except within its own nature; therefore, make use of this venerable nature. For it is from this that the art bursts forth, and not from another; and unless you grasp it and direct <note>original: *regatis*; a common alchemical term for governing the heat or the chemical process</note> it, you will possess nothing. Therefore, join the male **red servant** <term>serui rubei: a symbolic name in alchemy, often associated with gold, sulfur, or the solar principle</term> to his fragrant wife; and joined together, they shall give birth to the Art. To these, do not introduce anything foreign—neither powder nor any other thing. Let the conception suffice for you, and a true son shall be born. O, how most precious is the nature of that red servant, without which the process <note>original: *regimen*; the systematic treatment or procedure</note> cannot be maintained!

### DISCOURSE XXXII.

**BASSEN** said: After their marriage, introduce the **Citrine One** <term>Citrinum: a yellow or lemon-colored substance, often associated with the 'citrinitas' or yellowing phase of the alchemical work</term> with his wife into the bath. Do not heat the bath excessively, lest they be deprived of sense and motion. Cause them to undergo the bath until their body and their color become a single thing. Then, restore to it its sweat <note>Often referring to the condensation or the liquid byproduct of the heating process</note>, and once more deliver it to death, and establish rest for it, taking care that they do not flee <note>In alchemy, "fleeing" refers to evaporation or sublimation, where the volatile spirit escapes the vessel</note>. Then, honor the king and his wife, and do not burn them with too much fire; rather, direct them until they become black, then white, then red, and finally, they become the **dyeing poison** <term>venenum tingens: a paradoxical term for the philosopher's stone or final elixir, signifying its power to "infect" or transform base metals into gold</term>.

### DISCOURSE XXXIII. <note>original: *Sententia*; a formal opinion or decree in the context of the assembly</note>

**NEPHITUS** said: I speak briefly to you, seekers of the art: **Corfufle** <term>Corfufle: an enigmatic alchemical term, likely a corruption of an Arabic word, referring to the "stone" or the completed philosophical mercury</term> is the head of this work, not its beginning; rather, it is rightly called so after the "embrace" <note>referring to the chemical union of substances</note>. For this reason, **Corfufle** is the whole compound, which must be addressed <note>original: *affari*; possibly implying "to be treated with fire" or "to be exposed" seven times</note> seven times, and then it tints every body. It is called a coin, the flower of copper or of gold, or the flower of iron, even lead or tin; it is called by a thousand names by the Philosophers.

### DISCOURSE XXXIIII.

**BONELLUS** said: All things that live also die, God so willing. Therefore, that nature from which moisture has been taken away, when it is left through the nights, is like a dead thing. Then that nature requires fire until the spirit of that body returns; and then it becomes dust, like a dead man in his tomb. When this is accomplished, God restores its spirit and soul to it, and frees it from all infirmity, strengthens it, and improves it.

It is necessary, therefore, to burn that nature without fear until it becomes ash. This ash is made fit to receive its spirit and its moisture until it is turned into a most beautiful color, which conquers and surpasses all things. And if you direct <note>original: *regeritis*; to govern the heat or process</note> it with subtlety, many things will proceed from it, because **copper** <note>original: *æs*; usually referring to the "philosophers' copper," a symbolic starting material rather than common metal</note> has a body like a man, and a spirit of a man. Breathing is from the air; likewise, when moisture is breathed in, the copper receives life, and is multiplied and increased.

### DISCOURSE XXXIX.

**AGADMON**: Cook the **bronze** <term>bronze: Latin *aes*; here referring to the base metallic body or "matter" of the work</term> until it becomes a soft and impalpable body, and place it in its own vessel; then sublimate it <term>sublimate: a process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid, used here to purify the substance</term> five or seven times until the water descends, knowing that when the water becomes powder, it has been diligently ground.

Moreover, it must be known that unless you turn both into water, you will not arrive at the precious work; for the body must be occupied by the flame of fire so that it may be broken down and become weak while the water is in the water, until the whole becomes water. 

The ignorant, however, when they hear the name of "water," think it is the water of the clouds <note>original: *aquam nubis*; i.e., common rainwater</note>; but if they were to read our books, they would certainly know that it is the **permanent water**, which could not be permanent without its partner, with which it has been made one. This is the water which the Philosophers have called the **Water of Gold**, fire, the good poison, and the "sand of many names," which Hermes commanded to be washed many times so that the **blackness of the Sun** <note>original: *Solis nigredo*; a reference to the "Nigredo" or black stage of the work, representing the initial dissolution and "death" of the metal</note> might be washed away, which it had acquired during the dissolution of the body. And know that unless you take this body of mine, which lacks a spirit, you will by no means achieve what you desire, because [nothing] foreign...

**BONELLUS**: Sons of the Doctrine, mixing the **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: in this context, not the modern chemical, but a "prime matter" often described as a dark, heavy earth containing the potential for gold</term>, place it in its own vessel, and close the mouth diligently, and cook it with a gentle fire until it liquefies and is turned into water: for by the heat of the water, the whole will easily become water. Therefore, wash it and deprive it of its blackness, until it becomes a **stone** dry to the touch. 

For this reason, the Philosophers have said: Wash the Magnesia with fresh water and cook it diligently until it becomes earth and the moisture disappears, and then it is called **Bronze** <term>bronze: Latin *aes*; here representing the purified metallic body</term>. Pour the sharpest vinegar <note>original: *acetum acerrimum*; often used to represent a spiritual or philosophical acid used for purification</note> upon it, and allow it to be soaked by that vinegar, and it will be our **bronze**, which the Philosophers commanded to be washed with **permanent water** <note>original: *aqua permanente*; a specialized alchemical solvent that does not wet the hands and remains stable through fire</note>. 

Furthermore, they said: Divide the **poison** <note>original: *venenum*; alchemists often called their transformation-agent "poison" because it "killed" the base metal to transform it, or to signify its potent, medicinal nature</note> into two parts, with one of which you soak the body, and with the other you cause putrefaction, knowing that the whole work and governance is not accomplished except with water: because what we seek is one.

### DISCOURSE 46.

**ASCANIUS**: When we read in the books of the Philosophers that nature is only one, which overcomes all things, it is necessary to know that the one [nature] and the one [thing] are composed together. Do you not see that the composition of man consists of soul and body? Thus it is necessary for us to join two things: a mixture which the Philosophers have compared to spouses, from whose embrace results the golden water <note>original: *aqua aurea*; the liquid state of the transformed substance, often signifying the dissolution of the metals</note>. But this pertains to the second Work: concerning the first I will say a few things: Stir up a war between copper <note>original: *æs*; representing a base metallic body or the 'soul' of the metal</note> and quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury, the 'spirit' of the metal</note> until they reach destruction and are corrupted: then the copper, conceiving the quicksilver, coagulates it. But the quicksilver, conceiving the copper, is congealed into earth. Therefore, stir up the fight, and destroy the body of the copper until it becomes powder. Join the male to the female (which is made from vapor) and the quicksilver, until the male and female become **Etheel** <term>Etheel: a term derived from Arabic alchemical traditions, referring to the spiritualized or 'washed' essence of the matter</term>. For he who through Etheel turns them into spirit, and then makes them red, tints every body; for when the body is ground diligently, a clean, spiritual, and sublime soul is extracted from it, which tints every body, and it is the sulfur of nature <note>original: *sulphur naturae*; the active, life-giving principle that drives the transformation of matter</note>, which is known by various names.

## *DISCOURSE XLVII.*

**Dardaris**: Enough has been said by you regarding the regimen <term>regimen: the governed process of heating and treating the alchemical materials</term>; therefore, I shall say a few things concerning the conjunction. I signify to posterity that the hidden soul cannot be drawn out except through Ethelia <term>Ethelia: a technical term in the Turba representing a volatile spirit or "cloud" that facilitates the transformation of solid bodies into spiritualized states</term>, which turns bodies into non-bodies by the continuity of cooking and the sublimation of the Ethelia itself. Furthermore, you must know that quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note> is fiery, burning every body more than fire, and mortifying <note>original: *mortificans*; "killing" or breaking down the metallic structure</note> bodies; whatever body is mixed with it is ground down and given over to death. Therefore, when the bodies have been diligently ground and exalted <note>original: *exaltatis*; purified or raised to a higher state</note> as they ought to be, the nature of Ethelia is produced, which does not flee from the heat, but rather tints the copper <note>original: *æs*; copper, often used to represent the "body" of the Work</note>. This is what the Sages said previously: that it fixes the quicksilver until it is tinted, and once tinted, it [the quicksilver] tints others. Moreover, know that the body of copper is ruled by magnesia <term>magnesia: a symbolic "magnet" or mineral agent believed to draw out the spirits of metals</term>, and quicksilver has four [elements] within itself; yet it has no existence except in humidity, which is called sulfur-water <note>original: *aqua sulphuris*</note>, and which contains the sulfurs. For the sulfurs are the hidden souls in the four bodies; when these are extracted by themselves, they contain one another and are naturally joined. For if you rule the hidden thing which is in the "belly" of the sulfur with water and cleanse it well, that hidden thing rejoices to meet its own nature; likewise, the water rejoices with its peer. But these four [sulfurs] are not tinted themselves; rather, they tint the Fifth <note>original: *Quintum*; likely referring to the Quintessence or the final Elixir</note>. For this reason, the Philosophers have said that the four common coins <note>original: *numi vulgi*; referring to the four basic metals or elements used by the common people</note> do not tin...

**Mosius**: This one thing, which has often been mentioned, the Sages <note>original: *philosophi*</note> have called by many names: sometimes by two names, at other times even by three. Regarding this, the Sages <note>original: *Sapientes*</note> have said: "Unbar the door for the fugitive, lest he take flight" <note>This is a common alchemical paradox: by "opening the door" or relaxing the conditions, the philosopher allows the volatile spirit to be managed rather than lost to pressure or sudden escape</note>. Of these, the Philosophers also said: "They did not flee with those fleeing, and yet they were made fleeing." For this reason, they processed <note>original: *reiterauêre*; literally "reiterated" or "repeated the operation"</note> them, and they were made non-fleeing, but rather one single body, similar to the body from which they were first extracted.

Of this "One," the Sages said: "The tinting and the tinted have become one," and this spirit hidden within the other spirit is moisture <note>original: *humidus*</note>. Therefore, you must not be ignorant of the fact that of these moistures, one is hot and the other is cold; and although the cold moisture is incompatible with the hot moisture, they nevertheless produce a single thing. And for this reason, we have preferred those two bodies: because with them we perform the entire work, and we rule the corporeal things by the incorporeal, until the incorporeal things become bodies that do not flee from the fire. Then those bodies are better and more precious than all other bodies. Take them, therefore, which do not flee, and join them, and wash their bodies with the incorporeal <note>the spirit</note>, until the incorporeal spirit receives a body and no longer flees. **MORPHOLEUS:** It is necessary, wise men, that the humidity be first burned away with a slow fire, just as the example is shown to us in the generation of a chick <note>The "hatching of the egg" is a common alchemical metaphor for the slow, gentle heat required to transform matter without destroying its "spirit."</note>; and when the fire is increased, the vessel should be sealed on all sides, lest the body of the copper and its fleeing spirit be drawn out.

## PROPOSITION 57

OBSEMEGANUS: I say that the envious <note>A common alchemical term for those who wish to keep the art secret from the unworthy</note> have devastated this entire art with a vast multitude of names. Yet it is the art according to which the Philosophers commanded to make coinage-gold <term>aurum nummosum: gold in the form of coins or ready for striking; here referring to the metallic body of the work</term>, and to calcine it, sublimate it, fix it, grind it, whiten it, coagulate it, cook it, and turn it into red. They have called Ethelia <note>A term for a sublimated or volatile spirit</note> "fire," and the vessel a "sieve," and the water of sulfur a "bond" <term>copula: a union or connection</term>. All of this is nothing other than grinding <gloss>pulverization</gloss> and whitening.

Furthermore, I say that quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," or mercury</term> appears white to the sight. But when the smoke <gloss>vapor</gloss> reaches it, it is turned into red and becomes Combar <note>original: *Combar*; an Arabic-derived term for a red substance, often identified with red lead or cinnabar</note>, that is, a poison. The Philosophers hinted at this when they said that the nature of lead is easily converted. For this reason, they have frequently repeated this word "to grind," so that they might show in many ways how to draw out the spirits hidden in the vessel. By applying water, they prevent them from being burned; otherwise, the fire easily consumes them. 

But when water is added, the more the flame attacks them, the more the water penetrates into their innermost parts <gloss>visceribus</gloss> and prevents them from being burned by the flame. And for this reason also, the ancients treated much concerning sublimation, because unless the matter is strongly ground <gloss>broken down</gloss> by fire, the Ethelia <note>the volatile spirit</note> will not ascend. This is what Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> meant to hint at when he said: "Sift the things you know, and melt them more deeply."

<summary>Obsemeganus explains that the complex terminology of the "envious" ancients refers to simple chemical processes like grinding and whitening, focusing on how water protects volatile spirits from being destroyed by fire.</summary>

Therefore, first join nine parts of vinegar when the vessel grows warm, and again apply nine parts when the vessel has been heated.

### PROPOSITION 74

**FLORUS**: I will complete the arrangement of the cooking, and I say that the first sign of the decoction <note>original: *decoctio* — the process of boiling or heating a substance in a liquid</note> is the extraction of its redness. ## PROPOSITION LXXVIII.

**AGMON:** As a conclusion <note>original: *corolario*</note>, I say that whoever does not liquefy and coagulate errs in many ways. <header>PHILOSOPHERS</header>

<margin>+</margin>We do not doubt that this regarding the revelation of our **stone** <term>stone: the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary goal of alchemy said to transform base metals and perfect the human soul</term> is sufficient for the sons of doctrine <note>original: *doctrīnę filiis* — a traditional term for initiates or students of the secret arts</note>, whose powers cannot be corrupted. If it is placed in the fire, its strength is increased; if you wish to dissolve it, it will be dissolved; if you wish to coagulate it, it will be coagulated. No one can do without it, and everyone has need of it. And although it has many names, it is nonetheless named by one name, and where it is most visible, there it is most hidden. It is also a stone and yet not a stone; it is spirit, soul, and body. It is white, volatile, hollow, and smooth <note>original: *pilis carens* — literally "lacking hairs," signifying a refined or pure state</note>, which no one, once it has been chilled, can touch with their tongue without injury. If you make it fly, it flies; and if you say it is water, you speak the truth; and if you say it is not water, you speak falsely. Yet do not be deceived by the plurality of names, but hold it as certain that it is one single thing, to which nothing foreign is added. Therefore, investigate its natural place and introduce nothing foreign; let men multiply names as they wish, for if names were not multiplied, many would mock our wisdom.

Afterward, they return to it the **sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur* — in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, solar principle of a substance</note> which had been extracted from it, and it is ground into it until it turns into a stone; and thus the **Elixir** is completed, which shall be effective for the duration of this life. **Dyers** have a herb which they use in dyeing wool, taking only the dye and leaving behind the wood <note>original: *lignum* — the physical plant fiber or dregs</note>. Similarly, we have this in our art: we place the substance [there], grinding and sifting it, and frequently soaking it with the **urine of boys** <note>original: *urina puerorum* — a common alchemical reagent believed to contain essential salts and "spirits" for purification</note> until it becomes viscous; and so its dye will come from it. Afterward, we place it in **horse dung** <note>original: *fimo equino* — used as a steady, gentle heat source for digestion and fermentation</note> until its dye is purified and appears upon the body. Receiving this [dye] in a glass vessel, we store it. Then, grinding the body itself with its own moisture and placing it in a damp place, we do not cease to wash it until it is clothed in snowy whiteness.

<margin>+</margin>
Afterward, we join it [the body] to its own purified dye, which we drew away from it, and in the warm Sun we soak it with that dye; and thus it receives a miraculous power. And this is the description which the ancients narrated figuratively

When certain more eager disciples of the Philosophers had gathered once again around **Pythagoras**, among whom the elder was **Arisleus**, son of Abladi, then **Paris**, son of Belchioti, **Armenius**, son of Archias, **Meditantalus**, **Phalisæus**, **Echamisius**, **Parmenides**, and **Eximesias**, son of Admir, **Auerca** asked Arisleus whether he could succeed in explaining—by example or parable—how it might be possible for investigators of the art to gather fruits from that **immortal tree** <note>The "Immortal Tree" or "Philosophical Tree" is a common alchemical symbol representing the growing Stone or the completion of the Great Work, which bears fruit in the form of gold or health.</note> which the aforementioned disciples of the Philosophers and others in the **Assembly** <note>original: *Turba* — referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous gathering of ancient thinkers in alchemical lore.</note> had described?

And he replied: “I will gladly speak as best I can, though perhaps I may not satisfy your desire.” And **Pythagoras** spoke again: “Speak, then, as aptly as you are able.”

And he said: “I saw myself and certain others from the **Assembly** <note>original: *Turba*</note> riding toward the shores of the sea, and behold, the inhabitants of the sea were mating with one another, yet nothing was born to them; and they were planting trees, yet they bore no fruit; and they were sowing seeds, yet nothing grew. And I said: ‘What is wrong with you? Although you are many, is there no **Philosopher** <term>Philosopher: in alchemical texts, this refers to a "true seeker" or "adept" who understands the hidden laws of nature and the transformation of matter.</term> among you who might teach you?’ And they said: ‘What is a Philosopher?’”

### RIDDLE II.
#### Of the Stone.

There is in our sea a small round fish, lacking bones and skin, and it possesses within itself a fatness and a miraculous power. When this fish is cooked with a **silent fire** <note>A "silent fire" refers to a gentle, steady heat, often provided by a water bath or dung heap, rather than a roaring flame.</note> until its moisture and fatness are utterly worn away and consumed, it must afterward be ground most strongly and soaked in the water of the sea until it becomes soft. Then, let it be buried for a week; then roasted until it glows white-hot. And when it glows and becomes sufficiently white, its water is returned to it, and afterward it is soaked in its own proper moisture. At last, after the soaking of the moisture, it is roasted until it appears **citrine** <note>A lemon-yellow color, representing a stage of transition between the white (albedo) and red (rubedo) phases of the alchemical work.</note> in color. Thus it becomes the **eye-salve of the Philosophers** <term>collyrium: traditionally a medicinal lotion for the eyes; here it symbolizes the alchemist’s newfound ability to perceive the hidden truths of nature.</term>; by the liquid of which, when the eyes are anointed, the secrets of the Philosophers can easily be seen and understood.

This must be collected in its entirety, and the body—that is, the black dregs or scales remaining in the bath—must be thoroughly washed away. For that which is flowing and rest-

### RIDDLE IV.

Take a **viper**, and deprive it of its head and its tail: for in these two places its poison resides, from which it proceeds. <note>In alchemical symbolism, the 'viper' often represents the volatile or 'poisonous' raw matter that must be purified by removing its extremes.</note> Divide, therefore, the head and the tail, and place each by itself in a glass vessel. Then, join it to its head, and grind it with it for as long as any fluidity remains within it. Dry a body of this kind in the Sun or by a fire, so that you may see what you seek. ### R I D D L E   V.

->*Mercury speaks about himself.*<-

My mother bore me, and through me she herself is born: she once ruled over me, but henceforth I shall rule over her. <note>original: "Mater me genuit, & per me gignitur ipsa." This describes the cyclical nature of the "mercurial" substance, which is extracted from a base matter (the mother) and then used to transform or "perfect" that same matter.</note> This is because I have become the persecutor of my mother. Yet she now cherishes me like a pious woman and nourishes her son whom she bore, until he shall come to a state of perfection. Therefore, place me in a **humid fire**, <term>humid fire: a gentle, indirect heat such as a water bath (balneum Mariae) or a bed of fermenting manure, used to mimic the warmth of the womb.</term> and grind me until the end of the work is reached. Then, when the work is perfected, drive me toward **redness** <note>original: "rubedinem." This refers to the *Rubedo*, the final "red stage" of the alchemical process signaling the completion of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> with a strong fire. For the moisture of heat increases me, but the consumption of dryness kills me.

### R I D D L E   V I.

Upon the pregnant mother, place a **red servant** <note>The "red servant" typically represents sulfur or gold, which is added to the "mother" (mercury or the prima materia) to begin the chemical marriage.</note> in equal measure. Mortify the mother, cutting off her hands and feet. Bathe the servant himself, and betroth these two in a glass cloth, which is called a **Sera**, <note>original: "Sera." Likely referring to a specialized seal or a specific type of enclosing vessel.</note> and place a **Thonar** <term>Thonar: a variation of "Athanor," the "furnace of Arcana," designed to maintain a steady, prolonged heat.</term> over it, and block it well with the **Lute of Wisdom**. <term>Lute of Wisdom: A hermetic sealing paste (lutum sapientiae) made of clay, lime, and other binders used to ensure a vessel is airtight.</term>

And then take the glass with the bridegroom and bride, and cast them into the furnace, and cause them to roast for three days; and then the two shall be in one flesh. <note>This "one flesh" refers to the chemical union or *conjunctio*, where the separate substances merge into a single, new compound.</note> Finally, take that **white man** <note>The "white man" represents the *Albedo* or white stage, indicating the matter has been purified.</note> from the vessel and grind him by way of a mill, and add to him the **key of the art** <note>original: "clauem artis." Do this three times, and you possess the extreme limit of perfection.

# EXERCISES ON THE ASSEMBLY OF THE PHILOSOPHERS <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum." The Assembly (or Turba) of the Philosophers is a famous 12th-century text where various Greek philosophers are depicted debating alchemical principles.</note>

*In which certain hidden things, pertaining to the art, are explained.*

### DEFINITION OF THE STONE, AND of what principles it consists.

->EXERCISE I.<-

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial "T" containing ornate foliage and floral scrolls.</image-desc>
As we are about to treat the **Philosopher’s Stone**, it must first be seen from what principles, or from what elements, the Philosopher's Stone consists. # ON THE FIRST ELEMENT
## *Of the Stone, which is earth.*
### EXERCISE IV.
### *PYTHAGORAS.* <note>Pythagoras appears here as a legendary authority within the *Turba Philosophorum*, a text that presents a fictional assembly of ancient Greek philosophers discussing alchemy.</note>

On this point, all the Philosophers agree with one voice: that the purest and most subtle earthy substance should be chosen, whether red or white, with which red or white **Mercury** <term>Quicksilver; the essential fluid principle in alchemy</term> is joined in the smallest parts, and it must be **fixed** <term>fixetur; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</term> until they become one and inseparable. Moreover, this earthy substance belongs either to **Luna** <note>Silver</note>, or the **Sol** <note>Gold</note>, or some imperfect body, or to the **leaves of Mercury** <note>original: "foliis Mercurij"; likely referring to thin layers or a specific purified state of mercury.</note>. Regarding the Sun and Moon, I hold this opinion; regarding **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, **Arnaldus de Villa Nova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> holds it; regarding Mercury, **Geber the Arab** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy.</note> holds it. 

And again, if a judgment is to be made concerning the Moon or the Sun, there will perhaps be doubt whether their "earth" should be raw, or whether it should be the dregs left behind from sulfur. However, it must be judged that the earth is derived from the raw parts of either the Moon or the Sun—indeed, from the Sun alone. Yet, the mind of Arnaldus is not to be blamed, for his view relies on this reasoning: that every **tincture** <term>the potent alchemical medicine or agent capable of transforming metals</term> must contain the stone that enters into it, and must consist of that which it intends to transform. Therefore, if you wish to transform Venus with your stone, it will be necessary to have received the "earth" from Venus as well. 

This earth is created through **calcination** <term>heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to a powder or "ash"</term>, and it is turned into ash; and the ash, through **sublimation** <term>the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</term>, is turned into the **quintessence** <term>the "fifth essence" or purest, most potent spiritual core of a material</term>; and the quintessence, through solution, is turned into water; and the water, through coagulation, is turned...
