## ON THE LETTING DOWN OF WATER
->*or the Bedewing upon the Earth.*<-

### EXERCISE V.
->ARISTENES.<- <note>Aristenes is another of the legendary sages participating in this fictional alchemical gathering.</note>

On this point, it must be noted above all else: that neither simple **sea water** <note>In alchemy, "sea water" often refers to mercury or a specific saline solvent rather than literal ocean water.</note> alone, nor the **copper** <term>æs; while literally "copper" or "bronze," in this context it represents the "body" or metallic base of the work</term> itself alone, can do anything to produce the Philosophers' Stone, or constitute the Philosophers' Stone itself. Neither the stone itself, nor the **Elixir**, can consist of simple water alone or copper alone; rather, it is necessary that both—that is, the simple water and the copper—be joined together. 

But before you join or mix these two—namely the copper and the water—see to it that neither is crude nor **unrectified** <term>rectificatum; purified or refined by repeated distillation</term>. Instead, ensure that the water itself has been distilled several times and finally restored to its proper state and descent, and that the copper itself has been **burned** <note>original: "combustum"; referring to calcination</note>, made white, and rendered entirely pure. For once these things have been so prepared, one can proceed to the Elixir.

For since the **copper** <term>æs; here referring to the "body" or base metallic substance of the work</term> itself would not be pure, it would be certain that the **earth** <note>original: "terram"; the solid precipitate or "body" resulting from alchemical decay</note> which is drawn from it would be produced raw and impure—indeed, perhaps none would be produced at all. # *Natures and their Commixture.*

## EXERCISE VI.

### PARMENIDES. <note>Parmenides was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher; here he is cast as an alchemical master explaining the core operations of the Work.</note>

The method of the art of mutual conversion <note>original: "ad inuicem conuertentis"; the process of changing one substance into another, or spirit into body and vice versa</note> is as follows: First, dissolve the **Stone** into its own **Mercury** <term>Mercurium; not common quicksilver, but the "philosophical mercury" or universal solvent</term>. The authors call this the "metallic stone"; wash it, reduce it, fix it, and **incerate** <term>incera; the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency so it can be merged with others</term> it. That is to say: dissolve the coarse into the simple, wash the dark into the bright, reduce the moist into the dry, and **fix** <term>fige; to "fixation," making a volatile substance stable so it does not evaporate when heated</term> the volatile into its own body.

To "dissolve" is to divide and corrupt, and to create the **First Matter** <term>materia prima; the primordial, chaotic substance from which all things are made</term>. To "wash" is to **inhume** <note>original: "inhumare"; to bury in a "belly" or warm bath to encourage decay</note>, to distill, and to **calcine** <term>calcinare; reducing a solid to a fine powder through high heat</term>. To "reduce" is to enrich, to wax, and to refine. To "fix" is to **betroth** <note>original: "desponsare"; a reference to the "Chemical Wedding" or the union of opposing principles like Sulfur and Mercury</note>, to resolve, and to coagulate. Through the first, nature works inwardly; through the second, outwardly; through the third, above; and through the fourth, below. But the moderns <note>Parmenides refers to "modern" practitioners who have strayed from the ancient purity of the art.</note> disturb the end...

### SIMON.

<margin>13</margin>
This philosopher <note>referring to a previous speaker in the Assembly</note> seems to suggest that both perfect bodies should be taken for the composition of the **Elixir** <term>Elixiris; the medicinal or transmutative preparation sought by alchemists</term>, whether it is intended to be white or yellow. For the goal of the entire alchemical secret is that the Elixir should flow immediately before the "flight" <note>original: "fugam"; the evaporation or volatilization of a substance under heat</note> of **Mercury** <term>Mercurij; quicksilver, representing the volatile or spirituous principle</term>. Therefore, let anyone who wishes see what ought to be done and chosen.

This method does not please me very much. Because if it were done in this way, the Elixir would necessarily be neither white nor yellow, but of a mixed color. -># THE CLARIONS<-

...draws: because if the external heat is excessive, then the **unctuous moisture** <note>original: *humidum vnctuosum*; a fatty or oily substance believed to hold the vital spark of a metal</note> mixed with subtle earthy parts evaporates from the strong fire and does not remain in the body. It is necessary, therefore, that whatever is superfluous, coarse, and harmful be gradually purged, preserved, and refined through the power of a slow **decoction** <note>a process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or purify it</note>.

Furthermore, every object in the world—that is, every body composed of elements—contains within itself a **radical or formal heat** <note>the innate, essential heat that gives a thing its specific form and life</note> by which it persists; it is the fixed point of its existence and the means by which its seed is multiplied. In **Mercury**, this is its "middle substance"; in **gold**, it is its **sulfur** <note>in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle, while Mercury represents the passive and metallic</note>. These direct the matter toward its goal, its proper form, and its specific species. There is no thing so cold that it is not nurtured by heat—specifically, heat enclosed within it as if in its root—as the **Philosopher** <note>likely referring to Aristotle, the primary authority for medieval and Renaissance scholars</note> says.

Likewise, Mercury’s own earth is its own **tincture** <note>the potent substance capable of dyeing or transforming other metals</note>, which is very subtle. Within this, the fire of both the **Sun** <note>symbolizing gold or the solar principle</note> and the **menstruum** <note>a solvent or dissolving agent, often called 'the blood' of the work</note> is retained, along with the subtle "middle substance" of Mercury; this is the burden and the foundation of the **Mastery** <note>Latin: *magisterij*; the Great Work or the accomplishment of the Philosopher’s Stone</note>. This is the matter from which our **medicine** <note>the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone</note> is prepared, which takes its origin from **quicksilver** <note>Latin: *argento vivo*; raw Mercury</note> and must be created immediately from it. To this, you must not introduce anything foreign in any way, except that which was born from it according to its own natural properties. In this passage, it is truly shown to the "son of the doctrine" <note>a traditional term for an initiate or student of alchemy</note> that this material from which we compose the medicine is not quicksilver in its raw nature—since it has already been changed into sulfur—nor is it in its entire substance, since the extreme parts (the earth and water) have already been...

# CLANGOR

...truly it is coagulated and becomes earth. Behold, enemies <note>original: *inimici*; in alchemy, elements with opposing qualities (like fire and water) are called enemies</note> have come together into one nature; when they are driven together—that is, coagulated—they become friends; and when they are rarefied, they become enemies, namely in the separation of the elements. # THE TRUMPETS

Thus says the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarius*; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), one of the most famous alchemical texts</note>, and let it stand there for 40 days or longer according to the quantity of the material, until it is completed. All the Philosophers add this in general: because every general action has one specific time in which it is perfected and finished, as Aristotle says.

Mundus and Attamius say in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba*; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), a key early Latin alchemical text</note>: And put it into putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the stage where the matter breaks down and turns black, considered a death before rebirth</term> for forty days: that is, for 40 weeks, counting a day for a week, just as the seed stays in the womb, which is for nine months or thereabouts, according to the quantity of the material; then cleanse it of its blackness. And the *Rosary* says: Be especially careful in its purification against the loss of its virtue, lest the active force be suffocated in any way. For the seeds of all things born of the earth do not multiply, nor do they grow, if their generative force is removed by any external heat, as the Philosopher says. 

And purify it through distillation, first with a gentle fire: then, with a slightly stronger fire, distill the Mercury. This Mercury carries with it the soul of the Sun or the Moon <note>original: *Solis vel Lunę*; in alchemy, the Sun and Moon represent Gold and Silver, or the principles of Sulfur and Mercury</note>, depending on whether the Sun or Moon is present there. And do not distill with such a strong fire that the earth—that is, the element of earth—also passes over in the distillation; namely, it is enough that only the superfluous Mercury, which cannot be dried out with the body, passes over. And what remains below in the cucurbit <term>cucurbit: the lower, gourd-shaped vessel of a distillation apparatus</term> is our salt: that is, our earth, and it is black in color, the dragon devouring its own tail <note>The Ouroboros, symbolizing the cyclical nature of the alchemical work and the unity of the matter</note>: for the dragon is the matter...

# THE TRUMPET

<margin><image-desc>A faint ink sketch of a rectangular box or square containing a cross-like mark with a line extending from the side.</image-desc></margin>
...remaining at the bottom after the water has been distilled from it. That water is called the **dragon's tail** <note>original: *cauda draconis*</note>, and the dragon represents its **blackness** <note>original: *nigredo*; the first major stage of the alchemical Great Work, symbolizing death and decomposition</note>. The dragon is soaked in its own water and becomes solid, and thus it "devours its own tail" <note>This refers to the Ouroboros, the serpent eating its own tail, symbolizing the cyclical nature of the chemical process where matter is dissolved and reconstituted</note>. Do not despise the ash that remains at the bottom of the vessel, for it is the crown of your heart and the "ash of the permanent things," as **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit and alchemist often cited in medieval texts</note> says. Distill with such heat that the body is not reduced to a solid mass, nor becomes too dry or burnt. Distill with such a fire that when one drop begins to fall, you will count sixty-eight moments—as **Arnold** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says—or seventy (some say eighty) before the next drop falls. If the drops fall faster than this, withdraw the fire, as the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical sourcebook</note> says.

And if it falls more slowly, increase the fire slightly. Do not follow your own imagination about intensifying the fire at the end of the distillation, but keep it gentle. Hence the following verse:

->*Nature rejoices in a moderate path perceived by the senses.*<-
<note>original: *Sensibus æquato gaudet natura secundo*; an alchemical maxim emphasizing that the operator should follow nature's moderation rather than forcing the process with excessive heat</note>

And so, wait for the distillation with the patience required for completion.

The sign that the distillation is complete is when you have distilled through the **alembic** <term>alembic: a distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube; the "head" or cap of the still</term> half of the **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurij*</note> (or more) than you originally put in with the earth, and the earth remains soft and liquid, as Arnold says. Take this soft and liquid earth and put it into a good glass container with a long neck, and seal it with the **seal of Hermes** <term>seal of Hermes: an airtight, "hermetic" seal created by melting the glass of the vessel's neck shut</term>, and place it in hot ashes.

First, for eight days, let it sit slowly in hot ashes—

The more the matter has been **putrefied** <note>original: *putrefacta*; the process of "rotting" or breaking down the substance into a black mass</note>, the more strongly it will stick, as the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a key alchemical text</note> says. When it is said that our stone is made of the four elements, this is not to be understood literally—that it is [physical] earth, or water, or air, or fire—but rather that it is only one nature, which contains within itself the nature and properties of all the elements.

Likewise, the whole **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*; the complete process or "Great Work" of alchemy</note> is this: to divide the elements from the metals and purify them, and to divide the **sulfur of nature** <note>In alchemical theory, sulfur represents the active, combustible, and "soul" principle of a substance</note> from the metals. So says **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lully (Ramon Llull), a 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note>. But where it is said, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: "It behooves you to extract the four elements," this truly means nothing else than the **seminal virtues** <note>original: *seminarias virtutes*; the hidden potential or "seeds" within matter</note> themselves: that is, the active or passive qualities...

When you already have the dried earth, then place it in a glass vessel, and put upon it a sixth <note>original: "sotam," likely a typographic error for "sextam"</note> or seventh part of its weight of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"; also known as quicksilver</note>, so that it may be dissolved. However, if you place a greater weight of that "water" upon the body itself than a fourth part—provided it is not submerged or "drowned"—it will be even better. The substance will whiten the body, and it will be more subtle, more penetrating, and will convert metals with a greater weight.

Furthermore, when any substance is soaked in corruption, it cannot tolerate fire, nor can fire suffer corruption within itself. For this reason, it is necessary that the **Stone** <term>lapis; the Philosopher's Stone</term> be skillfully extracted, cleansed, and separated from all its corruptible **dregs** <note>original: "feculentijs"; the impurities or sedimentary waste</note> before you presume to **fix** <note>to make a substance resistant to evaporation by heat</note> it, until it becomes the pure element of the **first matter** <note>original: "primę rei"; the fundamental substance of all things</note>.

And note well that the medicine which converts Mercury is more subtle than that which converts solid metallic bodies. Hence, it should be known that there is greater labor in the **whitening** <note>original: "dealbando"</note> on account of the specific weights and mixtures required, than there is in the **reddening** <term>rubificando; the final stage of the work, known as Rubedo</term>. For once the whitening is achieved, no error follows until the reddening is complete. And for the making of the **red**, it is said that it must be done in the same way and with a similar **regimen** <term>regimine; the specific method of managing the heat and the vessel</term> in all respects, just as in the whitening of the substance itself...

They make it spiritual, clean from all earthiness, airy, and subtle.

### Likewise, a note concerning the ferment. 
Nothing is made from that which is already perfect, because it is already completed—just as this matter or craft <note>The "artificium" or alchemical art.</note> completes its work. We have an example of this: bread that has been leavened and baked is perfect in its state or being; it has reached its final end, and you cannot ferment it any further. 

So it is with gold: pure gold has been brought through the test of fire into a firm and fixed body. According to the Philosophers, it is impossible to ferment it any further unless one possesses the **First Matter** <term>prima materia; the original, undifferentiated substance from which all metals are formed</term> of metals, in which the gold may be dissolved back into its primary state and into its mixable elements. 

Let us therefore take that matter from which gold is made, and by means of the craft, let it be led into the **true ferment of the Philosophers**. Let us change this with skill into a perfect matter, or into the species of perfect bodies, and only then let us begin the operation. For this reason, many modern workers—even those working according to philosophical principles—are deceived, because they abandon the work exactly where it ought to begin.

**Note:** Water is the spirit that purifies, refines, and whitens the body. And the ferment is the soul, which grants life to the imperfect body through the mediation of water—a life it did not have before—and brings it back into a better form. Even if only one of these two were present in our Stone, the medicine would never easily flow, nor would it provide a **tincture** <term>tinctura; the potent color-changing essence of the Stone</term>. Even if it did provide one, it would fly away into smoke like **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius." Quick-silver, famous in alchemy for its volatility and tendency to evaporate when heated.</note>, because there would be no vessel within it to receive and hold the tincture.

And in the greatest hour of conjunction <note>The "marriage" or chemical union of the spirit, soul, and body.</note>, there appear

The **spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus"; the volatile or gaseous principle in alchemy</note> is not joined to the **bodies** until they have been perfectly cleansed of their impurities: that is, until the middle substance of **Mercury** and the **sulfur** of the body have been perfectly cleansed of their impurities. This means their conjunction is not possible unless they first become spiritual: that is, through the change of both from their original power and property, and through the conversion of their natures, they are joined in an all-encompassing union. Once purified in this way, they ought to be joined in the bodies: that is, with the **ferment** <note>original: "fermentum"</note> by means of **water**, which creates a marriage between them: that is, a conjunction or union. **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rafis"; Abū Bakr al-Rāzī (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and influential alchemical authority.</note> says: "Accidents cannot extend their qualities unless they are associated with substances."

Likewise, if you wish for a perfect and **transubstantiating** <term>transsubstantians; the power to change the underlying essence of a substance into another, such as lead into gold</term> **Elixir** to be made, which colors every body joined to it, this cannot be done except through its **solution** <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid</note> being frequently repeated.

Therefore, the **fifth essence** <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the quintessence, a pure, incorruptible substance thought to be the "spirit" of the world, separate from the four heavy elements</note> is a body that is distinct in itself from all **elements** and **compounds** <term>elementatis; things composed of the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</term>, as much in matter as in form, and in nature as in power. It contains no contrariety within itself, and thus has no cause of corruption. **Thomas** <note>Likely referring to a work attributed to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), as many alchemical "Compendiums" were spuriously credited to him.</note> writes this in his *Compendium*, where he sets out the difference between an element, a compound, and the fifth essence.

Cast away the other [part], because it is dross and slag; it is also called **white earth** <note>original: "terra alba"; a reference to the albedo or whitening stage of the work</note>. And always beware that you do not roast it unless it is dry. Whence **Hermes** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> says: Sow your **gold** in the **white foliated earth** <note>original: "terram albam foliatam"; a stage where the purified matter takes on a flaky or leaf-like appearance</note>, which through **calcination** <term>calcination; the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to achieve a powdery state, removing volatile impurities</term> has been made fiery, subtle, and airy—namely this much: sow the gold, that is, the **soul** and the **tinging virtue** <note>original: "virtutem tingentem"; the inherent power of a substance to transform the internal nature of another</note>, into the white earth, which by proper preparation has been made white and clean, in which there is no filth. From these things it is clear that the gold of nature is not the material of the **ferment** <term>ferment; a catalyst in alchemy that "leavens" the base matter to raise it to a higher state</term>; rather, the **gold of the Philosophers** is the tinging ferment itself.

Likewise, **Hermes**, the head of the Philosophers, says: When you **Alchemists** wish to mix natures together, mix the **stone of gold** with the liquid, which is the **permanent water** <note>original: "aqua permanens"; a key alchemical solvent that dissolves metals without wetting the hands</note>, and place it in its vessel over a gentle heat until it melts. Then leave it until the water dries up and they join together with one another. Let the water itself having been soaked—that is, dried—be a more intense fire than it was before, until it dries up and becomes **earth**—that is, powder. Once this is completed, know that this is the **beginning of the secret** <note>original: "arcani initium"</note>, namely, to perfectly soak with water and to dry.

Therefore, it is especially to be guarded against, lest the spirit becomes **volatile** <note>original: "volatilis"; literally 'flying'; refers to the spirit escaping the vessel as gas</note>: for if it flies from the body, the body will remain imperfect.

You must also be very careful to make the **Elixir** <term>Elixir; the transformative medicine or "philosopher's stone" in liquid or powder form</term> a middle state between hard and soft; for unless you know this, the **gold** <term>aurum</term> and **silver** <term>argentum</term> will not be fit for working—that is, for hammering or casting. For the medicine must be of a more subtle and more liquid substance than the metals themselves, because they possess greater stability and "retention" <note>the ability of a substance to resist being evaporated or changed by fire</note> than the **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term> does in its own nature, upon which the medicine is projected. Because **Euclid** <note>In alchemy, "Euclid" usually refers to a pseudo-epigraphical author rather than the Greek mathematician</note> says:

> Our final secret is to have a medicine which flows before the flight of **Mercury**. <note>meaning the medicine must melt and act upon the metal before the mercury evaporates from the heat</note>

Now, when you wish to compose the **Elixir**, make a lime <note>a fine powder produced by heating a substance to high temperatures</note> from that material of which the body is composed, and into it put its own **sulfur**, as I have said above: if it is **gold**, then use the sulfur of gold; if **silver**, then the sulfur of silver. For the marriage <note>original: "sponsalitium"; the alchemical "chemical wedding" or union of opposites</note> is nothing other than joining the **ferment** <term>fermentum; an agent added to the alchemical matter to "leaven" it, ensuring the entire mass takes on the quality of the desired metal</term> with its own body, from which you intend to make the **Elixir**. For the **Assembly** <term>Turba; referring to the "Turba Philosophorum" or Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts</term> says:

> Join these two: that is, the ashes—namely, of the perfected body—and the white **sulfur**: that is, the imperfect body—together with one another.

Wherefore the **Philosopher** <note>a title usually reserved for Aristotle, but often used generically for Hermes Trismegistus in these texts</note> says:

> First illuminate your body, and join it with the spirit and the clean body in equality: that is, by equal weight.

->*Note on the ferment.*<-

It must be noted that when the Elixir is joined with bodies, it is necessary that they be joined *by their smallest parts* <note>original: "per minima"; a physical theory suggesting that substances must be broken down to their most minute components to truly combine</note>, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a scholar and theologian to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> says. A powerful and useful **complexion** <term>complexionatio; the blending of qualities or elements into a new, balanced whole</term> can never be achieved with solid things unless they are first dissolved into "waters" <note>liquid solutions or acids</note>; then they should be mixed with one another, and in warm places, by the action of natural heat—or heat proportionate to it—they should connect to each other in a vaporous state over a suitable period of time. 

For it is necessary first to dissolve the Elixir, and afterward to prepare and dissolve the body just like the Elixir; later, one must take and join these solutions together—specifically, three parts of the Elixir and one part of the aforementioned bodies. Afterward, it is necessary to **congeal** <term>congelatio; the process of turning a liquid into a solid</term> this whole mixture, and again dissolve and congeal it, and so repeat the process until the whole is made into one without any separation. This entire work is completed through the benefit of our **mercurial water** <term>aqua mercurialis; a specialized alchemical solvent, the "water" of the wise, used to dissolve the Sun (gold) and Moon (silver)</term>: because with it the Elixir is dissolved and prepared, and with it the bodies are dissolved and prepar[ed]...

### *On the method of sweetening the stone with moisture.*

#### *Regarding the manner of performing the sweetening of this stone.*

Let the stone be taken and, by grinding, soak it in its own vessel. This **soaking** <term>imbibitio; the process of a solid gradually absorbing a liquid</term> should be done by the smallest amounts—that is, in turns, performed **in the manner of dew** <note>original: "modū roris"; a metaphor for very gentle, light application of liquid</note>—with one and a half parts of itself. After this, cook it with a gentle fire until that moisture has first been congealed into the substance of the stone.

Afterward, strengthen the fire of the coals little by little, until whatever has been released from it is refined, both regarding the **sulfur-water** <note>original: "aqua sulphuris"</note> and the moist **quicksilver** <term>argento viuo; mercury</term>.

Then, whatever has been **sublimated** <term>sublimatum; the material that has risen to the top of the vessel as vapor and solidified</term>, bring it back down upon the **dregs** <term>feces; the solid remains or "earth" left at the bottom of the vessel</term> by grinding and soaking it with the aforementioned spirit, which abounds more exuberantly in moisture. And repeat this with a dewy soaking...

When you wish to **wax** <term>ceration; from the Latin "incerare," meaning to soften a hard or brittle substance until it has the consistency of wax</term> the stone, you must add more of the **hot and moist** thing than you do of the **cold and dry**. And if you see that these things cannot be melted because of their **heaviness** <note>original: "grauitate"; likely referring to the density or stubbornness of the material</note>—namely through a failure of the waxing process—supplement it, and complete the waxing for it with the **oil of the stone**, adding it drop by drop over a light fire in an earthenware crucible, until it flows like wax, without smoke. Thus says **Raymond** <note>Referring again to the influential alchemist Raymond Lully</note>.

### *On the multiplication or augmentation of the stone.*

First, note what **augmentation** <note>original: "augmentum"; the process of increasing the power or amount of the alchemical medicine</note> is. For this reason, augmentation is the addition to a pre-existing quantity. And augmentation in quality and goodness consists of dissolving and coagulating the **tincture** <term>the refined essence of the Stone, capable of "staining" or transforming base metals</term> itself—that is, to moisten it with our **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio nostro"; refers to the "Philosophical Mercury" used as a solvent</note> and to dry it out.

Or like this: Take one part of the prepared tincture, and dissolve it in three parts of our Mercury; then place it in a vessel, and seal the vessel, and put it among warm ashes for the whole time, as expressed above, until it is dried out and becomes a powder. Then open the glass, and moisten it again, and dry it as above; and the more times you do this, the more parts you will gain, and it will tint further, as **Arnoldus** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a renowned medieval physician and alchemist</note> says.

Augmentation in quantity is: Take three parts of the **fixed matter** <term>substance that has been made stable and no longer evaporates or escapes when heated</term> which tints—that is, the prepared tincture—and one part of the **Mercury of the Philosophers**, and place it in a vessel, and seal the vessel, and put it among warm ashes, as above, and dry it until it becomes a powder. Then open the glass, and moisten it again, and dry it, and so forth, as above. And the water—that is, the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note> or Mercury—does not add or give more weight to the body except for as much as remains of the **metallic moisture** <note>original: "humiditate metallina"</note>.

These are the words of **Calidius, son of Isidorus** <note>Latinized name for Khalid ibn Yazid, a legendary early figure in Arabic alchemy</note>. Likewise, multiplication in quantity is done through the mixing of the medicine...

This quicksilver, through the addition of the Stone, is converted into a red and black powder. And repeatedly, let some of that powder of quicksilver be placed upon other quicksilver, and again it is converted into powder. And perform these repetitions of the powder of quicksilver upon other quicksilver until the quicksilver is no longer converted into powder, but instead is converted into a **perfect metal** <note>typically gold or silver, signifying the successful completion of the process</note>. And this is because the strength of the medicine is tempered by the addition of quicksilver.

Also, the **multiplication** <term>the process of increasing the quantity and quality of the alchemical medicine</term> of the **tincture** <term>the concentrated essence of the Stone</term> is nothing else but the increase and multiplication of the **natural heat** <note>the internal vital energy inherent in the matter</note>, which is **non-burning sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur non urens"; a pure alchemical principle that drives transformation without charring or destroying the substance</note> in the matter of quicksilver. For it is certain that quicksilver is the matter of metals in its substance, in which its clarity is fixed, because metals require nothing but a substantial nature. And it is necessary that the substance in which the tincture of sulfur is fixed be from matter preserved from all **burning** <note>original: "adustione"; the damaging effect of over-heating or impure fire</note>, and capable of perfect **fusion** <note>original: "fusionis"; the state of melting and flowing smoothly</note>, lovable and pleasing to all metals. And therefore it is necessary that the tincture of sulfur follows such a substance and is gathered within it, if you wish for it to be a tincture of metals; and the said substance must be such that it can be **fixed** <note>made stable and resistant to evaporation or heat</note> without the consumption of its humidity, and without it returning to earth, and without the burning of its own substance: and all this is quicksilver.

...of the powder: return it into that water through distillation until it has absorbed everything and is completely fixed in the earth <note>original: "fixa in terra"; in alchemy, "earth" refers to the solid, non-volatile residue remaining after distillation</note>. Afterward, saturate the whole with its oil and its tincture until it is well fixed and melts completely like **wax** <note>original: "sicut cera"; this indicates the medicine has reached the stage of "ceration," where it is solid but melts without evaporating</note>. Cast one weight of that medicine upon whichever body <note>i.e., a base metal like lead or mercury</note> you wish to transform, and you will certainly find its **tincture** <term>the color-giving, transformative essence of the Stone</term> multiplied a hundredfold by this method, etc.

**The medicine is further multiplied in two ways:**
By the **solution of heat** or by the **solution of rarity**. 

**The solution of heat** is as follows: Take the medicine placed in a glass vessel and bury it in our **moist fire** <note>original: "igne nostro humido"; typically refers to a water bath (balneum Mariae) or the gentle, steady heat of fermenting horse manure</note> for seven days or more, until the medicine is dissolved into water without any cloudiness. 

**The solution of rarity:** Take the glass vessel with the medicine and suspend it in a new bronze pot with a narrow opening. In this pot, let water boil, and keep the opening closed so that the medicine is dissolved by the vapor rising from the boiling water.

But note that the boiling water should not touch the glass vessel containing the medicine by a distance of at least three fingers. This solution may take perhaps one, two, or three days. After the medicine has been dissolved, remove it from the fire to be cooled, fixed, congealed, hardened, or dried. Let it be dissolved in this way multiple times; for the more the medicine is re-dissolved, the more perfect it will become. Such a solution is the **refinement** <note>original: "subtiliatio"; the process of making a substance more "subtle" or spiritually pure by breaking down its coarse physical form</note> of the medicine.

### *The method for projecting all the previously described substances may be tested in this way.*

Take one part of the medicine and ten parts of raw, purified **mercury** <term>mercury: also known as quicksilver; in alchemy, it represents the fluid, transformative principle of matter</term>, making sure the mercury is heated over the fire until it begins to smoke <note>original: "vsq; ad fumositatem"</note>. Soon, the entire mass becomes a **fixed** <term>fixed: a substance that is "fixed" can withstand the heat of the fire without evaporating or changing</term> medicine, suitable for making a further projection upon even more mercury. ### Prologue to the same.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring scrolling foliage and a central floral motif.</image-desc>

Since the improvement of all things is their augmentation <note>original: augmentatio; the idea that refining a substance increases its inherent power or quantity</note>: therefore it is written in many sayings of the Philosophers that nature is improved through art <note>original: per artem; "art" here refers to the "Great Art" of alchemy</note> beyond its own motion which it had in its first form. Yet no art can work except by means of nature, since nature itself works intrinsically and hiddenly within art through the management of the craftsman. From this it follows that the imitation of nature is the augmentation and labor of natural power, and the augmentation of the thing itself: because nature completes its own degree, which it can naturally complete, and cannot pass beyond it unless it is hindered by an opposing force. Although art does not truly transcend nature by creating a *new* nature through simple labor, it is said that art imitates nature—not that it builds a new nature, but that it refines <term>subtiliet: to make "subtle," meaning to purify, thin, or make more potent by removing heavy, impure matter</term> the power of that nature. Because of this, art begins to perfect where nature leaves off—namely, to uncover the "subtle" nature enclosed within a thing and to make it manifest. For this reason, the mineral ore generates metals, yet it cannot generate tinctures <term>tincture: a concentrated alchemical essence or elixir capable of transforming (dyeing) base metals into gold or silver</term>, even though it hiddenly contains a full tincture within itself. As the Philosopher <note>usually referring to Aristotle, or a general authority in the alchemical tradition</note> says...

The Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or a foundational alchemical authority like Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: Nature contains within itself those things which it needs and by which it is perfected, except that it must be set in motion by **art** <term>ars: in this context, the specific skill and laboratory techniques of the alchemist</term> and **operation**. Therefore, in our work, art is nothing other than an aid to nature. This is evident in many works of the arts of laypeople <note>original: laicorum; referring to common craftsmen rather than specialized scholars</note>, where nature first produces wood; second, the burning of the wood by fire turns it into ash; and third, art makes **glass** from the ash. This should be understood in the following way: if that **first matter** <term>materia: the fundamental substance or "building block" of a thing</term> of glass had not been hidden within the ash, art could by no means have created glass from it without nature's own skill.

And thus, consider that nothing can be extracted from any thing which does not already exist within it. Therefore, every thing in its own species, and every genus in its own genus, and every nature in its own nature, naturally completes its growth by its own power and bears fruit according to its own nature, and not in another nature contrary to itself. Since every **seed** corresponds to its own seed, as we say, regarding **generation**. Therefore, nothing is generated from a human except a human, nor from any animal except something like itself. 

And as for imitating perfected nature, no art performs the labor of serving nature simply, except through the composition of that specific nature. For if a foreign, inferior <note>original: peior; literally "worse" or "lower quality"</note> nature is introduced, art immediately ceases to simply imitate nature. Instead, those inferior, external natures corrupt that nature, and immediately that which was hoped for does not come to be from it. Since everything that works poorly in something...

### ON THE UTILITY OF STUDY

**Study** removes ignorance and leads the human intellect back to true knowledge and to the science of any thing. Therefore, it is first of all necessary to acquire knowledge of this "sweet work" <note>a common alchemical term for the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone</note> through study, and to sharpen the wit through **natural philosophy** <term>physica: in the medieval sense, this refers to the study of the physical world and the laws of nature</term>, since within these lies the knowledge of truth. If, therefore, those who labor do not despise study, they will sweetly taste the fruit coming from it. 

But those who shrink from studying and yet still wish to labor, let them see whether their art is truly an imitation of nature—which is what their art ought to improve. For it is impossible for such a person to prepare the secrets of the Philosophers to a perfect end. Of these people, the wise say that they "approach the practice like a **donkey to dinner**" <note>original: "asinus ad cœnam"; a proverbial expression for someone who lacks understanding of the task at hand</note>, not knowing toward what they stretch their snout, except insofar as their exterior senses (without the use of intellect) lead them to the fodder through sight and taste. Thus these very donkeys, without good and true principles, without fruitful studies, and without knowledge of natures, seek to perfect the works of nature and the secret of all **Philosophy** <term>philosophia: here referring specifically to Alchemical Philosophy or the "Great Work"</term>.

### *How many parts of minerals there are.*
## CHAPTER II.

Mineral bodies are specifically distinguished into two parts: namely, the metallic part and the mineral part. Into the metallic part: that is, into the metals which derive their origin from Mercury. And into the mineral part: those which do not draw their origin from Mercury.

An example of the metals [includes] gold, the Moon <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for Silver</note>, Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"; Quicksilver or hydrargyrum</note>, Jupiter <note>original: "Iupiter"; the alchemical name for Tin</note>, Mars <note>original: "Mars"; the alchemical name for Iron</note>, Saturn <note>original: "Saturnus"; the alchemical name for Lead</note>, and electrum <note>original: "electrum"; traditionally a natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver</note>.

An example of the minerals [includes] salts, inks <note>original: "atramenta"; often referring to vitriols or black metallic sulfates used in making ink</note>, alum, vitriol, arsenic, and orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide used as a pigment</note>.

Regarding the metals which derive their origin from Mercury: all metals which have drawn their origin from Mercury are malleable <term>malleable: "ductibilia," meaning they can be hammered thin or drawn into wire</term> and liquefiable <term>liquefiable: "liquabilia," meaning they can be melted or fused</term>. This is because their material is a watery substance mixed with an earthy substance in such a strong combination <note>original: "commixtione forti"</note> that one cannot be separated from the other. For this reason, that watery substance is congealed more by cold after the action of heat, and they will therefore be malleable or workable by the smith. Furthermore, water alone is not congealed except by an earthy dryness which alters the wateriness, since the moisture in them is not oily <note>original: "unctuosus"; in alchemical theory, "unctuous" or oily moisture was associated with Sulfur, while "watery" moisture was associated with Mercury</note>. Because their solidification is caused by earthy dryness, they are not easily dissolved <note>original: "soluuntur"; melted or broken down</note> except through the action of a vehement heat within them, according to how strongly and powerfully they are mixed.

### *How metals are generated specifically from Mercury.* CHAPTER III.

The nature and substance of all liquefiable things is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuo"; literally "living silver," the standard alchemical term for Mercury</note>, because this same quicksilver is solidified <term>coagulated: "coagulatur," the process of a liquid or vapor becoming a solid body</term> by the vapor or heat of white or red sulfur that does not burn. Hence Aristotle says in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*: If the sulfur is white and not burning, it solidifies Mercury into good silver. But if the sulfur is pure with a clear redness, and if there is in it a simple, non-burning heat, it solidifies [the Mercury] into the purest gold, better than what a mine produces. This happens because every dry thing naturally drinks up its own moisture so that it may be made continuous in its parts. 

The vapor of the sulfur that solidifies the quicksilver consists of a substance that is fire-like, subtle, and airy; it is boiled <note>original: "decocta"; refers to the process of refining or "ripening" through heat</note> and digested from the first mixture, united to itself by the action of heat, and afterwards raised, boiled, and digested until it possesses the sulfur-like power of solidifying quicksilver into metallic bodies. 

But when the sulfur is impure or burning <note>original: "adurens"; referring to sulfur that is too "hot" or chemically aggressive, which "scorches" the metal into an imperfect state</note>, it causes either perfection or imperfection in the metals, as the example of these things later makes clear. Their primary matter is quicksilver because when they are liquefied, they are converted into it by heat. It is certain that they were quicksilver before, because every thing is made of that into which it can be resolved. An example of this is ice <note>Just as ice can be melted back into water to prove its origin, the author argues that metals can be "resolved" back into a liquid state resembling Mercury</note>.

### *On the generation of Mercury and which metals are generated from it. CHAPTER IV.*

Mercury <note>original: "Argentum viuum"; literally "living silver," the standard alchemical name for quicksilver</note>, in its primary root, is composed of a white, subtle, and highly sulfurous earth, strongly mixed with clear water until it becomes a single substance. It does not rest on a flat surface, nor does it stick to what touches it, because the "dryness" has transformed the wateriness within it. It is, however, uniform <term>homogenium: of the same nature throughout, rather than a mixture of visible parts</term> in its nature: for either the whole of it remains in the fire and becomes fixed <term>fixatur: the state of being resistant to heat and no longer evaporating</term>, or the whole of it flies away as smoke, since it is incombustible and airy. This is a sign of its perfection. For this reason, when it is first heated and runs through sulfurous earth, it ascends to the top. Thus, its nature is to be refined by heat.

Nevertheless, through continuous sublimation <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the condensed solid</term>, it is greatly purified, "boiled" or refined, and thickened, and is gradually solidified by white and red sulfur. Since sulfur is dissolved many times, the sublimated mercury is first solidified and made "waxy" <term>inceratum: an alchemical stage where a substance is softened to the consistency of wax</term> by the action of heat. This continues until, through the work of nature over perhaps thousands of years, it is successively solidified into a perfect metal.

Within mineral vessels <note>original: "vasis mineralibus"; a metaphorical reference to the natural hollows or veins within the earth where metals "grow"</note>, nature herself produces metals from this substance. Therefore, in these operations, whoever wishes to complete the medicine—bringing it from imperfection to perfection—must imitate nature. This is true even though the metallic bodies generated from mercury differ from it in their composition, depending on how pure that mercury was,

<page-num>553</page-num>

### *Concerning the formation of wonders which do not take their origin from Mercury.* CAP. V.

There are, moreover, minor or intermediate minerals, according to what has been said, which do not take their origin from Mercury. And of these, some are those which are easily liquefied by moisture, such as alum, simple salt, sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum: ammonium chloride, a white crystalline salt used by early chemists to clean metal surfaces and in the process of sublimation</term>, rock salt, and all types of salts. 

And some are potent <note>original: "virtuosa"; referring to substances with strong chemical or medicinal properties</note>, and do not easily liquefy by moisture alone, such as orpiment <term>auripigmentum: a deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide once used as a pigment and thought to contain the "seed" of gold</term>, arsenic, and sulfur. This occurs when the wateriness of sulfurous bodies is mixed with a viscous earth through a strong combination and the boiling of heat, until they become potent and have been previously solidified by cold. 

Vitriols <term>atramenta: literally "inks," but in this context referring to the family of metallic sulfates (vitriols) used to make pigments and dyes</term>, however, are composed of salt, sulfur, and stones. It is believed that within them resides the mineral power of certain liquefiable bodies which are made from them, such as chalcanthum <term>calcantum: blue vitriol or copper sulfate, prized for its vibrant color</term> and "field olocar" <note>original: "olocari ager"; likely a corruption of an Arabic-derived term like "alchor" or a specific type of earthy mineral sulfate such as colcothar</note>. These are generated from larger grains of vitriol and do not dissolve unless the saltiness <note>original: "falsedo," likely a typo for "salsedo" (saltiness)</note> within the sulfur itself is dissolved with them; they are first congealed in the cold. 

This substance then receives a mineral power from certain bodies naturally existing in the earth. That which receives the power of iron will be red and earthy, like *olocar*. However, that which receives a copper-like <note>original: "aëream"; likely a reference to "aes" (copper/bronze) rather than "aer" (air)</note> power will be the green chalcanthum. Therefore, it is possible for these two—namely *olocar* and *chalcanthum*—to be generated from the same source, since all these aforesaid things share in a mineral power along with the metals.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of minerals and metals. <page-num>554</page-num>
<header>CORRECTION</header>

But metallic bodies cannot be produced artificially from these [minor minerals], since they are of a different nature; they did not take their origin from the proximate first matter <term>prima materia propinqua: the immediate, base substance from which a specific class of things is formed; in alchemy, mercury was considered the proximate matter of metals</term> alongside metals—namely Mercury—but from quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuo"; while often synonyms, the author here distinguishes between the "mercury" that serves as a philosophical principle and the common liquid metal</note>. I do not deny that metals can be purged or dissolved with these minerals, or that a sophistic form <note>original: "forma sophistica"; a deceptive outward appearance that masks the true nature of a substance</note> can be introduced through them to deceive people—for instance, the blackness of lead can be wiped away—yet lead always remains lead. Thus, craftsmen can perform "congelations" <term>congelationes: the process of turning a liquid substance into a solid, often by removing moisture</term> through them: that is, to extract the moisture from Mercury with dry substances so that the Mercury appears coagulated <note>solidified</note>, but that coagulation is of the worst sort.

> Whence Aristotle <note>This famous quote actually originates from Avicenna’s *De Congelatione*, which was frequently attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages. It was the primary authority used to argue that alchemy could only mimic the appearance of metals, not change their essence.</note> says: Let the Alchemists know that they cannot change the species of things, but they can make things similar to them: that is, they can tinge a red substance with yellow so that it appears to be gold, and tinge white with whatever color they wish until it becomes very similar to silver: as do those who join together tin, copper, and mercury, and from these make sophistic silver <term>argentum sophisticum: counterfeit or "fake" silver that looks real but lacks the essential properties of the metal</term>.

And while the purging of metals through minerals is also performed and is not impossible—and reason does not stand against this—it does stand against the creation of true gold and silver. This is by no means permitted to happen in nature or art except through the reduction of bodies into their first matter <term>prima materia: the primitive, formless base substance from which all matter was thought to originate</term>. In this way, the species of things can be transmuted, as Aristotle later adds. And this is not achieved by simple melting alone, but by the resolution of congealed Mercury, when, through the mixing of its own spirit, the body is transformed into Mercury.

## On the difference in the generation of common sulfur, simple [sulfur], and Mercury.

### CHAPTER VI.

Since it has been stated that the sulfur which causes metals is an element of metals alongside Mercury, I now set forth the difference between the generation of Mercury and that of sulfur, although both certainly contribute to the creation of a metal—namely, through essential Mercury <term>Mercurio essentiali: the inner "matter" or "soul" of the metal</term> and through sulfur on the accidental side <term>ex parte accidentali: in Aristotelian terms, "accidents" are the outward qualities like color or hardness, rather than the core essence</term>. However, that sulfur is itself twofold: namely, "living" <note>original: "vivum"; also known as "quicksulfur," the philosophical principle of sulfur found in nature before being processed</note> and "burning." Living sulfur causes metals to form, although they still differ significantly from one another according to how much they are infected by the viscosity <term>viscositate: a sticky, oily, or "thick" quality of earth that alchemists believed hindered the perfection of metals</term> of the earth. Yet, simple living sulfur, which causes the formation of gold and silver, is nothing but a hot and dry vapor, generated from the purest terrestrial dryness, in which fire predominates in every way; and this is called an "element" together with the Mercury of metals.

But the generation of common sulfur <note>original: "sulphuris vulgi"; the yellow, smelly brimstone used in everyday crafts, which alchemists distinguished from the "philosophical sulfur" that forms metals</note> differs from the generation of Mercury, as was said above: because the wateriness of common sulfur is mixed with a most viscous earthiness along with boiling heat, and they have become oily. Thus, the generation of Mercury differs in its second stage from the generation of this sulfur, since it is generated from a most subtle, white, sulfurous earth, combined with very clear water; because it shines through due to a very strong mixture <note>The author is describing the metallic luster and fluidity of Mercury as a perfect marriage of "clear water" and "subtle earth"</note>, such that one cannot be separated from the other, as long as it does not rest on a flat surface,

### *How it is possible for the lesser metals to be made into [perfect] metals artificially. CHAPTER VII.*

But because it was determined in the preceding chapter that it is impossible for lesser metals <note>base metals such as lead, tin, or copper</note> to be made into [perfect] metals artificially, it remains here to be proved. First, in this way: because the lesser metals were not generated from the primary matter of metals, which is Mercury; because their generation differs from the generation of Mercury primarily in form, in nature, and in composition, therefore they also cannot be made into [perfect] metals: because for things of one species, there is but one primary matter and seed from which they are generated.

It should not be believed that the nature of earth can be artificially changed into a watery moisture, even if the earth is soaked with water. These include afterbirth <note>original: "secundinas"</note>, the eyes of animals, eggshells, hair, the blood of a red-haired man <note>In medieval alchemy, the blood of a red-haired person was often (falsely) rumored to have magical or transformative properties.</note>, the Basilisk (both the artificial and natural kind), worms, herbs, roots, and even human dung.

We point these out to the ignorant so that they might avoid such deceptions. For from these things—which we will discuss later—they have spent a long time extracting what they call "artificial quicksilver" <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury</term>, as well as oils and waters which they have named the "four elements" (namely water, air, earth, and fire), and also sal ammoniac, arsenic, sulfur, and orpiment <note>a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>. They could have bought these better in the market and achieved their results much sooner! 

They have also sought a tincture <term>tinctura: the elusive "dye" or spiritual essence intended to transform base metal into gold</term> in vegetable and sensible things—substances that lack the proper moisture and are merely dry, combustible, and corruptible—a quality which these things simply do not have. These men, having been thus ruined...

That they convert things into their own nature through dyeing is proven by the rule that every generating thing generates its own kind. But since here the tincture of the four spirits is the "generator," the earth will therefore generate its own kind, which is earthy just like itself.

## *How red sulfur is in the Sun, and white*

Since it has been said that the red sulfur of the Philosophers exists in the **Sun** <note>original: "Sole"; refers to Gold</note> through a greater digestion, and white sulfur exists in the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; refers to Silver</note> through a lesser digestion. # THE BOOK ON THE CHEMICAL ART by an Unknown Author.

## ON THE GENERATIONS *of Metals in the Bowels of the Earth.*
### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'O' featuring stylized foliage and vines within a square border.</image-desc>The opinion and judgment of all who philosophize correctly is the same: that all **metals** are generated from the vapor of **sulfur** and **quicksilver**. For when the "fatness of the earth" <term>fatness of the earth</term><note>An alchemical term for the oily, combustible principle (sulfur) found in the soil.</note> is heated and encounters the substance of water gathered together in a mass, it solidifies those most beautiful bodies—**gold**, **silver**, **copper**, **tin**, **iron**, and **lead**—within the veins of the earth. This happens through both natural power and the rays of the celestial bodies <note>Alchemists believed the planets "ripened" metals in the earth; for example, the Sun's rays produced gold.</note> and the movement of the heavens, depending on the purity or impurity of the ingredients.

### *Concerning nature and art.* CHAPTER II.

There are, moreover, two effective causes within this "dome of the world" <note>original: "Mundi teſtudine"; a poetic term for the vault of the sky or the universe.</note>: **nature** and **art** <term>art</term><note>In alchemical texts, "Art" specifically refers to the practice of alchemy—the human imitation or acceleration of nature's work.</note>. Nature produces and generates new things daily; Art, however...

...[modes], impressing the likenesses of those things through conception, it follows the traces and lineaments of nature in a wondrous way. So much so that if the ingenuity of man did not sometimes assist in certain matters, nature itself [would seem to] have openly failed in its operation. For **Art**, with the help of nature, sometimes corrects, completes, and in a certain way (especially in this magnificent discourse on **mineral things** <note>original: "mineralium rerum diatribe"</note>) seems to surpass nature. This has long been consecrated in the memory of those ancient **Philosophers**.

There are two kinds of **Philosophers**. Some, investigating nature merely for its own sake, have passed down in literary records the virtue and power which **sublunary things** <term>sublunary things</term><note>Objects existing in the realm below the moon—the Earth—which were believed to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note> possess, both from their elementary qualities and from the heavens and stars—such as **Physicians** <note>original: "Medici"</note>. And there are certain others who have described the natures of living creatures, trees, herbs, **metals**, and precious stones.

The other kind, far more splendid indeed, penetrating most sagaciously and acutely not only nature, but finally the very secret of nature and its innermost sanctuaries, have claimed for themselves the name of **Philosopher** in a truer sense. But because nature produces all metals from two things—**sulfur** and **Mercury**—and has left to us the **superior bodies** <term>superior bodies</term><note>In alchemical theory, "superior bodies" refers to the perfect metals, gold and silver, which correspond to the Sun and Moon.</note> generated from them along with the **inferior bodies**, it is certain that diligent seekers can produce the same things from their three operations, and are able to lead the **inferior bodies** <note>The base metals, such as lead, iron, or tin.</note> to the nature and perfection of the **superior bodies**.

### He refutes the opinion of certain people in this art, and the Philosophical art is explained in very few words. CHAPTER III.

And since it is accepted among most students of **Philosophy** <note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers to Natural Philosophy or Alchemy, the study of nature's hidden workings.</note> that **metals** themselves are generated from **sulfur** and **Mercury**, some have thought that since sulfur and Mercury are the root and matter of metals, they ought to be taken and cooked for so long until they are bonded together into a metallic body. Indeed, if these people had descended deeper into the sanctuary of nature, they would never have arrived at such foolish opinions. 

For although **sulfur** and **Mercury** <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> were in a way the root of metals before their first **coagulation** <term>coagulation</term><note>The process by which a fluid or "spirit" becomes a solid body.</note>, they are no longer so now, since they have been led to another nature. From this, it follows that no metallic body can be made from them [in their raw state]. Likewise, the **bond** <note>original: "vinculum"</note> is unknown by which **Venus** <note>The alchemical name for Copper.</note> and **Mercury** might join in the proper proportion. 

Therefore, those raw materials are not to be taken, but rather that which has been fully cooked from them in the "belly of the earth," and that thing is indeed the purest. You will find a similar example of this in **vegetable** nature. It is clear that all small trees, flowers, and herbs are produced from water and the union of subtle earth. Yet, if you attempt to grow a tree or a herb, you do not take raw earth or water; but rather you take that which comes from them, such as a sprout or a seed. These, when entrusted to the womb of the earth—the parent of all—and by the nourishment of their own nature...

### CHAPTER IV.

Moreover, we eagerly assert that the most powerful reason why those ancient **Philosophers** <note>The "natural philosophers" or alchemists of antiquity</note> investigated this science was the **inspiration of God**. For when the Philosophers saw that all vegetable and animal things, as well as other things, multiply and produce after their own kind by a certain **spirit** <note>original: "spiritu" — in alchemy, the "spirit" is the volatile, active principle that gives life or form to matter</note> of their own, and that **transmutation** <term>transmutation</term><note>The fundamental alchemical process of changing one substance—usually a "base" metal like lead—into another, like gold.</note> occurs in this lower world through the air (which over a long time seemed to corrupt individual things) and that the nature of one thing altered itself through movements, this question arose among them: Namely, why the **spirit** in metals could not propagate its own kind, whereas many branches might grow together from one shoot, and from one small grain count...

...mere grains, as it were, might multiply themselves. It was finally decreed by divine oracle that this spirit is confined by a coarser matter; if this spirit is separated by a certain **sublimation** <term>sublimation|The alchemical process of heating a substance until it vaporizes, then cooling it to purify it</term> through fire, and kept in its own natural seat, it acts as a **seed-like virtue** <note>original: "seminaria virtus" — the internal power or "spark" that allows a substance to reproduce itself like a plant seed</note> which can, without any falsehood, generate its own kind. From this, the **Philosophers** <note>Meaning the "natural philosophers" or alchemists</note> thought to bring the light and brilliance of the most perfect body <note>A reference to gold, considered the most "perfect" and "solar" of all metals</note> into the lower bodies, once they found that metallic bodies differ from one another only by a greater or lesser degree of **decoction** <term>decoction|The internal "cooking" or maturation of metals within the earth by natural heat over long periods of time</term>, and that **Mercury** was the primary origin of all metals. By extracting the metallic gold from the Mercury, they reduced gold to its first nature. Since this reduction is both easy and possible, the Philosophers concluded that the **transmutation** of metals is likewise easy and possible.

<margin>AB</margin>
And when those original Philosophers had reduced gold to its first nature, they employed **celestial influence** <note>The alignment of the planets and stars, believed to be essential for the success of the alchemical "Great Work"</note> so that it would not return to being the same metal it was before. Then they purified its nature, separating the impure from the clean. Having done this, they called that substance the transmuting **Philosopher's Stone**. To prepare it, various operations were invented by different Philosophers so that what had been left unfinished by nature might be completed by art, for nature itself is always striving toward its own perfection.

### A Thorough Discussion of What the Philosopher's Stone Is, and Treating First its Primary Part
### CHAPTER V.

And because the Philosophers declared this skill so obscurely—wrapped in the veils of words and the bonds of figures—it has been doubted by many what the **Stone of the Philosophers** <note>original: "lapis Philosophorum"</note> actually is, and from what substances it is composed. Therefore, if you are willing to listen carefully: we divide the Stone into two parts. 

Its first part we call "earthly," which both the ancient Philosophers and more recent ones clearly confirm to me with their testimonies in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba" — referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the most famous and foundational Latin alchemical texts</note>. Without the **Earthly Sun** <note>original: "Sole terreno" — a reference to gold, which alchemists believed held the power of the celestial sun in physical form</note>, the Philosophical work is not completed. Since all assert that no **tincture** <term>tincture|A potent alchemical substance or "dye" capable of transforming the properties and color of base metals into gold</term> is true without its own copper: because in it is the **purest sulfur of the wise** <note>original: "sulphur sapientum" — not common sulfur, but the active, spiritual "fire" or "soul" extracted from gold</note>, in which wise nature contains its own mind. 

And just as the Sun pours out and pierces its most lively and penetrating rays into this elementary world, so the Philosopher’s Stone—composed by philosophical operation from the **gold of the Sun**, his son, so to speak—spreads itself into other metals, and will match them in power, color, and weight forever. And because all metals are contained in gold, we rightly take gold before all others. For when we wish to create gold or silver, it is necessary to take those very same substances. From a human, a human is generated; from a tree, a tree; from a plant, a plant...

### Concerning the second part of the stone, where the spirit is compared to the most glorious Virgin Mary. CHAPTER VI.

We call the second part of the stone **Living Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium vivum" — often called quicksilver, but here referring to "Philosophical Mercury," the transformative fluid principle</note>. Because it is living and raw, it is said to dissolve the bodies [of metals] themselves, for it naturally clings to them in their innermost depths. This is the stone without which nature performs nothing. 

For this reason, the Philosophers advise us that we should not work except with the **Sun** <note>original: "Sole" — alchemical code for gold</note> and **Mercury**, which, when joined together, constitute the **Stone of the Philosophers**. Who, then, is capable of honoring the merits of Mercury with sufficient praise, since he alone is the one who makes gold thin <note>Meaning to "subtleize" or break down the solid structure of gold</note>, and who holds such power that he can reduce the Sun itself back to its primary nature? No other thing in this world is known to possess such power. Of Mercury itself, it is said:

->Whatever the wise seek is found in Mercury.<-
->Mercury destroys all leafed gold,<-
->dissolving it and softening it, it draws the soul from the body.<-
->If it is sublimated, then the **water of life** is generated.<-
<term>water of life|original: "aqua vitę" — in this context, a purified alchemical solvent or distillate used to "vivify" the metallic base</term>

Therefore, if anyone should ask you: "What are the stones?" You shall answer: "The Sun and Mercury are the philosophical stones." These truly are the stones...

...[the bodies] are dead upon the earth, and they perform nothing, unless the industry of man is administered to them. The profound likeness of gold. The **Ethereal Heaven** <note>original: "Cœlum Æthereum"</note> was closed to all men, so that all men descended to the infernal seats <note>The underworld or hell</note>, and were detained there perpetually. But Jesus Christ opened the gate of the **Ethereal Olympus** <note>The author uses classical Greek imagery—Olympus—to represent the highest Christian heaven</note> and has now laid open the **Plutonian realms** <note>original: "Plutonia regna" — the kingdom of Pluto, god of the dead; here meaning the gates of Hell</note>, so that souls might be rescued, when in the virginal womb—with the Holy Spirit cooperating—by an ineffable mystery and most profound sacrament, the Virgin Mary conceived that which was most excellent in heaven and on earth; and at last she brought forth for us the **Savior of the entire World**, who by his most exuberant goodness shall save all those given over to sin, if only the sinner turns himself toward him.

Yet she remained a virgin, unharmed and undefiled; for which reason **Mercury** is not undeservedly compared to the most glorious divine Virgin Mary. For Mercury is a virgin, because it has never propagated any metallic body in the womb of the earth, and yet it generates a new **Stone** <note>original: "lapidem" — the Philosopher's Stone</note>. By dissolving "heaven"—that is, gold—it opens and leads out the soul (by which you should understand its divinity); and it carries this soul in its womb for a short time, and at last, in its own time, transmits it into a purified body. Whence for us a child—that is, the Stone—is born, by whose blood the **inferior bodies** <note>The "imperfect" or base metals, such as lead, tin, or copper</note>, having been **tinctured** <note>The process of "tincturing" involves the Stone's power to change the color and nature of a metal through contact</note>, are brought back alive into the golden heaven; and Mercury remains a virgin without stain, just as it ever was before.

### *He determines why the Philosophers have hidden this skill, wherein the praise of the art is set forth, and he rails against the biting critic Zoilus <note>Zoilus was an ancient Greek grammarian known for his harsh, "biting" criticism of Homer; his name became a shorthand for any cynical or unfair critic</note>. CHAPTER VII.*

Hamul <note>Referring to the Arabic alchemist Muhammad ibn Umail al-Tamimi, known in Latin as Senior Zadith filius Hamuel</note>, in the book *Senior*, sets forth the principal reason why the Philosophers entrusted this science to posterity and the "sons of wisdom" <note>original: "sapientiæ filijs" — a traditional term for alchemical initiates</note> through distant metaphors and obscure allegories. It was so that they might attribute it to the glorious God, who would reveal it to whom He willed, and withhold it from whom He willed. Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis" — Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, a Persian physician and one of the most important figures in the history of medicine and alchemy</note> also relates this in his *Book of Lights* <note>original: "librum Luminũ"</note>. For if I wished to explain everything exactly as it is, there would no longer be any place for prudence, since the foolish man would be made equal to the wise. It is also read at the end of the *Turba* <note>original: "Turbæ" — referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," a foundational alchemical text translated from Arabic into Latin</note>: "For unless names were multiplied in the Philosophical art, children would mock our wisdom."

For this reason, we do not highly value those who mock this divine skill as being "adulterous" <note>meaning false, counterfeit, or illegitimate</note>—this art from which the most famous Philosophers used to take their knowledge of almost all things. Just as in the past, sculptors used to take the "thefts and threads" <note>original: "furta & fila" — a metaphor for the secret techniques and structural proportions</note> of their own art from the statue of Polykleitos <note>A famous Greek sculptor whose statue, the "Canon," was considered the perfect model of human proportion</note>, it would likewise be most absurd to suspect that those ancient Philosophers of venerable authority have committed any falsehood to memory—especially in this discourse on natural things. These were men who always applied the greatest effort to investigating the truth, even if they did not ascend to the sublimity of the nature of the soul-saving faith and the highest peak of the divine essence <note>The author acknowledges that while these ancient "pagans" were masters of nature, they lacked Christian revelation</note>. # ON THE ART

...[would even a] Zoilus <note>A reference to Zoilus of Amphipolis, an ancient critic known for his relentless attacks on Homer; here, he represents any cynical detractor of alchemy</note> not praise this science, and follow it with singular favor? From it, nearly all the arts of the detractors are drawn; from it, so many colors highly suitable for the painter's art took their beginning. I am silent regarding the art of coinage; I am silent regarding that learned distillation used by physicians, through which the virtue—which they call the **fifth essence** <note>original: "essentiam quintam"—the "quintessence," a refined substance thought to be the pure "spirit" of a material</note>—is usually drawn out. What shall I say of those bronze vessels by which thunderbolts and thundering are accustomed to be summoned among mortals <note>This refers to cannons and gunpowder, which were viewed as "alchemical" inventions that mimicked the power of nature</note>—if only they were used against the sacrilegious enemies of the Christian faith! There is, besides, a **science of the Stone** <note>Alchemy, specifically the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone</note> so sublime and magnificent that in it almost all of nature and the whole universe of things may be seen, as if in a certain clear mirror.

For it exists in the likeness of the **Minor World** <term>microcosm; the idea that a small system (like the human body or an alchemical flask) reflects the structure of the entire universe</term>, where there are the four elements and the fifth essence, which they call "heaven." In this heaven, another most noble essence has placed its seat, which certain Philosophers were accustomed to compare—I speak with reverence—to Almighty God, the most holy and undivided Trinity. This essence is neither of the nature of heaven, nor of the nature of the elements; and they called it by the peculiar name of the **middle soul of nature** <note>original: "animam mediam naturam"</note>. And just as God, the craftsman of the world, is present everywhere in this **Greater World** <term>macrocosm; the universe as a whole</term>: so this essence, which is judged by the title of "God," is everywhere in the whole World: that is, in the **philosophical glass** <term>the glass vessel or flask in which the alchemist performs his work</term>. And just as Almighty God is immense and infinite, so that thing seems almost innumerable in the procreation of its own kind, even until the end...
