### CHIMICA.

...the final end of the **Great World** <term>Macrocosm; the universe as a whole, as opposed to the "minor world" or microcosm</term>. For then the generative nature will be taken away from every procreative thing. From which words a person skilled in nature can gather that the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> can tinge many parts, by which also many other difficulties can be dissolved.

Let that **Aristarchus** <note>original: "Aristarchus"; an ancient critic of Homer, here used as a generic name for a pedantic or hyper-critical scholar</note> the Theologian be gone, who does not blush to confess himself an interpreter of divine letters, and yet does not fear to attack with his most impudent insults this skill of nature established by God—a skill than which God has bestowed nothing more magnificent or sublime upon this world after the Holy Scriptures. Tell me, by the immortal God, what is more unjust than for men to hate what they do not know? And even if the matter deserved hatred, what is more futile? What is more abject? What greater madness or insanity is there than to condemn that science in which you have smelled absolutely nothing? You, who have learned neither nature, nor the majesty of nature, nor its properties, nor the hidden **operations of metals** <note>The chemical processes used to refine or transmute metallic substances</note>?

In the same way, that lawyer and court-room **brawler** <term>rabula; a loud-mouthed, low-tier advocate or "pettifogger"</term>, a **great hater of philosophy**, croaks and blathers; he who strikes coins for himself with the hammer of a venal tongue from the tears of the wretched. Passing over the most sacred aspects of the laws, he has pursued the whole world with his deceits through the winding paths of **glosses** <note>original: "glossematum"; interpretive commentaries or marginal notes on legal texts that the author implies are used to distort the original law</note>. But why do I pursue these mocks and satires? Let those rough men and their followers remain forever in their own opinion—men who taste nothing that is pure, nothing that is pleasant, nothing that is fe[licitous/fruitful]...

*Chapters 8 and 9 treat the first essence of all things, and here it is discussed: What nature is, what the soul is, middle nature, and what the **Soul of the World** <term>Anima Mundi; an intrinsic connection between all living things on the planet</term> is. Now let us descend into **practice** <term>praxis: the practical, laboratory application of alchemical theory</term>, which we shall divide into two works. In the second, we will deal with **conjunction** and **fixation**, where consideration will be given to that most secret **augmentation** <note>The process of increasing the quantity or the power of the alchemical medicine (the Stone).</note>, which you will find in no other book in the world. 

But here, I wish to introduce the steps of the work in a general sense. For first, we **compose**; we **putrefy** <note>The stage of breaking down the matter, often associated with a black color.</note> that which is composed; we **dissolve** that which is putrefied; we **divide** that which is dissolved; we **cleanse** that which is divided; we **unite** that which is cleansed; and thus the work is completed. Our discourse will labor on these steps in detail. 

However, the Philosophers judge that in the practice of the **stones** <note>The raw materials or stages of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, less than a twelfth part of **Mercury** <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> should be taken. Also, among them, there is a danger to the "dissolved body" if compression were to happen through its skin <note>This likely refers to filtering the mixture through a piece of leather or cloth to separate the liquid mercury.</note>. Likewise, some of the more recent practitioners thought that dissolution could happen in a shorter time if long-term pounding or grinding of **gold leaf** were first performed in a certain mill or mortar.

### ALCHYMY

->607<-

...might be obtained. Of this purified water <note>original: "aquæ purificatæ," likely referring to the mercurial solvent described previously.</note>, let several parts be right well mixed with one part of most pure **Sun** <term>Sol: the alchemical name for Gold</term> drawn into leaves or thin plates. Let these be placed in a rather long glass **flask** <note>original: "ampulla"</note>, stopped up with small cloths and the sign of the cross. Let the glass be covered with ashes up to the level of the water, and let a very light fire be applied, so that the water does not seem to rise, but remains "alive" with the gold, and is maintained as if in a **balance** <term>trutina: a scale or balance, here signifying a state of perfect thermal equilibrium</term>. Let this heat be balanced until there sweats out upon the **Water of Mercury** <note>original: "aqua Mercurij"</note> a certain vaporous and subtle earth, which is usually recognized by its wondrous color when it is to be extracted. 

This **Sulfur** <term>Sulphur: in alchemy, the active, combustible, and "soul" principle of a substance</term> itself shines through the waters like a **rainbow** <note>original: "iridis instar." This refers to the *cauda pavonis* or "Peacock's Tail" stage, where a spectrum of colors appears in the flask.</note>, though not according to all the colors seen in the rainbow of this **Greater World** <term>Mundus maior: the Macrocosm or the universe at large</term>. The arc of the rainbow itself stands midway in the pure, liquid, and flowing water, and midway above the earth. From this, the entire property of the sulfur and its natural likeness is expressed through the rainbow; nor is the rainbow perceived in the sky except when the Sun is shining, which rain is also known to follow. 

However, when mists or dark clouds arrive, the Sun itself—and likewise the arc of the rainbow—is hidden. It has pleased **Natural Philosophers** <note>original: "Physicis," referring to those who study the physical laws of nature.</note> to explain the rainbow thus: when the image of the Sun colors a moist, hollow, and dense cloud, just like a mirror, and intersects the middle of its sphere—an explanation which comes quite close to this divine and wondrous skill of ours. Yet, one must not think that the sulfur itself turns black when you have extracted it, as some have mistakenly believed.

## CHAPTER 14.

There remains now the other part of the Philosophical practice, which is indeed far more difficult and far more sublime. In this stage, we read that all the strengths of genius—indeed, all the mental efforts of many Philosophers—have grown weary. For you would find it more difficult to make a man come back to life <note>original: "reuiuiſcere"</note> than to seek death. Here, the work of God is sought: it is indeed the greatest mystery for souls to wander, and [the goal is] to fashion an inanimate body into a living statue <note>The "living statue" refers to the animated "Philosophical Child" or the perfected Stone.</note>.

Do you think it is within the power of a lively intellect to lead the soul back to the spirit, then the spirit to the soul, and again those two back to the body? In this body of ours, it is fitting to know how much is spirit, how much is soul, and how much is of the body. Furthermore, [one must know] how much of the soul’s "middle nature" resides in the spirit and how much in the body, so that you may join these two natures—which are related and akin to one another—in the proper proportion. Therefore, we must join two waters: the **sulfur of gold** <term>Sulfur of gold: the active, "combustible" masculine principle extracted from gold</term> and the soul and body of its **Mercury**, the **Sun** and the **Moon**, the male and the female.

The body must be dissolved in the midst of the most subtle air; likewise, the body is dissolved by its own heat and humidity. In this state, the soul—acting as the "middle nature"—holds sovereignty everywhere within the glass vessel amidst the heat of blackness. This natural blackness was named by the ancient Philosophers the **crow’s head** <note>original: "caput corui"; a famous alchemical symbol for the *Nigredo* or black stage of transformation</note>, or the **Black Sun** <note>original: "Solem nigrum"</note>.

Regarding this, a certain man once brought forward this proposition: "I saw three circles revolving; I saw three Suns in the firmament having three faces: namely, a **Black Sun**, a **White Sun**, and a **Red Sun**." That blackness was also called by the names of all black things, because after it, all the colors of the world that can be conceived by the mind are accustomed to appear; these are finally referred to **true whiteness** <note>original: "albedinem veram"</note> as if to a center and a pivot. In the white, all colors exist, and from it all others, if I may say so, seem to receive their color. White and black are themselves the natural colors, and indeed the extremes: from the manifold [interaction] of these with one another...

The Philosophers call their natural fire "fiery," or their "Sun," or **horse vapor** <note>original: "fumum equinum"; this refers to the gentle, moist heat produced by fermenting horse manure, a traditional alchemical method for maintaining steady temperatures</note>. Moreover, the stone is usually placed in a triple clay vessel so that a gentle little flame can be maintained, which is—I say—very similar to the heat of a hen while she hatches her eggs. And from this heat the **dragon**—which is the **earth of gold** <note>original: "terra auri"; the base material or "prima materia" at a specific stage of the work</note>—<term>mortifies: the alchemical process of "killing" the matter, causing it to break down and turn black</term> itself when it gives off its elements and spirits. Conversely, it brings itself back to life when it receives those spirits back into itself. 

For this reason, the process is compared to **Christ**, who voluntarily offered Himself to death for us, and afterwards, through the glory of the resurrection, restored Himself to life by His own power, never to die again. We also say in this place that the dragon spits out from itself all darkness and poison, and afterwards drinks it back in and <term>becomes white: known as the "Albedo" stage, where the matter is purified of its blackness</term>. 

And since we said above that heaven must be joined with earth, this question arises: whether heaven ought to descend to earth, or earth ought to ascend to heaven. It is certain that the earth cannot ascend unless heaven has first descended; however, the earth is said to be **sublimated into heaven** <note>original: "sublimari"; in chemistry, sublimation is when a solid turns directly into vapor, but here it represents the spiritualization of the material</note> when, having been dissolved by its own spirit, it is finally made purer along with it. With this comparison I might satisfy you...

### CHAPTER XV.

We said in the preceding chapter that the Sun and Moon must be joined. We believe you are wise enough to know what the Sun is, and what <term>Phoebe: a poetic name for the Moon</term> herself is. <term>Cynthia: another name for the Moon, referencing her mythological birthplace on Mount Cynthus</term>—that is, the Moon—opens <term>Phoebus: a title for the Sun, meaning "bright" or "radiant"</term>, the Sun. Phoebus, in turn, encloses and <term>coagulates: the process of thickening or solidifying a substance</term> his sister—that is, his Moon. 

Understand this proposition within the very union of the Sun and Moon: **In the shadow of the Sun is the heat of the Moon, and in the heat of the Moon is the coldness of the Sun.** Truly, when the moisture of the Moon receives heat and light from the Sun, the Sun is said to "enter" the Moon. As he enters, the Moon receives an increase and begins to grow warm. The Sun, however, begins to grow cold and moist; because he has taken the water into himself, he loses his heat and dryness, and as a result, being deprived of his light, he grows dark. 

But when the Moon goes into the Sun, the Sun himself begins to come back to life and to shine, because light is restored to him; the Moon, widowed of her splendor, grows thin and is overshadowed. Therefore, I assert that the Sun’s shadow is the coldness and moisture of the Moon, while the Moon’s shadow is the day. Remove, therefore, the shadow from the Sun, and his entire light is dispersed everywhere.

### C H A P T E R  X V I.

It is my pleasure now, son of wisdom, to bring that Philosophical boat to a happy port: come then, pull the oars: expand the sails, give a swift and fertile wind; the port of salvation must be sought. ...from those things which were discussed in their schools, they might release them to the common people. Therefore, he <note>Referring to Pythagoras</note> made his listeners keep silent for a five-year period, so that it was neither permitted to question the teacher about these matters, nor to debate among themselves. Following this custom, the Pythagoreans—as their memory eventually began to fade—started to commit those things which they had learned from the teacher to writing, both concerning the first principles of things and concerning divine matters; they did this in such a way that the secret core <note>original: "medulla," literally the marrow or pith</note> of those matters lay hidden within the mysteries <note>original: "sacramentis"</note> of numbers. 

Evidence that Plato also did this—who concealed his teachings through distant metaphors and mathematical figures—is found in his letter which he wrote to Dionysius regarding the nature of the "first being." "One must write," he says, "through obscurities and riddles <note>original: "per ambages & ænigmata"</note>, so that if by chance the book should happen to be tossed about on sea or land, he who reads it might not understand it." I believe this also gave poets the occasion for storytelling, so that sublime matters would not descend to the ignoble commoners; they hid the sweetest nourishment of Philosophy inside, beneath the outer shell of fables. 

We read that the Egyptians, in order to keep their dogmas in their sanctuaries, concealed them with unknowable letters—that is, with certain figures of animals—as a kind of seal of nature. If I remember correctly, a vulture was depicted. A dragon drawn into a circle and biting its own tail <note>This is the Ouroboros, a classic alchemical symbol of eternity and the cyclical nature of the universe</note> represented the image of the passing year. Do not certain more inquisitive men strive to assign a specific character <note>A symbol or sigil</note> to any given thing, by which...

Thus it happened that those ancient Philosophers judged it best to hand down this divine art <note>The "divine art" refers to alchemy, often called the Ars Sacra or Sacred Art.</note> in more obscure words. The Philosophers say that their **stone** is found everywhere, in mountains and in caverns. From that poorly understood proposition, I am persuaded that all errors flowed down to posterity—those who have worked with sheep's blood, hair, and other vain and foreign things <note>The author is criticizing "puffers" or false alchemists who interpreted metaphorical ingredients literally, using organic waste instead of metallic principles.</note>. 

Understand it thus: just as the celestial **Sun** itself is everywhere in this **Greater World** <note>original: "Mundo maiori," referring to the Macrocosm or the universe at large</note> through its rays, so that earthly Sun—that is, **gold**—is everywhere in the whole **glass** <note>original: "vitro," referring to the alchemical flask or vessel</note>, that is, in the **Lesser World** <note>original: "Mundo minori," the Microcosm, here represented by the controlled environment of the laboratory vessel</note>. 

In the mountains: that is, in the **head of the glass** <note>The upper part or "cap" of the distilling apparatus</note> and the heavens; and in the caverns: that is, in the **bottom of the glass** and the earth. They say the stone is born in two mountains. In the mountain of heaven and the earth—understand this as within the glass. 

Furthermore, they claim that their stone is in all things: that is, in all **metals**, which are their "things." Likewise, the stone is in every thing: that is, **nature** is in every thing; and because nature holds all names within itself, and nature is the whole World. Therefore, the stone has many names, and is said to be in every thing, although it is closer in one thing than in another, since the Philosophers demand only the **generative nature of metals**. That stone heals nature. In the propagation of gold, the heavens have labored most greatly, and likewise the **Sun** itself, and **Jupiter**. ### CHAPTER XIX.

Combine the **masculine value** <note>likely referring to gold, the "noble" or "precious" masculine metal</note> in leaves or filings with **Mercury**, using a ratio of twelve parts [of Mercury] to one of the value. Place it over a slow fire, and continue the heat until **Venus** <term>Venus: the alchemical name for copper, or here, a specific green or iridescent film that rises during the process</term> is seen swimming on top in the dissolving Mercury. Extract this until no "body" <note>solid material</note> remains at the bottom: and you have the first part of the philosophical work. 

The second part of the work concerns the **sulfur**. Place it in a glass without water, and the "water of the body," in which is the **soul of the Moon** <term>anima Lunæ: the "soul" or essence of silver, representing the white stage of the work</term>, by distilling. Join this water to the sulfur, and allow it, through many forces, to sometimes rise and sometimes sink <note>Referring to "circulation," where a liquid is boiled and condensed so it repeatedly washes over the solids at the bottom.</note> with the other, until **Venus** has conceived her water. This happens when it turns a most brilliant white color, and you then possess the **elixir for the white** <term>elixir ad album: a substance capable of transmuting "base" metals into pure silver</term>.

### On another way of operating.

Furthermore, it is pleasing to grasp that divine expertise in short statements and with wonderful skill. Dissolve the body, take the **sulphur** <note>original: "sulphur"; in alchemy, this represents the active, combustible, and "masculine" principle of matter</note>, purify it, sublime the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritum"; the volatile essence of a substance</note>, join the spirit with the sulphur, and you will have the philosophical art. In every perfect alchemical work, however small, it is necessary to have the spirit and the sulphur of gold. The spirit tints with a golden color. The sulphur gives golden weight and also coagulates <note>solidifies the liquid components</note>. If one were lacking, the work would achieve nothing. In the **Venus** <term>Venus: the alchemical name for copper, though here used allegorically to describe a hidden "green" or "base" quality within the gold itself</term> of philosophical gold, they say the whole secret of nature lies hidden, and they speak most truly. For this reason, it is usually called the **rennet** <note>original: "coagulum"; an agent like those used in cheesemaking to turn liquid to solid</note>, when it is said: Take the rennet from the body, and you have the **mastery** <term>magisterium: the completed "Great Work" or the Philosopher's Stone itself</term>, than which there is nothing greater in nature. Likewise, purify the rennet and remove the impediments, and you shall tint <note>the act of transmuting or coloring a base metal into gold</note>. But because an unclean cloth, not unlike sulphur, cannot be purified without water: so the nature of sulphur is not washed without water. To wash is to dissolve, to dissolve is to purify; the water is **Mercury** <term>Mercurius: quicksilver, representing the fluid, "feminine," and transformative principle</term>, he is the key: he alone opens the body and whitens the sulphur; once it is whitened, he [Mercury] departs with the filth. I would say you flourish with singular learning if you are able to remove that filth. It is itself the impediment and eternal death. # THE BOOK ON THE COMPOSITION OF ALCHEMY,
## WHICH MORIENUS the Roman produced for Khalid, King of the Egyptians: which Robert of Chester translated from Arabic into Latin. <note>Khalid ibn Yazid (died c. 704) was an Umayyad prince; though his role as an alchemist is debated by modern historians, he was legendary in the Middle Ages as the first Muslim to take an interest in the art.</note>

### PREFACE BY ROBERT OF CHESTER. <note>Robert of Chester (active c. 1140s) was an English scholar and a crucial figure in the transmission of Arabic science—including algebra and alchemy—to the West. His translation of this text in 1144 is considered the formal birth of alchemy in Latin Europe.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'L' featuring scrolling floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

*We read in the histories of the ancient divines that there were three Philosophers, each of whom was called Hermes. The first of them was Enoch <note>The author is synchronizing biblical history with pagan mythology to provide alchemy with a holy lineage.</note>, who was known by the name Hermes in one place and by the name Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius." In the medieval mind, the Greek god Hermes and the Roman god Mercury were identical with the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> in another. The second was Noah, who was similarly called by the name Hermes and by the name Mercury. The third of them, however, was the Hermes who reigned in Egypt after the flood, and held his kingdom for a long time. This man was called “The Triple”* <term>Triplex</term> <note>original: "Triplex." This is a translation of the Greek "Trismegistus" (Thrice-Greatest). Medieval scholars interpreted this "triple" nature as Hermes being the greatest King, the greatest Philosopher, and the greatest Priest.</note> *by our predecessors, on account of the threefold collection of virtues attributed to him by the Lord God. He was both King and Philo-* <note>The text ends mid-word, intended to be "Philosopher."</note>

<summary>This page introduces the "Book on the Composition of Alchemy," famously translated by Robert of Chester in 1144. The preface establishes a mythical genealogy for alchemy, identifying the legendary Hermes Trismegistus as a successor to the biblical patriarchs Enoch and Noah.</summary>

<keywords>Robert of Chester, Morienus the Roman, Hermes Trismegistus, Khalid ibn Yazid, Enoch, Noah, origins of alchemy, translation history</keywords>

--- Page 694 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction of Hermes Trismegistus (the "Third Hermes") as the legendary founder of all human knowledge. Robert of Chester explains that while he won't detail Hermes' entire life, he credits him as the original author of this alchemical work, which he claims aligns perfectly with Holy Scripture.</meta>

->### P R E F A C E.<-

*[...philoso]*pher, and Prophet. This indeed was the Hermes who, after the flood, was the first inventor and publisher of all arts and disciplines, both the liberal <note>The "liberal arts" (grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy) were the core of medieval education.</note> as well as the mechanical <note>The "mechanical arts" referred to practical, manual trades like metalworking, weaving, and agriculture.</note>. For all those who came after him strove to walk in his path and follow in his footsteps. Why say more? It would be long for us, and even difficult, to recall to memory at present the ornaments of virtue and the deeds of so great and eminent a man. Since we have not undertaken this kind of teaching in the translation of this divine book; nor could the weakness of our talent, or our study, or the labor of writing be sufficient to explain these things to you. 

But we have introduced his name in the Prologue of this book for this reason: because he was the first to discover and publish this book. For this is a divine book, and most full of divinity. In it is contained the true and perfect proof of the two testaments (namely the Old and the New). If anyone, indeed, shall have studied much in this book and understood it fully, the truth of both testaments, as well as the way of life for both, will be sufficiently revealed and cannot remain hidden from him.

<summary>Robert of Chester identifies Hermes Trismegistus as the post-flood father of all arts and the original author of this text. He asserts that the book contains a divine truth that perfectly aligns with and proves the Christian Bible.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, liberal arts, mechanical arts, divine book, Old Testament, New Testament, Robert of Chester, lineage of knowledge</keywords>

--- Page 695 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction where Robert of Chester explains that those who followed the legendary Hermes Trismegistus strove to walk in his footsteps. Having established Hermes' authority, he now introduces the specific text at hand and provides the first definition of alchemy to his Latin-speaking audience.</meta>

->### P R E F A C E.<-

*[...followed]* him. And this is the book, which is named the **Book on the Composition of Alchemy**. And since your Latin-speaking world <note>original: "latinitas." Robert is addressing the scholars of Western Europe who, in the 12th century, had little to no knowledge of alchemical science.</note> does not yet truly know what **Alchemy** is, or what its composition might be, I shall clarify it in the present discourse. I have put forward this word—even though it is unknown and strange—so that it might become clear through a definition. 

Indeed, **Hermes the Philosopher**, and others who lived after him, define this term as it appears in the book *On the Change of Substances*: **Alchemy** is a physical substance composed from one and through one, joining more precious things together through kinship and effect, and naturally transforming them into better natures <note>original: "ingenijs melioribus." This refers to the alchemical goal of perfecting "base" metals into "noble" ones like gold.</note> by the same natural mixing. 

In the following sections, what we have said will be explained, and its composition will be fully treated. But we—although our intellect is young and our mastery of Latin is very modest—have nevertheless undertaken to translate this so great and so significant a work from **Arabic into Latin**. 

Therefore, for the singular grace bestowed upon us by God among the moderns <note>By "moderns," Robert refers to the scholars of his own time (c. 1144 AD) who were rediscovering ancient knowledge through Arabic sources.</note>, we give thanks to that highest living God, who exists as **three and one**. However, my name at the beginning...

<summary>Robert of Chester provides the first formal definition of alchemy for the Latin world, crediting Hermes the Philosopher. He notes his role in translating this fundamental text from Arabic into Latin, framing it as a divine gift.</summary>

6 PREFACE.

->### P R E F A C E.<-

*I did not think it right for the prologue to be kept silent* <note>original: "Prologi taceri non placuit." Robert is emphasizing that the introductory remarks are essential to establish the book's context.</note>, *lest someone else take this work of ours for themselves, and even claim its praise and merit as if it were their own. What more? I humbly ask and beseech everyone that no one among our people wastes away with envy of mind* <note>original: "mentis liuore." In the competitive world of 12th-century scholarship, translators often worried about rivals stealing their work or slandering their reputation.</note> *toward my name (which many are often accustomed to doing). For the God of all knows to whom He bestows His grace; and the Spirit proceeds from grace, which inspires whom He wills. Therefore, we ought to rejoice rightly, since the Creator and Founder of all shows His own particular divinity, as it were, to everyone.*

[...dwell]. <note>The syllable "tet" completes the word *habitaret* from the previous page, referring to where the hermit might reside.</note> I hope, therefore, that the goodness of the divine will not abandon me in the life of this **World**; for the entrance to that place is very narrow, and no one can enter it except through the affliction of the soul. The King then said: "All that you say is undoubtedly true; but because these things come from a faithful soul, they seem false [to me]." The King said this because he was still a worshiper of idols. 

Morienus replied: "If you concede that what I say is true, you must also concede that the soul from which they come is true and speaks the truth. For truth proceeds from truth; falsehood from falsehood; the eternal from the eternal; the transitory from the transitory; good from good; and evil from evil." 

The King then said: "O Morienus, many things have been reported to me concerning you, your constancy, and your faith; wherefore I marvel greatly, now that I see and hear that these things are indeed true. This was the reason why I had long desired to see and hear you so much. For I wish for you to instruct and teach me with certain other **proofs** <term>documentis: in this context, it refers to instructional demonstrations or evidence of his knowledge</term> regarding the matters we are about to discuss." 

Then Morienus said to him: "O King, may almighty God turn you toward better things; for I am not one at whom you should marvel much. I am but one of the **sons of Adam**. <note>original: "filijs Adæ." A common medieval phrase emphasizing the shared, fallen, and mortal nature of all humanity.</note> We all indeed proceeded from one, and again to that one we shall return, albeit by a different path. Truly, the long passage of time confounds and changes man, who is subject to time. Nor do I yet only..."

...[so much] <note>The word "tantum" completes a thought from the previous page, likely referring to the degree of Morienus's spiritual or physical transformation.</note> I have been changed, so that many others who came before me might not be changed more. But a dreadful death follows the final change, which is surely judged to be no worse punishment. Then the King said to him: "O Morienus, from these things you were just saying, I see that you think I wish to mock you. According to this opinion, although you appear old and wise, you are more to be mocked than praised."

After this, the King called me and said to me: "O Khalid <term>Calip: a variation of Khalid, referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, the Umayyad prince who is historically credited with being one of the first patrons of alchemy</term>, good servant, go and seek a house for this man, beautiful both inside and out, and adorned with much ornament, and let it be near the palace. At the same time, seek a man who is a practitioner of his own faith, learned, elderly, and refined in character, by whose words and advice he may be comforted, and his mind may rest in peace. For I see that he is as if terrified, and has very little confidence in me."

I did, therefore, as the King commanded me. The King, indeed, came to him every day and sat with him for several hours. For he spoke with him and comforted him, yet he asked him nothing of his **mastery** <term>magisterio: the Latin term for the alchemical "Great Work" or the secret of the Philosopher's Stone</term>. After, however, great acquaintance and affection grew between them, Morienus placed great trust in the King and confided in him. Then the King began to ask about the **Romans**...

It happened, therefore, while they were talking together one day, that the King said to Morienus: "O wisest of all old men, know that for a long time I have sought the mastery of Hermes <term>magisterium Hermetis: the 'Mastery of Hermes' refers to the Great Work of alchemy, the secret process of transmuting base metals into gold or achieving spiritual enlightenment</term> from many people, but until now I have been able to find no one who could reveal its true nature to me. 

For this reason, on that other occasion when you secretly departed from our borders—after I had read the letters you had written around the vessel in which the 'mastery' had been placed, and had grasped their meaning—I immediately ordered the heads to be cut off <note>original: "iussi capita amputari." The King’s violent reaction to the failed alchemists highlights the high stakes and the historical trope of the 'cruel patron' who executes those who cannot deliver the promised gold.</note> of all those whom I had kept with me for many years for the sake of this science. 

I ask you, therefore, O good and most wise old man, that you explain to me its true logic, as well as its appearance and substance, so that my long-held expectation may be joyfully fulfilled through you. If you indeed do this, you will win both me and everything I possess; and if it pleases you, we shall return together to your own country. For I do not want you to doubt me in any way from now on, nor should you harbor any fear in your mind based on any suspicion."

...for the better. Now, however, I understand well why you sent for me: for you needed me greatly, and for that reason you sent for me. I, for my part, have come to you joyfully, so that I may both teach you this <term>magisterium: 'mastery' or 'the Great Work,' referring to the successful completion of the alchemical process</term> and clearly demonstrate the wondrous power of God. 

As for the fear of which you spoke a little while ago, I am not afraid, nor do I despair of you thus far. For everyone who fears is not perfect in truth. It is especially unfitting for a wise man to fear anything. For if he fears, he will soon despair; and if he despairs, his mind will waver, and he will in no way achieve the effect of his intention. 

And since I now understand that you embrace me with no small love, and I see that you are very strict in character regarding your inquiry, and pious in deed, and patient, it is not right for me to hide or conceal this mastery from you any longer. Now, more easily than all others, you have reached your purpose and the end of your long inquiry. Blessed be the name of the Lord for ages unto ages.

At these words, the King smiled and said: "Now indeed I know that God grants patience to every man. He who acts cruelly is confounded, for haste is from the devil. <note>original: "Festinatio enim ex parte diaboli est." A foundational alchemical principle stating that the natural process of metallic transformation cannot be rushed by human greed.</note> I am the grandson of Machoya <note>Machoya refers to Muawiya I, the founder of the Umayyad Caliphate.</note> and the son of King Gezid <note>Gezid refers to Yazid I. And there is no strength except with the highest God, who alone is most high."

Then Morienus said: "O good King, may God turn you toward better things. Attend now to the judgment of this mastery, and you shall know it well, and understand it.

But remember to study deeply its entrance and its exit; for with the Lord’s favor, you will more easily attain everything pertaining to it.

For this thing, which you have sought for so long, is not received or accomplished through force or anger. Instead, it is received through patience, humility, and a certain and most perfect love. For God bestows this divine and pure knowledge upon His faithful servants: specifically those to whom He has disposed to grant it from the primeval nature of things by His wonderful power. And when it has been bestowed upon any of His faithful, it is fitting for that person to first foresee to whom he might later entrust and reveal it. For this thing is nothing but a gift from God Most High, who entrusts and shows it to whichever of His servants and faithful He wishes, just as He wills. Therefore, it is fitting to be humble and entirely subject to Almighty God in all things.

Then the King said: "Indeed, we truly know and recognize that there is no perfection in things without the help of the Divine and its demonstration. For He Himself is the Most High and the Unchangeable."

Afterward, the King adjured me <note>The narrator here is Galip, the King's servant and scribe, recording the encounter.</note> and said: "O Galip, good servant, sit quickly, and with your pen commit to memory <note>In this context, to 'commit to memory' means to record the words in writing so they are preserved for the future.</note> all the things about which we shall now confer."

For this is the knowledge which draws its master away from the misery of this world, and leads him back to the knowledge of future goods. In past times, they always inherited this wisdom in turn among themselves; but afterward, this knowledge was almost held in contempt. But many books of the ancient masters remained, in which that knowledge is contained entirely true and without falsehood; yet no one was found who could clearly bring it to fruition then, because of the many and diverse names which had long ago been imposed upon the things pertaining to it by the elder sages. <margin>The Matter</margin>

KING KHALID <note>Khalid ibn Yazid (d. c. 704), an Umayyad prince who, according to legend, was the first Arab to take a serious interest in alchemy.</note>: O Morienus, it first pleases me to ask what and of what kind is the principal substance and matter of this sort of thing <note>referring to the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note>; and whether they are many or several, or if it is composed of only one alone.

MORIENUS: Every matter is proven more true by the testimony of many, until such time as it is distinguished by its own effect. But before I bring the older testimonies to you at present, I will explain this indeed which we have often proven concerning its principal substance and matter. If you look rightly upon those things I shall say to you and the testimonies of the ancients, you will clearly recognize that we all agree in one point, and that all things we say are true. Therefore, accept what you have asked in this way: The first and principal substance and matter of this thing is one, and from it is one, and with it it is made, nor is anything added to it or taken away. Behold, you now have what you asked. Now indeed I shall bring to you the testimonies of the ancients, so that we may all be judged to agree as one. Hercules <note>In alchemical literature, "Hercules" often refers to a wise philosopher-king or a symbolic figure, rather than the Greek hero of myth.</note> indeed, a certain wise King and Philosopher, when he was asked by some of his people, said: "This mastery <term>Mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the technical process of producing the Philosopher's Stone.</note> indeed proceeds first from one root..."

<summary>King Khalid asks Morienus whether the Alchemical Work requires many ingredients or just one. Morienus responds that the primary matter is entirely singular and self-contained, citing the ancient "King Hercules" as a witness to this truth.</summary>

The philosopher Arsicanus <note>Arsicanus is a name frequently appearing in medieval alchemical texts, often thought to be a corruption of a Greek name like Archigenus or Anaxagoras.</note> also says: the four elements—that is, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—proceed from one source, and some of them are made from others of those same things. Likewise, Arsicanus says to Maria <note>Maria the Jewess, or Mary the Prophetess, a legendary early alchemical figure credited with inventing the bain-marie (water bath).</note>: "Our water," he says, "holds mastery over our earth, which is great, bright, and pure. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of the Hermetic tradition and alchemy.</note> also says: Earth is the mother of the elements; from the earth they proceed, and to the earth they return. Hermes says again: Just as all things proceed from one, so my mastery <term>magisterium: the Great Work or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> is made from one substance and matter. And as the four elements are contained in the human body, so God created them positioned and distinct, yet joined; collected also and diffused throughout the whole body. Because one body merges them and retains them as one, and yet each one of them performs a work unlike the work of another. And although they are in one body, they nevertheless have different colors and different dominions. In the same way, therefore, it must be understood concerning this mastery. ...of which things we will speak. King Calid: How, and by what reasoning is it possible, that there is but one root, one substance, and one matter for this mastery <term>magisterium: the Great Work or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>, when among the Philosophers so many and varied names for this root are found? 

Morienus: Indeed, the names of this root are many, but if you examine the things said above in the correct order, you will find its single root, substance, and matter. So that you may understand this more easily, I will recount for you yet more testimonies of the ancients. 

King Calid: Complete the telling of the mastery of this work for me. 

Morienus: A certain Hercules <note>likely referring to a legendary alchemical authority rather than the hero of Greek myth</note> said to some of his disciples: "The stone of a date <note>original: "lapillus dactili"</note> is nourished by the palm tree, and the palm by its own stone; and from its root many branches grow together, which multiply and increase their number because of it." 

Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> also says: "Look upon the perfect Red <note>original: "Rubeum completum"</note>, and the Red diminished of its redness, and all redness. Consider also the perfect Yellow <note>original: "citrinum completum"</note>, and the Yellow diminished of its yellowness, and all yellowness; and also the perfect Black <note>original: "nigrum completum"</note>, and the Black diminished of its blackness, and all blackness." <note>These colors refer to the stages of the alchemical process: Rubedo (reddening), Citrinitas (yellowing), and Nigredo (blackening).</note> 

Similarly, the ear of corn proceeds from the grain, and many branches come out of one tree, even though the tree takes its origin from its own seed. A certain wise man, who had left the whole world for God's sake, brings a similar example to us. For he says: "The first creation of man is..."

...you will be able to find what you have sought. Likewise, I advise you to observe thoroughly those things which were spoken of above.

**King Calid:** O Morienus, now declare to me the quality of this arrangement <note>original: "dispositionis" — refers to the specific setup or procedure of the alchemical work</note>. For God will now be in our help.

**Morienus:** I shall tell it to you as it has been handed down to me by the ancients: for you ask well. In the direction, therefore, of this composition, you must observe these parts of the arrangement, reasonably established in their own order, and by no means omit them.

The first of them is **union** <note>original: "coitus" — in alchemy, this refers to the "Chemical Wedding," the joining of opposing principles like sulfur and mercury</note>: the second is **conception**: the third, **pregnancy**: the fourth, **birth**: the fifth, **nutrition**.

If, therefore, there is no union, there will be no conception: and if there is no conception, there will be no pregnancy: and if there is no pregnancy, birth will in no way follow. For this is the direction of this arrangement, which is likened to the creation of man.

For the Almighty, highest Creator, the Great—whose name be forever blessed—created man, not from constitutive parts like a house, which consists of its constitutive parts: for there is no [pre-existing] thing that establishes the being of man. A house, however, consists of its constitutive parts: such as the wall, the roof, and the foundation. For these are the parts of a house, and they are called **contrived things** <note>original: "res inventæ" — literally "found things," here meaning artificial objects constructed by human craft rather than divine nature</note>.

But man does not consist in this way: because he is a **creature** <note>original: "creatura" — something brought into being by God from nothing, rather than assembled from parts</note>. For when the essence of man is changed, he is seen to pass from one thing to a better thing: and thus man always persists in creation, which is seen to differ greatly from contrived things: and thus

# ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

...proceeds from day to day, and from month to month, until the highest, great Creator completes His creation, namely at a certain time and on defined days. Because even though the four elements were previously in the seed <note>original: "spermate" — used here in the biological sense of the starting point of life</note>, God the Creator nevertheless set a defined time for it, in which it is to be completed: and when that time is finished, the creature itself is established. Such is the strength and wisdom of God the Most High. 

It is also fitting for you to know, O good King, that this <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium" — the alchemical "Great Work" or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> is nothing other than the hidden mystery and secret of secrets of God the Most High and Great. For He Himself entrusted this secret to His Prophets, whose souls He has placed in His Paradise. If, however, the wise men who came after them had not discovered their own explanations regarding the quality of the vessel in which it is prepared, they would never have reached the perfection of this mastery. Therefore, commit these things to your memory. 

For I showed above that this mastery is not far distant from the creation of man; now I also tell you that nothing was ever animated, or created by birth, nor growing, except after <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putredinem" — the "nigredo" or blackening stage, where the matter decomposes before it can be reborn</note> and its transformation. Whence the wise man says that the entire strength of this mastery exists only after putrefaction. ...adhering, and the **tincture** <term>tincture: an elixir or substance capable of transforming and "dyeing" base metals into noble ones</term> will then work more effectively within it. If all these things have been handled well, the tincture will operate well within it, and its gold will emerge most pure and red—so pure, in fact, that you could find none better or more pure. For if the alchemical medicine is ever completed, let one part of it be placed among nine parts of silver, for the whole will be converted into the purest gold. Therefore, blessed be God, Amen, for all ages.

Having offered all the service possible for me to give, venerable Doctor and honored lord. Therefore, venerable Doctor, let us now visit one another through such replies and little books, since we are unable to be joined in physical presence. ### BERNARD OF TREVISAN
->60<-

...[if it] has been outside of **natural digestion** <term>digestio: a process of slow, internal maturation through heat, analogous to biological digestion</term>, it will not effect nor generate a heat like a fever within the mineral species. It will inappropriately attempt to make hot from cold and active from passive; hence the error will be incurable and the work will be in vain. 

For example: fools <note>original: "fatui"</note> produce and extract **corrosive waters** <note>These are mineral acids, such as nitric acid or sulfuric acid, which were newly discovered in the medieval period.</note> from lesser minerals, into which they throw various species of metals and corrode them. For they believe that because of this, the metals have been dissolved by a **natural solution** <term>solutione naturali: a dissolution where the solvent and solute merge into a new, living substance, rather than the solvent simply eating away at the solid</term>. Yet such a solution requires the simultaneous permanence of both the solvent and the solute, so that from both—namely, the **masculine and feminine seed** <note>Alchemists often described the "Great Work" as a marriage; the masculine seed (Sulfur) and feminine seed (Mercury) must combine to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note>—a new species may result.

...dwells proportionally in the air, and therefore it dissolves the air itself. But this liquefaction is not a **true dissolution**; rather, it is dissipative <note>Meaning it causes the substance to scatter or lose its integrity rather than transforming it into something new.</note>. This is because the elements within it are homogeneous, mixed in a fixed proportion through digestion, and one is generally drawn out from the potential of another by the remainder. 

And so this occurs in **pure bodies** <note>In alchemy, "pure" or "clean" bodies usually refer to refined metals like gold or silver.</note> in which the elemental natures are fixed. For this reason, in these bodies, the flame of fire causes liquefaction and dissolves the entire compound into a **flow** <note>original: "ad fluxum"; this refers to melting into a liquid state like molten metal</note> but not into a separation. This is because fire cannot flow unless its substantial air also flows; nor does air flow unless water is dissolved; nor does water flow unless the earth also flows. 

And conversely, just as earth is dissolved by water, so vice versa, water retains and congeals the air; and in the same way, ascending upwards, air retains fire in **congealment** <note>The process of a liquid becoming solid, or a gas becoming more "fixed."</note>. This happens because the more fixed and **fixing** elements <term>fixing: the ability of a substance to resist the heat of fire without evaporating or changing</term> acting together—namely earth and water—bring about fixation; conversely, fire and air act together toward dissolution. 

But this process is called the **liquefaction of the compound** and not properly its solution, because the parts are not dissolved from one another so as to be separable in the generation of the compound. This is unlike what happens in the **third and true Philosophical solution**, when the compound is dissolved in the aforementioned way, yet the parts remain unseparated—though they are separable—so that the virtue of the most highly digested...

<meta>This page continues the argument of Bernard of Treviso regarding the internal composition of metals. On the previous page, he established that gold is essentially "matured mercury" perfected by natural heat. Here, he distinguishes between the "external heat" applied by the alchemist and the "internal heat" (the active elements of fire and air) already present within mercury itself, arguing that nothing foreign is actually added to the metal's substance during its transformation.</meta>

<page-num>67</page-num>
<header>ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS</header>

In the art <note>The "art" here refers to alchemy, specifically the "Great Work" performed by the practitioner above ground, as opposed to the natural processes occurring within the earth.</note> practiced above ground, an external addition is found to aid the digestion of **Mercury** and its thickening into the golden state or the form of metals. For this reason, the **Philosophers** <note>Alchemical authors often referred to themselves and their predecessors simply as "The Philosophers."</note> said that **sulfur** and **Mercury** create the **Sun** <note>original: "Solem"; in alchemical shorthand, the Sun always represents gold.</note>, that is, *corporeality and permanence.* And therefore, one does not conclude from this that the external artificial heat—which excites and assists the proportional internal heat to digest and ripen the remaining two elements that are less digested and immature within Mercury (namely **water and earth**)—is part of the substance of the compound. For external heat is not permanent within the quantity or weight of the thing, nor does it add anything to them.

*Internal heat, however, which is proportional and natural, is simple and permanent with the quantity and weight of the Mercury digested by it: because that heat is an intrinsic and essential part* of the Mercury itself, namely the two more active elements within it, such as *air and fire*. Therefore, fools poorly and absurdly understand that Philosophical saying, that **sulfur** and **mercury** generate the **Sun** <note>gold</note>: because (as is well enough known) just as air—neither in the first mercurial composition nor afterward in natural metallic digestion—departs or is separated from water and earth: so neither does **sulfur** (which is the same as <term>air and fire</term> <note>Treviso identifies sulfur not as a separate ingredient, but as the active, fiery principle already present within mercury.</note>) depart nor is it separated from **Mercury**, which is the same as *water and earth*. He who thinks otherwise, or asserts the contrary, is not a Philosopher.

BERNARD TREVISAN

<margin>/</margin>Therefore, the masculine seed, or **our sulfur** <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle, while "mercury" represents the passive, fluid, and feminine principle.</note>, does not return after the coagulation of Mercury, as some falsely assert. Some think this occurs primarily by the power of the **Sun** <note>original: "Solis"</note>, and that the form of gold is perfected chiefly by its heat in subterranean places. Nay, it is rather by the power of the motion of the globe and its orbit, and the universal motion of the entire heaven. This is *because solar rays only warm the surface of the earth and not its deep interior* reaches, in which the generation of mineral species occurs. The influence of the heaven does not reach those lowest places through rays, although the subterranean movement of the elements proceeds primarily *from the movement of the heaven, and not from the rays* of its light, nor from their heat, or any other influence besides *motion*. How this occurs, however, and what the cause of such subterranean motion might be, I think does not escape your Reverence's notice; therefore, I shall now desist from further explanation.

<margin>/</margin>*The Sun, therefore, is not the primary cause of gold, or of its form*, although there is a similarity of names between them. *Because just as the Sun is hotter than the other planets, gold is hotter than the other metals*, and they share a similar difference of properties. The other metals have also received names similar to the planets, from which arises the **error of fools** <note>original: "error stultorum"; a common alchemical phrase used to dismiss those who take metaphorical or astrological correspondences too literally.</note>. For they believe that each of the seven planets, both generally and specifically through its own influence, generates one metallic species, which it matches by a certain property and resembles in nature.

In subterranean places and among plants <note>original: "vegetabilibus"</note>, however, it happens in a different way, where the heaven or the **Sun** is the cause of their generation and growth not only because of its movement, but indeed also by reason of the heat of its rays. For the **Sun** warms the plants themselves and the surface of the earth; that is to say, the **elements** are reflected more intensely as far as the very surface of the earth by its rays, because those rays are able to reach that far. 

For example: from the twelfth heaven <note>The outermost sphere in medieval cosmology, often identified as the Primum Mobile or the Empyrean, representing the highest point of the universe.</note>, which contains the highest degree of height, proceeding downward, spheres that are always denser or "less subtle" <note>In alchemical philosophy, "subtle" refers to matter that is refined, thin, or spirit-like, while "dense" refers to heavy, physical matter.</note> follow one another until the hollow of the sphere of the **Moon**. It is here that things capable of local change exist; or rather, it is where the elements—mixed under the hemisphere of things that can be generated and corrupted <note>A reference to the "sublunary" world, where all physical things are subject to birth, decay, and transformation, unlike the eternal stars.</note>—begin and end. 

Therefore, in that same place, a more subtle and simpler **fire** <note>original: "ignis"</note> is found, though it is not entirely pure. For simply pure fire can in no way be found separately among changeable species, just as none of the other elements can; although in any composite body, simple fire is found mixed with other simple elements. If it were otherwise, there would not be several elements, but only one. 

Therefore, the rays of the stars of heaven, and most especially of the **Sun**, pass through these aforementioned regions without being refracted <note>Passing through without bending or losing strength.</note> until, descending further downward, they are reflected in the fire because of its density. Then, descending further through the sphere of fire, [carrying] the fire itself into the air...

...it is, just as water is very easily joined to another water identically and quickly through a union of mixing without resistance. And even if they were part of the mixture, they are still not part of its "proportion" <note>In alchemy, "proportion" refers to the specific, balanced ratio of ingredients that defines a substance's identity; anything outside this ratio is considered "extra" or "superfluous."</note>: for whatever belongs to the proportion of a thing is never superfluous.

Since such drosses are combustible when subjected to the test of fire <note>The "examen ignis" or assay by fire, which burns away impurities to reveal pure metal.</note>, they are therefore separable. What wonder is it then if they hinder the natural mixing and permanent unity of those metals which they have accidentally contaminated, whether with congealed Mercury or with other raw Mercury? <header>BERNAR. TREV.</header>

<margin>NB.</margin>
...for this reason, gold itself—however [pure] it may be—remains far more difficult to join and cannot adhere as easily to impure or drossy <note>original: "scorioso"; containing slag or waste impurities from the smelting process.</note> Mercury, whether it is coagulated or not, as it can with that which is pure and clean. This is because a simple nature will rejoice and be perfected by adhering to another simple nature that is similar and identical to itself in its homogeneity and elemental proportion. For as has been said, gold is nothing other than Mercury thickened <note>original: "inspissatus"; thickened or made dense through heat and time.</note> by its own proper digestion and elemental action. Therefore, although in the earth there is a difference in maturity between gold and Mercury (because gold is more mature than Mercury), there is nonetheless no diversity in their underlying matter. 

Consequently, whatever gold has acquired through the ripening of its digestion, that same Mercury can also acquire for itself without any foreign substance being added to it. Art <note>The "Art" refers to the practice of alchemy.</note>, however, in order to shorten and condense the labor, joins gold to Mercury, as has been stated. Through artifice, it produces and generates from these two seeds <term>spermatibus: the "seeds" or essential germinating principles of metals in alchemical theory</term> that very same thing which Nature, in the mineral realm, created from a single seed in actuality. Throughout this process, the identity of the matter is always preserved everywhere, though not the potential of Art alone.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion from page 85 regarding the internal composition of gold and the Philosopher's Stone. The author is elaborating on the concept of "anatization," a specific alchemical state of elemental balance where the qualities of the four elements are perfectly harmonized even if their physical weights are not.</meta>

# BERNARD OF TREVISO

Since it is an anatized <term>anatized: from 'anatizatis,' referring to a state where the four elements are so perfectly blended and balanced that they form a single, inseparable substance.</term> work of nature, all four elements—both the active and the passive—are present in actuality and remain in an unequal proportion. For "goldness" <note>original: "aureitas"; the essential, shimmering quality or "spirit" that makes gold what it is.</note> is nothing other than the four elements anatized. This is not to say, however, that the form and matter are called anatized, but rather the potency and the act. 

That is to say: they are not anatized and equalized in **quantity**, but in **quality**. This is because the active element does not exceed the passive in its acting, nor on the other hand does the passive element exceed the active by being "overpowered" <note>original: "plus patiendo"; literally "suffering more," referring to the passive element's capacity to be acted upon by the active ones.</note> in its endurance. Because there is an equal proportion of measures in gold (or in our medicine), there is a double measure of heat, a double measure of moisture, a double measure of cold, and a double measure of dryness. All are present in the reality of action and passion—namely fire, air, water, and earth—as has already been stated. 

However, all these are said to be anatized and equalized in **quality** and not in **quantity**, because they are equally active and passive, and therefore they remain durably within the gold. In gold, the passive component permanently resides within the active; and conversely, the passive does not rebel against the active. 

Nor is it necessary for them to be anatized in quantity—that is, that there be just as much of the "matter" of fire as there is of the "matter" of earth. For if that were the case, the fire (due to its intense quality) would have an activity far greater than the passive earth everywhere, rather than being equalized with it. Therefore, in gold, there is much more of the heavier and more passive element—meaning in terms of its physical matter, not its quality—than there is of the lighter and more active element. That is to say: in terms of **quantity**, the quantity of earth in gold is greater than the quantity of water; and

<summary>Bernard explains that gold's stability comes from a "quality" balance (anatization) of the four elements, where their active and passive forces are equalized even though their physical quantities (weights) differ. He argues that if the physical quantity of fire equaled that of earth, the fire would destroy the balance due to its superior intensity.</summary>

For from the Elixir, **azoc** is drawn and extracted, just like oil is from water, and not vice versa; as is mentioned elsewhere.

For example, take the medical art: pure spring water, through a simple first boiling <note>original: "elixationem"; the Latin word for boiling or decoction, which shares a linguistic root with "Elixir."</note>, is joined with the flesh of a chicken. From this first stage of boiling, a perfect and good juice and broth <note>original: "ius & decoctum"</note> emerges; this occurs by dissolving the moist, watery, and airy parts of the chicken into the water, even though other elements are also present in action.

However, to create a much more perfect medicine, one more potent for restoring health to a sick human body, the chicken meat (already boiled and altered into broth) is crushed, and then distilled by a stronger boiling. This produces a much more noble and powerful broth that participates in the nature of the entire chicken.

In this second boiling, not only are the moist parts of the chicken dissolved, but also the hot parts: that is, the airy and fiery elements are mixed and dissolved into the broth itself. Therefore, the entire virtue <note>original: "virtus"; the inner power or essence of a substance.</note> of the chicken is extracted into that liquid by such a boiling.

**Similarly, this occurs in the Philosophical work <note>original: "opere Philosophico"; a common term for the Great Work of Alchemy.</note>, because the crude mineral spirit, acting like water, is joined with its own body, dissolving it through a first boiling: from which**

It is named **Rebis** <term>Rebis</term> <note>original: "Rebis"; a name derived from the Latin "res bina," meaning "a double thing." That is to say, it comes from the act of dissolving, even though the substance and matter are ultimately one. Hence the verse:

> *The Rebis is a twofold thing joined, yet it remains one,*
> *It is dissolved so that the first parts appear: either the Sun or the Moon’s seed.*
> <note>original: "Sol aut spermata Lunae"; in alchemical symbolism, the "Sun" (Sol) represents Gold or the masculine principle, and the "Moon" (Luna) represents Silver or the feminine principle.</note>

> *Elixir in Greek is called the second part of the art,*
> *For from the liquids themselves, purified bodies are fashioned.*
> <note>The author provides a folk etymology here, attempting to link "Elixir" to the Greek word for "part" and the Latin "lix," meaning liquid or lye.</note>

This is done through a stronger and repeated distillation. This azoc reflects and shares in the nature of the body from which it was drawn (which is hot), and it retains that body’s power within itself. It possesses an oily nature that is hot and moist, for it is effectively fire and air in action, even though all the elements are present in its essential composition.

Therefore, from these metals, various medicines can be composed through different techniques to cure the diseases of living creatures. However, these are irrelevant to the Work of the Philosophers. This is true even though they are of higher natures relative to one another according to their degrees—just as the soul is higher than the crude spirit, since...

It happens that writers have sometimes erred and treated the truth of nature poorly or ambiguously. Then, through **revivification** <term>revivification</term> <note>The process of restoring a chemically altered metal back to its original metallic state.</note>, it becomes hot and moist, similar to the human **temperament** <note>original: "complexioni"; referring to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) in the human body.</note>. "What wonder will it be then," you might ask, "if it is joined with the **Sun** <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" (Sol) is the standard symbol for Gold.</note>, so that it surely takes on the nature of the **Sun**?" For Mercury is of a changeable nature, just like the celestial Mercury <note>The planet Mercury was traditionally viewed in astrology as "neutral," taking on the qualities of whatever planet it was positioned near.</note>, which is of such a character as the planet with which it is joined in the heavens. For that Arnald, although he was a revered Doctor and ingenious in other sciences, perhaps in this art he handled experiments without the **doctrine of causes** <note>The theoretical framework or "why" behind the physical "how."</note>. Regarding the fact that in the first purification, he says the crude spirit is sublimated from minor salty minerals, and that Mercury itself (which is cold and moist by nature) is made into a powder that is hot and dry in nature (as he says), this nevertheless benefits our **Philosophical work** not at all. Let it be so, indeed, that he makes such a powder from Mercury as he says—namely, dried and heated through sublimation from salty substances. Yet those purifications are vain and irrelevant—indeed, harmful to the completion of our work. For even if minor minerals share a nature with metals, they do not share the same species and proportion.

I wish this to be said in reverence and honor of the aforementioned **Arnald** <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>; however, it is the truth of nature and of experience that I contemplate and defend.

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK
## THE LADDER OF THE PHILOSOPHERS
### so called.

As the venerable Ramon Llull <note>original: "Raymūdus Lulij"; a 13th-century Majorcan polymath to whom many influential alchemical texts were attributed.</note> says: The intention of nature for performing our Great Work <term>Great Work</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the systematic process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is that the Stone <term>Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapis"; the elusive substance capable of transmuting metals and perfecting life.</note> is to be divided into the four elements, so that each one by itself, according to the requirements of nature, can be purified. And that is the preparation of things which precedes the operation of perfect preparation, and it is properly called the Separation of the Elements <term>Separation of the Elements</term> <note>original: "Separatio elementorum"; the stage where the raw matter is broken down into its constituent parts—Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.</note>, since it divides all the impure parts from the pure parts, so that with the lighter and purer parts our perfect preparation may successively take place through a natural union. 

This union is achieved by the bringing together of the moist with the dry—prepared immediately and directly through the benefit of the separation of the elements. Otherwise, the moist would not "love" the dry, nor would the body love the spirit, if they were not first well washed of their infections by means of distillations <term>distillation</term> <note>Purifying a liquid by heating it into vapor and condensing it back into liquid.</note>, and calcinations <term>calcination</term> <note>Reducing a solid to a fine powder through high heat.</note>, solutions <term>solution</term> <note>Dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note>, and coagulations <term>coagulation</term> <note>Turning a liquid or dissolved substance back into a solid.</note>. 

For through the separation of the elements, the "falseness" of its burning sulfurous nature <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphureitas"; in alchemy, sulfur often represents the active, combustible principle, but "burning sulfur" here refers to impurities that must be removed.</note> is burned away, which came to it through the original stain of our "menstrual blood" <term>menstruum</term> <note>original: "menstrualis"; a term used here metaphorically to describe the "corrupt" or "unrefined" state of the initial matter, comparing it to the biological cycle of generation.</note>, which is the corruption of our stone. Therefore, the "earth of the bodies" is calcined after the extraction of the "air," so that it may be perfectly purified from false sulfurous qualities and combustions. Therefore...

->### PHILOSOPHY<-

In the third month, **Mars** works by acting upon the matter with its heat and dryness, dividing and separating that mass, and arranging the limbs. <note>Mars represents the energetic separation of the "pure" from the "impure" in the alchemical vessel.</note>

In the fourth month, the **Sun** <note>original: *Sol*</note> works, which nourishes the spirits, and the offspring begins to live.

In the fifth month, **Mercury** works, who creates the openings and the breathing passages.

In the sixth month, **Venus** works: for she arranges and orders the eyes, the eyebrows, and the testicles.

In the seventh month, the **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*</note> works with her coldness and humidity; she labors to expel the infant, and if it is born then, it can live; but if it is not born, it is weakened.

And in the eighth month, **Saturn** works again by constricting; the fetus is formed in the <term>womb</term> <note>original: *matrice*; in alchemy, the "matrix" refers to the flask or vessel where the transformation occurs.</note>, and if it were born then, it could not live. <note>Saturn, associated with lead and coldness, represents a period of contraction or stabilization that is dangerous if interrupted too early.</note>

But in the ninth month, **Jupiter** again nourishes with heat and humidity, restoring strength to the fetus, and thus it is born completely and lives well.

Therefore, it must be known that for three months, **water** preserves the fetus in the womb. **Air** also fosters it for three months; and **fire** guards it for just as many. <note>These 3x3 months complete the nine-month cycle of the Great Work.</note> When these are completed, the blood of that which is fostered in the <term>umbilical cord</term> <note>original: *vmbilico*</note>—once it is cut—goes out to the breasts, and there it assumes the **whiteness of snow**. <note>This "whiteness of snow" refers to the *Albedo*, the stage of the work where the matter is purified and turned white.</note> Therefore, the way out will never open for the infant until the breath of air draws it out.

Then, however, the exit is opened, as is its mouth, and it is nursed. From these three <note>likely referring to the three elements—Water, Air, and Fire—previously mentioned</note>, it is necessary for us to understand and, with sharp intellect, know how to compose and extract.

<margin>*two: for from two, a third is not extracted <unclear>a third</unclear>, well in reverse.</margin> Therefore, let all those who desire to know sharpen their wits to acquire the [fu]ture treasure from three words, in [which] the stone is hidden, in which is also hid[den humi]dity and dryness, the <term>tincture</term> <note>A "tincture" in alchemy is a substance capable of deeply penetrating and changing the color and nature of another substance, usually turning base metals into gold.</note> and the depth of the [tin]ctures, and the hot oil, and the conjunctive hu[midity].

It must be known that there are four prin[ciples] of the governance of our stone: namely, to dissolve, to [wa]sh, to conjoin, and to fix.

**To dissolve** is to divide the bodies and to create the ma[tter].

**To wash** <note>original: *abluere*; also known as "ablution" or purification.</note> is to bury <note>original: *inhumare*; this refers to "inhumation," placing the vessel in a warm bed of dung or ashes to maintain a steady, gentle heat.</note>, to distill, to asce[nd] and to descend. **To conjoin** is to impre[gnate], to whiten, and to redden. **To fix**, however, is to fer[men]t and to betroth. <note>original: *desponfare*; alchemical "betrothal" or "marriage" refers to the chemical union of the "male" (sulfur/sun) and "female" (mercury/moon) principles.</note> **Solution** converts the sto[ne] into its first matter: that is, its wa[ter]; **ablution** into air, **conjunction** into fire, and **fix[ation into]** spiritual and dyeing earth. Whence [Ari]stotle <note>Alchemical texts frequently attributed sayings to Aristotle to gain authority, though many are apocryphal.</note> says: "When you have water from air, [ai]r from fire, and fire from earth: then you will ha[ve] the full art." Because the four elements [are] then well and perfectly prepared, and eve[ry] master of the work and of the fire performs well in o[ne] vessel, in four stages, namely four c[ertain] kinds of conversion, as will be said be[low].

Fire, according to Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and famous authority in medieval alchemy.</note>, is dissolved [so that] it may be converted into **Mercury**, and be divided into the four ele[men]ts, so that it may ha[ve] its first origin.

Then a mixture is formed which fire cannot separate or overcome, even if it acted upon it continuously for a thousand years; for they are mixed so thoroughly in their smallest parts <term>per minima: a philosophical term meaning mixed at the most fundamental, microscopic level</term> that by no ingenuity, once they have thus begun to [join...]

# THE LADDER

...[con]taining within itself qualities in act or in potency <note>original: "actu vel potentia"; Aristotelian terms referring to something being currently manifest (act) or having the hidden capacity to become so (potency)</note>. 
Wherefore **Avicenna** <note>original: "Auicenna"; the Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational to European alchemy</note> says: The posterior quality draws its entity from the quality which is its prior. 
The **Solution of the Stone** <note>original: "Solutio lapidis"; the process of dissolving the "philosopher's stone" or its base materials into a liquid state</note>, however, is its reduction into the mineral water from which it was composed by the operation of nature; indeed, this stone does not bear fruit until it is reduced to nothing, like running water. Since it is fitting that the reduction happens by dissolving the stone, it is easier and more appropriate for it to be reduced to a state of **neutrality** <note>original: "neutralitatem"; a state of chemical or symbolic balance where the material is stripped of its previous specific form</note>, and afterward to its first watery nature, or otherwise finally reduced to some other **subtlety** <note>original: "subtilitatē"; referring to the refinement or thinning of a substance into a more spiritual or volatile form</note>. 

And what can be done by fewer means is done in vain by more. Wherefore the **Philosopher** <note>original: "Philosophus"; likely referring to Aristotle or a high alchemical authority</note> says: If you are able to complete the work from **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"</note> alone, you will be the investigator of a most precious work. And you should know that that thing is not foreign into which it has to convert itself through the **natural mastery** <note>original: "naturale magisterium"; the expert process of mimicking or perfecting nature’s own methods</note>, just as is evident with frozen ice, which when it is resolved, is turned into water: it is clear, therefore, that it was water before. Wherefore he says: Unless everything is turned into water, there is no way to reach **perfection**. 

Hence **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermes"; Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note>: Nature is not amended except in its own nature, the amendment of which nature is done by the ingenuity of art, and art in nature does not correct what nature cannot. Nature must therefore be aided by art in that which was omitted by nature. For that which nature only manages to perfect below in the span of thousands of years, we, by the industry of the highest art in a lesser span than a single year, have...

<summary>This page explains the alchemical stage of Solution, arguing that materials must be returned to their "watery" or neutral state to be perfected. It emphasizes that alchemical "Art" (human skill) can accelerate natural processes, achieving in a year what nature takes millennia to complete.</summary>
