### PHILOSOPHY

...than to perfect what is perfect, and thus nature is helped by ingenuity, and ingenuity by art.

For **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristoteles"; although many alchemical texts were falsely attributed to him, the author here uses him as the ultimate authority on natural law</note> says: Unless I saw gold and silver with my own eyes, I would say for certain that Alchemy was not true; unless I saw the perfection of nature's work through speculative observation <note>original: "speculatiuè"; meaning to observe the underlying principles of nature's own processes</note>, I would not consider Alchemy to be true.

It must be known that there are many ways of solution, yet of all these only one solution is necessary for us, which only takes place—as I have said—from itself with itself, etc.; it is raw, clear, and without violence.

Wherefore the **Philosopher** says: A solution is better when it is raw rather than cooked, dewy rather than dry, voluntary rather than violent, tempered rather than hasty, fragrant <note>original: "flagra"; likely a variation of "fragrans," contrasting with "fœtida" (stinking)</note> rather than foul-smelling, clear rather than thick, and black rather than red.

<margin>Note Well</margin>
And therefore, in every solution, one must be deeply cautious against the **vitrification** <term>vitrification: the accidental turning of the alchemical matter into an inert, glass-like substance, which was considered a failure in the process</term> of the matter along with the odors and tastes of imperfect bodies, and also lest the generative power of that form be smothered in any way by burning corrosives. Therefore, assist the solution by means of the **Moon** <note>original: "Lunam"; symbolically representing Silver and the feminine, cooling, or moist principle</note>, and the coagulation by means of the **Sun** <note>original: "Solem"; symbolically representing Gold and the masculine, heating, or drying principle</note>. The **digestion** <term>digestion: a stage of the work involving gentle, continuous heat, similar to a stomach digesting food</term> of this solution is very necessary for us.

<margin>Note Well</margin>
And our "digestion" is defined as the thinning of moisture, a destructive ripening, the loosening of things connected, the awakening of disposition, and the enablement of separation, which can be done in various ways, as will be discussed later.

But as **Avicenna** says: To dissolve the body and to congeal the spirits is our first work <note>original: "Soluere corpus, & congelare spiritus, est opus nostrum primum"</note>.

# THE LADDER

...because the body is not dissolved unless the spirit is congealed. Nor is the spirit congealed, except through the dissolution of the body. For if they are joined together, each acts upon the other, just as water acts upon the earth mixed with it: therefore, you should refine <term>subtilietis: to "subtle" or refine a substance, reducing it to its most pure, volatile, or spiritual state</term> it in its own manner.

For the earth is not refined unless the water is thickened <note>original: "inspissetur"; meaning to make dense or concentrated</note>, nor is the water thickened unless the earth is refined. Thus, between the congealing <term>congelationem: the process of turning a liquid or "spirit" into a solid or "fixed" state</term> of the spirit and the dissolution of the body, there is no difference in time, nor is the work different, because each acts upon the other in its own way. For action and reaction <note>original: "actio & passio"; literally action and "suffering" or undergoing, a standard Aristotelian pair</note> do not result from things that are contrary in species but similar in genus and nature; and when one of the contraries exceeds the other, it destroys or alters the remainder. When the body is mixed with moisture and placed over a slow fire <note>original: "lento igni"; a gentle, steady heat, often compared to the warmth of a brooding hen</note> for a long time, it is dissolved: because the moisture turns upon it and dissolves it. Meanwhile, the body—with its cold and dry qualities—encloses, retains, and thickens the moisture, turning the dry part to ash; and yet the moisture cannot leave the body unless it absorbs itself <note>original: "imbibat"; the process of 'imbibition' where a dry solid soaks up a liquid</note> with the fire.

For when the proper heat works through putrefaction <term>putrescendo: the stage of "death" or decomposition, usually marked by the matter turning black, which was considered essential for rebirth</term>, the moist is turned into the dry. And therefore, when you have dissolved the body, you congeal the moisture, and this happens with a delay: which is chiefly because of the four warring elements <note>The four elements (Fire, Air, Water, Earth) were thought to have opposing qualities like Hot vs. Cold. The alchemist’s goal was to balance them</note>, so that peace may be made between them, etc.

### PHILOSOPHY

In this third step of the **Ladder of the Wise**, things are separated: and therefore this step is called our **separation**. This is the separation or purification of the watery or liquid vapor from the dregs <note>original: "faecibus"; the sediment or waste matter left after a process</note>, the refining of the subtle parts, the extraction of coarse parts, the division of things joined together, the production of primary principles, and the segregation of like substances.

Hence the Psalms say: *He brought forth water from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone* <note>original: "Eduxit aquam de petra, & oleum de saxo durissimo"; a reference to Psalm 81:16, used here to symbolize extracting precious substances from base matter</note>: because this work must be done in appropriate baths, and afterward in dry stoves <term>stuphis: heated chambers or drying ovens used for controlled evaporation</term>, according to the requirements of reason. In these baths, their "phlegm" <note>original: "phlegma"; the watery, inactive, or tasteless part of a substance</note> is first separated and drained away.

Then these four principles are separated from the beginning according to the required signs—and especially **Luna** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for Silver or the "feminine" principle</note>, the male before the female—and thus, with their "mother" left at the bottom in the first distillation, you shall set aside the **yellow sapphire** <term>saphiram citrinam: here referring to a specific yellow-colored distillate or residue, not the gemstone</term>. Afterward, the **orpiment** <term>auripigmentum: "gold pigment," a yellow arsenic mineral often used in alchemical attempts to create or color gold</term> is rectified <note>original: "rectificatur"; a process of purifying a liquid by repeated distillation</note> separately in the dry stove as many times as needed—both from its moisture and by itself—until no "southern redness" <note>likely referring to a reddish vapor or "bloom" associated with heat</note> ascends, and the orpiment remains clear and white. This is achieved by the third or fourth repetition.

The signs of its perfection are greenness, whiteness, and purity without dregs (unless perhaps white ones). This greenness is created from the abundance of the soul's coldness. For **Habakkuk** <note>Habakkuk is a biblical prophet; in alchemical literature, such names are often used to lend ancient authority to specific chemical maxims</note> says: *Fire is the black earth left in the bottom of the vessel, which while it is black, corrupts.* Therefore, the earth itself is **calcined** <term>calcinatur: heated to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce a substance to a powder and remove volatile impurities</term> until it glows white, and its "oil" entirely departs, so that it is deprived of all "fatness" <note>original: "pinguedine"; in alchemy, "fatness" refers to combustible or oily impurities that prevent the substance from reaching a pure, "fixed" state</note>, lest from...

# SCALA
### 134

...prevented from being hindered in its work, so that it might become dry and fiery—that which was previously cold and moist, like earth. Whence **Senior** <note>original: "Senior"; likely referring to Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century alchemist whose "Chemical Tables" were widely cited in the Middle Ages</note> says: **Our Earth** <term>Terra nostra: in alchemy, this refers not to common soil, but to the purified, solid material that forms the foundation of the Great Work</term> is taken from two natures; likewise, water is taken from two bodies, and thus the subtle is separated from the dense. For he who is ignorant of how to extract many things from one, is also ignorant of how to compose one thing from many; only then shall the **union of desire** <note>original: "coniunctio concupiscentiæ"; a poetic and technical term for the "chemical marriage," the perfect bonding of opposing elements like sulfur and mercury</note> be perfected.

Because of this, the **soul** of the substance is produced, which enters with life and spirit through the attraction of its "air," resulting from **repeated distillation** <note>original: "reiteratione distillationis"; the process of vaporizing and condensing a liquid multiple times to increase its purity and potency</note>. Through this repetition, the substance becomes fiery; and secondly, it possesses a heat stronger than that of fire itself. This is indeed the preparation of which many are ignorant: for the Philosophers have hidden the preparation of the **Stone**, which is the key to the art and to the most difficult of matters.

Therefore, prepare by preparing and purging; separate by rectifying and seeking the **mastery** <term>magisterium: the "Great Work" or the ultimate realization of the Philosopher’s Stone</term>. Divide the Stone into two principal parts: namely, into the upper part, which ascends upward and is spiritual and airy, and the lower path, which is earthy. And yet, these two parts are of a single nature, the division of which is necessary to perform the miracles of a thing of one nature: that is, the generation of the **Philosopher's Stone**. For its lower, earthy part is its nurse and **ferment** <term>fermentum: a substance that triggers transformation in another, much like yeast causes bread to rise</term>, **fixing** <note>original: "figens"; the alchemical process of "fixation," which makes a volatile or liquid substance solid and resistant to heat</note> the entire stone; and its upper part is the soul, **vivifying** <note>original: "viuificans"; the act of giving life, animation, or chemical activity to a "dead" or inert substance</note> the whole stone. To perform this division in the **Philosophical furnace** specified below, it is required—

# PHILOSOPHY
### 135

...due and nourishing heat, and continuous—namely for ten and fifteen days—and the longer it continues, the better the **digestion** <term>digestio: a process of slow, consistent heating, similar to incubation, used to mature the alchemical matter</term> of the **water** is perfected, from which our **copper** <term>æs nostrum: literally "our bronze" or "our copper"; in alchemy, this refers to the purified metallic base or the "body" of the Work, not common copper</term> arises.

And every copper is **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur"; in alchemical theory, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and "soul" principle of a substance</note>, but not every sulfur is copper: because the sulfur of nature is contained within sulfurs; and all gold is copper, but not all copper is gold: just as every man is an animal, but not every animal is a man: because from the genus to the species, as **Plato** <note>referring to Platonic logic regarding categorization; the author argues that while gold belongs to the category of "alchemical copper," the category itself is broader than just gold</note> says, the consequence is not necessarily valid. For this **water of ours** is the key of the art, and the head of the work; and the spirit, the soul, and the body compose our copper. And they are called elsewhere **uterine brothers** <note>original: "fratres vterini"; a metaphor indicating that the different components of the Stone—mercury and sulfur—originate from the same primary matter or "womb"</note>, because they proceed from the same womb.

And when you have water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth, then the separation is made perfect. For you have fire from earth through **rarefaction**, **calcination**, and **liquefaction**; and you have earth from fire through **congealing** and **thickening**.

And when you have the tempered substance—that is, a substance of equal **complexion** <term>complexionatũ: the balanced temperament or ratio of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry)</term>—within the **Philosophical vessel**, place a natural fire beneath your vessel, by whose heat all things are to be heated, tending toward the center of the fire. When these things have been raised up into the **heaven** <note>the upper part of the distillation flask</note>, gathered, and reside upon the **peaks of our mountains** <note>original: "cacumina montium nostrorũ"; a metaphor for the top of the alchemical apparatus where vapors condense</note> for a short time, that air is made into a "generation," converting all things into its own nature; its light parts succumb to the heavy, and the light things which previously had conquered [rest] with them, and within those same things they descend into the earth in that **heavenly dew** <note>original: "rore cœlesti"; the condensed liquid or "spirit" that drips back down during reflux distillation</note> to be multiplied infinitely.

## The fourth step of our Ladder of wisdom is, and is called, Conjunction.

Therefore, once the four distinct elements have been separated, as was previously stated, and **rectified** <term>rectificatis: the process of purifying a substance by repeated distillation or sublimation until it reaches its most potent state</term>, we join and connect those four: and our **conjunction** <term>coniunctio: the "chemical marriage" where the previously separated and purified principles (soul, spirit, and body) are reunited into a single, stable substance</term> is called a mixing of qualities, a coupling of those embracing, a folding back of things dispersed, an equalization of principles, and an arrangement for overcoming opposition.

For the **Rosarius** <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), one of the most famous illustrated alchemical treatises of the 16th century</note> says: Arrange the **airy substance** <note>original: "substantiam aëream"; referring to the volatile or spiritual part of the matter</note> through discernment, so that earth may thus be obtained from two natures, and water, as previously said, from two bodies: because in this way the subtle is separated from the gross, and the rare from the dense: namely, that which we have spoken of must be performed gently, and with great ingenuity.

### PHILOSOPHY

...by nature <note>original: *ingenio*; here referring to the natural character or innate quality of the substance</note>: that is, by a due and nutritive heat. For in our work, water is not necessary unless it is bright-white; nor is oil, unless it is white, clear, and lemon-yellow in color; nor is earth, unless it is pale and whitish. This is because, at that stage, the earth is fit for binding, the water for dissolving, and the air is superabundant for **tinting** <term>tingendum: the process of projecting the alchemical tincture onto a base metal to transform its color and nature</term>.

And there are two earths and two waters in our work. The first earth, which remains at the bottom during the first distillation, is properly pale; it is upon this that our **rectification** <term>rectificatio: the purification of a substance through repeated distillation</term> is performed, once the oil has been separated from this earth (as was hinted at somewhat unclearly above) and likewise from the water. Then the oil is distilled by itself, and what remains at the bottom is called fire, which is sometimes referred to as the "Second Earth."

It is of these two earths that **Aristotle** <note>In alchemical literature, "Aristotle" often refers to pseudo-Aristotelian texts like the *Secretum Secretorum* rather than the historical philosopher</note> speaks—namely, of earth and fire—which are **calcined** <term>calcinatae: reduced to a powder through high heat</term> together into a white state. These are "vinegary" <note>original: *acetiuae*; likely referring to the sharp, solvent-like quality of the substances</note>, and they are the two waters: namely, water and oil. Sometimes the author uses the name of one for the name of the other, so that unworthy seekers may deviate from the path of truth.

Again, Aristotle says: "Join to it two operative virtues, namely water and oil; by rectifying the water and air, the earth and fire will also be rectified." I have added this here because I said too little about **separation** in the preceding chapter. I have also done this for the sake of those who are accustomed to "deflower" books <note>original: *deflorare*; a common historical metaphor for readers who skip through a text to find only the "best parts" or secrets without studying the whole</note>, so that they might not find everything they require laid out in order in a single chapter. # SCALA
<note>Latin for "The Ladder" or "The Staircase," signifying the ascending stages of the alchemical work.</note>

...the active and the passive, the rare and the dense, the male and the female, sulfur and mercury, matter and form.

Whence the Philosopher <note>In this context, "the Philosopher" refers to Aristotle, whose theories of matter and form underpinned medieval alchemy.</note> says: "In both matter and form, the generation of nature is contained." Likewise, he says elsewhere: "It is enough for the operator of this art to reduce the matter to the simple purity of rarity and density, though not individually within the elements."

Therefore, join Gabricus <note>original: *Sabricum*; Gabricus is the alchemical prince or brother, representing the solar/sulfur principle.</note> to Beya <note>The alchemical queen or sister, representing the lunar/mercurial principle.</note>, so that they may beget their own likeness between themselves, whose seed shall be multiplied like the stars. And thus it is clear that a **binary conjunction** <term>dyptatiua coniunctio: a two-fold union, specifically the "chemical marriage" of male and female principles</term> is sufficient for the Mastery.

A **triple conjunction** <term>Triptatiua coniunctio: a three-fold union involving the three philosophical principles of body, soul, and spirit</term>: that is, the union of the trinity, is made of body, spirit, and soul. For according to the Philosophers, just as the soul is the bond of the spirit, so too is the body the bond of the soul; this is because the spirit penetrates, the body **fixes** <note>original: *figit*; the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</note>, and the soul joins them together. Thus this trinity is a unity in essence, because they are at once co-eternal and co-equal.

A **fourfold conjunction** <term>Tetraptatiua coniunctio: a four-fold union that balances the four elements (fire, air, water, earth)</term> is called the correction of the principles, so that one of them may be achieved within the other. For this reason, for the most law-worthy conjunction, it is necessary that just as in our work there are four elements, they be in a composition that is liquid, fresh, warm, and duly proportioned.

# PHILOSOPHY
<note>Header: PHILOSOPH. indicates this section belongs to the "Scala Philosophorum" or the "Ladder of Philosophers."</note>

...his wife [consisting of] nine [parts], whose tail the male, when he has ascended upon her, shall hold in his beak. They must remain in the required **philosophical vessel** <term>vas philosophicum: a specially sealed glass container, often called an "alchemical egg," designed to withstand long periods of heat</term>, placed in the **philosophical furnace** <term>furnus philosophicus: also known as an "athanor," designed to maintain a constant, steady temperature</term>, and carefully sealed with the aforementioned moisture placed beneath. And it must be known that the seed is never placed into the **womb** <term>matrix: the interior of the alchemical vessel where the "conception" of the Stone occurs</term> except all at once, and the womb is immediately closed until [the offspring] is brought forth into the light.

And when it has remained in **eclipse** <note>original: *eclipsi*; this refers to the *nigredo* or "blackening" stage, where the matter decays and turns black before it can be purified</note>, namely for five months, as the darkness recedes and the clear light arrives, the heat should be increased moderately—and especially so on the "days of abstinence"—until the shining **Sun** <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" (Sol) represents the completed Gold or the Red Tincture</note> rises. From that point on, it should be nourished continuously in triple heat, because it then no longer fears the pains of the "fighting fire."

And thus the body is the cause of retaining the water, and the water is the cause of saving the oil from burning, and the oil is the cause of retaining the fiery **tincture** <note>The "tincture" is the active power of the Philosopher's Stone to transform or "dye" base metals into gold</note>, for the sake of the appearance of color. And so the thick substance will strive to retain the subtle, and the **soul** <note>original: *anima*</note> will strive to fight with the fire and endure it, and the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*</note> will strive to be submerged and melted into the bodies.

And then like applauds its like, because of the great desire for material adherence and the **sulfurous form** <note>Sulfur was considered the "form" or active, masculine principle that gives shape and properties to the "matter" of Mercury</note>. Whence Vometras <note>A philosopher frequently cited in medieval alchemical compendiums, likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic authority</note> the Philosopher says:

"Two sulfurs dwell in the body, like fire in wood and stones, which must be extracted by a most subtle art without burning. For he who does not distinguish between the two sulfurs, and sulfur...

...ning <note>original: *combustura*; finishing the word from the previous page</note>, it knows nothing; yet the work begins and ends with a single odor.

There are, however, two modes of composition: namely, one moist and the other dry, and through **decoction** <term>decoctio: a process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or cause a chemical change</term> they become one. Therefore, neither should leave the other: because the moist easily makes an impression and loses it. And when the moist and the dry have tempered one another, the dry will acquire from the moist an easy impression, and the moist will acquire from the dry the ability to firmly retain every impression, while enduring the fire. Hence, by means of the moist, it moves from its fluidity toward perfection. Therefore, it does not act as a **tincture** <note>original: *tingens*; a substance capable of transforming or "coloring" base metals into gold</note> until the **Sun and Moon** <note>Sol and Luna: symbols for Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles of the work</note>, and the **spirit**, and the **soul**, are convertedly joined into one body: that is, into earth. 

An example of this is the **potter's work** <note>original: *opus figuli*</note>, the reliability of which consists in two things: namely, the dry and the moist. The dry is used to transform the moist, and the moist to dissolve the dry; and thus, with the spirit mixed with the body, a temperament is formed that is not as thin as the spirit, nor as dense as the body. For **to dissolve and to conjoin** <note>original: *soluere & coniungere*; a reference to the famous alchemical motto *Solve et Coagula*, meaning to break down and build back up</note> are the principal starting points of this art and work, and are a single power. For he who does not dissolve and **coagulate** <term>coagulo: to thicken or solidify a liquid into a stable mass</term> errs in many ways.

Which is celebrated for forty-six nights in the **shadow of purgatory** <note>In alchemy, "purgatory" refers to the *nigredo* or black stage, where the matter must "die" or decay to be purified</note>. And putrefaction is necessary because it is the corruption and [the beginning] of regeneration...

Similarly, when they [the philosophers] say: "water and waters," they mean by this one water, which is the spirit from which the waters bring forth; understand this to be true.

### *The sixth step is called Whitening Coagulation*
### *and naturally fixing.*

And coagulation is the hardening of what is soft, the concealment of moisture, the **fixing of the spirit** <term>Fixatio: a process where a volatile substance is made stable and resistant to fire</term>, the joining of diverse things, the continuation of like things or homogeneity, and the appropriate adaptation of things fleeing from the fire toward the fire, as shown by the universal **tincture** <note>original: *tinctura*; the concentrated essence or "medicine" capable of transforming metals</note> whose extroverted nature is made perpetual in the other.

And it should be known that through the **mortification** <term>Mortificatio: the "killing" or chemical breakdown of a substance until it loses its original properties, usually marked by a change to a black color</term> of the coarse earthy part in the moist, **blackness** <note>original: *nigredo*; the first major stage of the alchemical process representing decay and prima materia</note> is generated; and from the constricted cold-moisture into the dry, **whiteness** <note>original: *albedo*; the second major stage, representing purification</note> is generated.

For dryness proceeds by whitening, just as moisture proceeds by blackening, with heat acting as the mediator; for without nutritive heat, life cannot be given to the world. Redness is truly more black than white when combined with fire without heat; Saffron-yellow <note>original: *Croceum*</note> comes from pure black and much white with the air of moisture.

Citrine-yellow <note>original: *Citrinum*</note> is more white than black, with an abundance of the airiness of water dried by fire rather than by fire alone, because that which is black does not come to citrine, nor to red, unless it was first white: because there is no passage from the first stage to the third, except through the second.

And it should be known that the elements are not united except in the white color. And when the white has been preserved, it does not require great heat, but is ruled by a strong fire, so that when completely **digested** <term>Digestio: a process of slow, consistent heating, similar to biological digestion, to mature the substance</term> it is totally turned into fire, so that it fears no fire.

Now, by this **sublimation**, one understands the preparation <note>original: *habilitatio*; the process of making the stone "fit" or capable of its task</note> of the stone and the perfect joining of the **ferment** <term>ferment</term> <note>original: *fermenti*; a substance added to "leaven" or trigger the transformation of the base metal, much like yeast in bread</note> with the stone itself.

At this stage, it is also a simple **medicine**, but it is neither perfect nor most perfect until the medicine is ennobled through **exaltation** <note>original: *exaltationem*; a process intended to raise the "dignity" or potency of a substance</note> and raised up, as appears below.

And it must be known that we perform sublimation for four reasons:

**First**, so that the **body** <note>the solid, material part of the work</note> might become **spirit** <note>the volatile or gaseous part</note> from subtle matter.

**Second**, so that **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*; referring here to the "spirit" or quicksilver</note> might incorporate itself with the body and become one with it.

**Third**, so that the whole may become white; and thereafter red and pure, and the "falseness" <note>impurities or combustible elements</note> of the **sulfur** is diminished.

And **especially** so that the innate moisture of the stone might be restored—which it first lost when it was reduced to **lime** <note>original: *calce*; the dry powder produced by intense heating</note>—and that it may be effectively prepared for very rapid **liquefaction** <note>the ability to melt or flow easily</note>. For the medicine ought to be a simple powder of the most subtle and pure substance, adhering to the **quicksilver** <note>original: *argento viuo*; mercury</note> by its very nature. It must be of the easiest liquefaction, of hidden refinement, and of the thinnest entry—much like water—and it must stand fixed against the battle of the fire before the "flight" <note>evaporation or volatilization</note> of the Mercury. 

Then, whatever is added to it will be of the same **complexion** <note>the fundamental nature or temperament of a substance</note> as that to which it is added: so that if you add water to it, the whole will be dissolved in water; but if you put it in the fire, the whole will belong to the fire. And when you have **fixed** the **Elixir** <note>made it resistant to evaporation by heat</note>, you must bring back over it the prepared spirit, so that they are mixed together and liquefied.

### PHILOSOPHY

...be purified and enlivened: just as spiritual accidents cannot show their permanent virtues unless they are first united and perpetuated with fixed bodies. It is then that the body embraces the spirit, teaching it by strengthening it to battle against the fire. And the spirit teaches the body to actively penetrate thick substances, to thin out the dense, to improve the imperfect and bring it to perfection, and also to generally provide a final remedy for all the infirmities of bodies <note>In alchemy, the "infirmities of bodies" refers to the impurities in base metals that prevent them from being gold.</note>.

Furthermore, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical texts were foundational to Western alchemy</note> says that the body and the ferment <term>fermentum</term> <note>a substance added to the alchemical base to "leaven" it and trigger transformation, much like yeast in bread</note> which you mix therein must be a simple and subtle powder. However, you should not complete their mixing until both of them are dissolved into water, because it is only in that state that mixing occurs "by the smallest parts" <term>per minima</term> <note>original: *commixtio per minima*; a philosophical term for a mixture so intimate that the components are combined at the atomic or most fundamental level</note>. This is because it is easier to separate wine from earth than it is to separate it from water. But when water is mixed with water, it receives that water as its own nature, so that they are never separated from one another; for "Nature rejoices in nature" <note>original: *Natura naturâ lætatur*; one of the oldest and most famous maxims in the alchemical tradition</note>, and Nature seeks, desires, conceives, embraces, nourishes, renews, directs, strengthens, whitens, and reddens nature.

According to **Avicenna**, you must prepare the ferment by washing, calcining <term>calcination</term> <note>the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a fine, dry powder</note>, and dissolving it, so that it may be joined with the subtle work or the body—namely, the white with the white, and the red with the red <note>Referring to the *Albedo* (whiteness) and *Rubedo* (redness), the final two major stages of the Great Work.</note>. Yet the ferment does not change the powder of the stone into any form other than its own; rather, it gives it "flavor" and "odor," along with the strength to transmute other bodies into its own nature.

For since the nature has been converted, each part becomes one with the individual elements whose essence it first embraces. This occurs because as long as the ferment <term>fermentum</term> <note>original: *fermentum*; in alchemy, a substance that "leavens" or triggers a transformative chain reaction in a base metal</note> is prepared to receive every form, it is always adapted for solution. Therefore, the philosophers posit "solution" and give a definition to this solution: for the ferment is the fourth part of our copper <note>original: *æris nostri*; this refers to "philosophical brass/copper," a specialized substance rather than common metal</note>. And it should be known that in any tincture, the dyeing part is a thousand times more effective in a liquid substance than in a dry one, as is evident in saffron when it is placed in a liquid. Thus, the ferment reduces whatever is applied to it into its own nature, color, and flavor in every way—namely, from potentiality to actuality <note>a reference to Aristotelian philosophy where a thing moves from a state of "could be" (potential) to "is" (actuality)</note>. For it whitens the confection, or multiplies it; it strengthens its spirituality and annihilates combustion <note>prevents the substance from being destroyed or "burned" by the alchemical fire</note>; it contains the tincture so it does not flee <note>prevents the volatile "spirit" or color from evaporating</note>; it lightens the bodies and makes them enter and join one another. This is the end of the work, without which the Elixir is not completed, just as dough is not leavened without ferment; it is called the "ferment of the ferment" and the "coagulant of the coagulant."

And it should be known that every dissolution <note>the process of turning a solid into a liquid state</note> occurs according to affinity. For everything that dissolves the Moon <note>alchemical code for silver</note> also dissolves the Sun <note>alchemical code for gold</note>, because the body is extremely hot, and nothing can penetrate it except the subtlest spirit, which is also called "air." And all these things are called the "second spirit," which creates a homogeneity between the two bodies, much like that between God and man: because once the superior spirit is bounded, it receives the second. It is a spirit <term>spiritus</term> <note>original: *spiritus*; in alchemy, this refers to a volatile substance or the vital, active essence of a metal</note> composed of two humors <note>original: *humoribus*; the basic fluids or elemental components</note>, and the spirit is their ferment. Therefore it is clear that through quicksilver <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; the metal Mercury, considered the foundational "mother" of all metals</note> one does not coagulate the white [substance] while enduring the fire, nor does it join with pure silver; it demands nothing for the whiteness: and the same is true for pure gold regarding the red: because it will profit neither itself, nor another, nor the world. Yet the operation of both is one and the same, except that the white work <term>white work</term> <note>original: *opus album*; also known as the *Albedo*, the second major stage of alchemy aimed at creating silver</note> is the work of winter, as I have said, and the red [work] <term>red work</term> <note>original: *opus rubeum*; the *Rubedo*, the final stage of the Great Work aimed at creating gold or the Philosopher's Stone</note> is the work of summer: wherefore in the time of summer, and of floods, the inundation of waters ruins the third mastery <note>original: *magisterium tertium*; likely referring to the third stage or "degree" of the alchemical process</note>.

The Sun <term>Sun</term> <note>original: *Sol*; the alchemical symbol for Gold</note> does not dye, as I have said before, unless it is dyed itself, nor does it dye unto completion unless it is more fully dissolved. Moreover, it is fully dissolved if they are fixed <note>made stable or non-volatile</note> in the fourth degree through sublimation. And thus it is clear that without the ferment, neither the Sun nor the Moon <term>Moon</term> <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical symbol for Silver</note> will emerge.

For according to Plato <note>Alchemists frequently cited ancient philosophers like Plato to lend authority to their chemical theories, though the quotes were often apocryphal</note>: "Unless there is something in it that amends it, that which you seek will not happen." Wherefore we command that the stone <term>stone</term> <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note> be joined with its own body, so that it might generate its own likeness: that is, with pure silver or gold, which are the ferments of our final Elixir.

And it should be known that ash <term>ash</term> <note>original: *cinis*; the dry, calcined remains of a substance after intense heating</note> is the ferment of gold, and gold is their water, and their water is the ferment of the body, and their bodies are their earth. And the ferment of this divine water is the ash, which is the "ferment of the ferment." Therefore, mix gold with gold: that is, water with ash.

Likewise, join the spirit <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus*; the volatile, active essence of the substance</note> with its own blanched earth <term>blanched earth</term> <note>original: *terra dealbata*; earth that has been purified and whitened through chemical processes</note> and lime <term>lime</term> <note>original: *calx*; a powder produced by heating a substance until it loses its moisture and becomes brittle</note>, which is its ferment, and prepare the whole with its own water, until it is fermented, and it becomes like fermented dough. ### *The tenth step is called Exaltation.*

This is the ennobling of our blanched magnesia <term>magnesia</term> <note>original: *magnesia*; in alchemy, this refers not to the modern element magnesium, but to the "prime matter" or a specific mineral used as a starting point</note> within the fire, which is achieved chiefly through the augmentation of the spirit, the sublimation of the earth, and the signaling of liquefaction, by exalting the rectified elements and vivifyingly constituting from them the fifth essence <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: *quintam essentiam*; the "quintessence," a celestial and incorruptible element beyond the four earthly elements</note>.

Wherefore Aristotle <note>The famous Greek philosopher, whose theories on the elements formed the basis of alchemical science</note> says: "When you have water from air, air from fire, and fire from earth, etc." This stone, however, is said to be [contained] in the elements by the final operation, not by manual labor. First, it loses the water which it has from the air after its resolution into it: for air and water are contiguous and middle elements, wherefore they are lighter in the mixture and better in the operation of fire. When cold overcomes heat, air is turned into water; but when heat overcomes cold, water is turned into air: indeed, having air from fire, through resolution, putrefaction <term>putrefaction</term> <note>a stage where the material is broken down and rotted, often turning black, to allow for new life or growth</note>, and much con-

And the air was made a **solar substance** <note>original: *substantia solaris*; a refined, luminous state of matter that participates in the nature of the Sun</note> bringing harmony between opposing forces so they do not destroy one another—namely, between water and fire. An example of this is the **egg** <term>Philosophical Egg</term> <note>original: *ouum*; a central alchemical symbol representing the sealed vessel or the microcosm where the elements are reconciled</note>, which is a single thing containing many within itself: specifically, the **white** <note>original: *albumen*</note> and the **yolk** <note>original: *vitellum*</note>, representing matter and form, as well as the shell. The white and the yolk represent the body, spirit, and soul. Regarding the four elements, however: the shell represents the earth; furthermore, the lower membrane represents the cold, subterranean air, which separates the earth so that it does not sink into the water.

Next, the white stands for the quality of water; afterward, the upper membrane represents the warm air beneath the sun, bringing harmony between the opposing forces—namely between the water and the fiery yolk—lest they destroy one another through their conflict. Yet all are one. The lower and colder air, however, stays above the earth—that is, [above] the denser water and [below] the loftier air.

Therefore, the higher air of the heights is warmer, thinner, and more subtle than the lower air. And thus within one thing, five are contained: namely, a group of four—earth, water, air, and fire—and the **point of the Sun** <note>original: *pũctus Solis*; the "quintessence" or fifth element, often depicted as a red dot at the center of the work</note>, which is red and in the middle. And this chick is the **Bird of Hermes** <note>original: *auis Hermetis*; a famous alchemical symbol for the volatile spirit or the Stone itself during its transition</note>.

For this reason, our **Stone** has been so named by all the Philosophers among all our ancestors, especially because of its whiteness and dryness, and its evident watery nature surrounding it, while secretly enfolding its most intense redness within.

For **Aristotle** <note>The text appeals to Aristotelian physics, which taught that elements could only transform into one another through a shared quality or a middle state</note> says that a direct passage between extremes cannot occur except through a middle point.

Therefore, that which is hot is not turned into that which is cold, except by way of the **moist** <note>original: *humidum*</note>, which serves as the medium between them. Nor indeed is water turned into fire, unless it is first turned into air; nor is earth turned into air, unless it is first turned into water. For fire and water are contrary elements—or extremes—while air and earth are their mediators. This is because just as water is positioned next to air from below, so air is positioned next to fire from above. Therefore, water is the contrary to fire, just as earth is to air, for the reason that water and air meet in the quality of the moist, while fire and earth meet in the quality of the dry. Earth is immediately changed into fire <note>Both share the quality of "dryness"</note>, just as water is changed into air <note>Both share the quality of "moisture"</note>; but fire and water, or air and earth, do not cycle <note>original: *rotantur*; the "rotation of the elements" is a key alchemical process for purification</note> unless the earth is first converted into water, and the air into fire. 

Indeed, according to **Roger Bacon** <note>A 13th-century English philosopher and friar, legendary in alchemy for his works on nature and experimental science</note>, fire in its highest state is naturally hot and dry in the **fourth degree** <note>In medieval science, qualities like heat were measured in four degrees of intensity; the fourth is the most extreme</note>. If you wish to turn these into water, you must bring the body back to a **balanced state** <term>temperament</term> <note>original: *temperamentum*; a state where opposing qualities are perfectly proportioned or neutralized</note> so that it becomes receptive. Reduce it into **lime** <note>original: *calcem*; the product of calcination or burning a substance to a fine powder</note>, then subject it to fire, and then water must be added, which is cold and moist. In the fourth degree, however, there is a balance that is neither hot nor cold; and thus water mixed with fire creates a balance that is neither moist nor dry.

In the same way, by means of qualities that diminish or increase, earth and air are led toward a balanced state. And so, when the spirit is mixed with the body—as I said before—a balanced state is achieved: one that is not as thin as the spirit, nor as dense as the body.

Furthermore, when you are engaged in the work, you should strive—

Remember in your mind all the natural signs that appear in any decoction <note>original: *decoctione*; the process of heating a substance to extract its essence or transform it</note>, and investigate their causes. But if the work is led to the final red state <note>original: *rubeum*; the *rubedo* is the final stage of the Great Work</note> before the due limit of whiteness <note>original: *albedinis*; the stage of purification that must precede the final reddening</note> is reached in the administration of the work, you must realize that you have erred corruptly—which God forbid! Then, as a remedy, take away the redness by imbibing <note>original: *imbibendo*; the process of adding moisture to the dry matter</note> it with fresh white water, burying it <note>original: *inhumando*; placing the vessel in a warm, dark place like a dung-pit or sand bath</note>, and by converting that which is buried into blackness <note>The *nigredo* stage</note> with heat. Beware especially of that premature redness because of the danger <note>In alchemy, "skipping" to the red stage too early was thought to result in a "brittle" or failed stone, or even an explosion of the vessel</note>. This appears around the matter along the sides of the yellowish vessel, where previously, after the greatest blackness, a white circle appeared. 

And do not care for the colors appearing before the true whiteness, for they are not true. For it turns black twice, it becomes base twice, it turns white twice, and it turns red twice. When it is composed and putrefied for four days, it will give a dark black color if left for a long time; secondly, a yellowish black; thirdly, a blackish red; fourthly, a red similar to clear, dried saffron; fifthly and finally, it reaches the heat of correct whiteness, beyond which you will achieve no further effect <note>meaning this stage is the completion of the *albedo*</note>.

### *The eleventh step is called Multiplication.*

Which is the increase of goodness, the exaltation of color, and the artificial accumulation of infinite quantity.

And why this medicine of ours <note>The "medicine" is another name for the Philosopher's Stone, reflecting its supposed power to heal both metals and the human body.</note> ought to be multiplied into infinity, this is the reason:

For the medicine itself is like fire in wood, and like musk among fine spices. Therefore, it grows more the more it is worked with; for this reason, you must always leave a part of it behind, since you are enriched thrice by it, just as one who has fire is enriched by fire <note>The author suggests the Stone acts like a flame—one candle can light many others without losing its own heat.</note>.

The medicine can be multiplied in two ways. First, through solution and repeated coagulation; and this is its virtual multiplication in goodness <note>In this context, "virtual" refers to the "virtue" or inner power and potency of the substance.</note>.

The second is through fermentation, and this is its multiplication in quantity. More quickly, however...

...the species <note>The "species" refers to the specific form or essence of the alchemical substance.</note> increases through fermentation, because a dissolved substance does not work well <margin>⸫</margin> until it is first fixed in its own ferment <note>Ferment: in alchemy, a substance (usually gold or silver) added to the "medicine" to stabilize it and give it a specific direction or "flavor."</note>. Therefore, our medicine is more perfectly multiplied through solution <note>Solution: the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note> and exaltation; and in this way by the spirit and—

After the first solution, exaltation, and coagulation <note>Coagulation: the stage where the liquid substance is thickened or solidified again.</note>, one part in the first projection <note>Projection: the final act of casting the Philosopher's Stone onto base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note> falls upon 100 parts; the second stage upon 1,000; and thus further by tenfold, always exalting it even unto infinity, which is the most precious gift. 

Thus it is concluded that the work operates more abundantly in a great amount of fermented and dissolved medicine, because the ferment alone is made more refined—even though it could be multiplied to infinity through fermentation alone. This is for this reason: because the ferment draws whatever is added to it into its own natural color and flavor in every way. 

Therefore the Philosophers, seeing that the substance did not flee when it was made volatile <note>original: *fugiens*; literally "fleeing." Alchemists used this to describe substances that evaporate or escape when heated.</note> with other volatile things, repeated the process with a similar non-volatile <note>original: *non fugiens*; "not fleeing," referring to a substance that remains stable under heat.</note> body. They brought it into that very thing from which they could not escape because of the close kinship of their natures. 

Surely the soul enters its own body more quickly than if it were placed in another. For if you strive to place it elsewhere, you will labor in vain, since there is no communication between darkness and light. Therefore, they have returned to a body similar to the bodies from which they were drawn, and they are able to remain: because thus the dyer and the thing to be dyed <note>original: *tingens & tingendum*; refers to the "Tincture" (the Stone) and the base metal it transforms.</note> become one.

Therefore, once the things are mixed so that they may be multiplied through fixation <term>Fixation (confixationem): The process of making a volatile or "fleeing" substance stable and resistant to heat, so it no longer evaporates.</term>, place the vessel on the fire. It will then become a single fixed body—clear and white, or red—depending on how the medicine...

->*dren’s play, as it is called, begins auspiciously.*<-

The progression of the labor is called the "work of women" <term>Women's Work: An alchemical metaphor for the stage of "coction" or cooking, implying a process that requires patience and a steady, gentle heat, much like tending a kitchen hearth.</term> and "children’s play" <term>Children's Play: A metaphor suggesting that once the correct "starting matter" is found, the rest of the Great Work is so simple it could be compared to a child's game.</term>. After the entrance into the work, the subtle investigator of divine nature continues the progression. Therefore, these words are not fables, nor are they worthy of contempt; indeed, you should pay such attention to these words so that the texts of ancient books do not deceive you, for they sometimes transpose words, as the Philosopher <term>Apuleius: Likely referring to Apuleius of Madaura, though in alchemical contexts, many works were "pseudo-Apuleian," attributed to him to lend them ancient authority.</term> says in his book *On the Secrets of Nature* <note>original: "de Secretis naturæ"</note>.

Moreover, a threefold children's play ought to precede the women's work. For children play with three things. First, frequently with very old walls <note>Alchemists often extracted niter (saltpeter) from the efflorescence found on old stone walls or in cellars.</note>. Second, with urine. Third, with coals. The first play provides the matter of the stone <note>original: "materia lapidis"</note>. The second play increases the soul. The third play prepares the body for life. For from the "flower of blood" <note>An alchemical code for a specific mineral or chemical state, often associated with the redness of certain salts.</note> comes saltpeter <note>original: "sal petra"</note> by means of the first children’s play. When this is done, it remains to animate it, and frequently to dissolve it into water with its partner <note>original: "compari"</note>, by means of the two other children's plays which are necessary, up until the third heat of our Elixir in the women's work—for their work is to cook; who therefore

Let him who is able to understand, understand <note>original: "potest capere capiat." A common alchemical and biblical phrase indicating that the secret is hidden in plain sight for the wise.</note>. Moreover, our stone, which all the **Philosophers** have sought, contains within it the first elements of minerals; in it are the tincture, the lime <term>Calx: The powdery residue left after a substance has been heated or "calcined"; it represents the physical body of the material.</term> and the soul, the spirit and the body, both fixed and volatile. It contains a **Mercury**, not just any kind, but that one around which nature began its first operations and determined those first operations toward a metallic nature, but left that thing imperfect. 

If, therefore, you extract it from that thing in which it is found, and begin to work with it by starting where nature left off, you will find a perfect thing within that imperfect one, and you will rejoice, just as **King Geber** <term>Geber: The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 8th-century polymath and foundational figure in alchemy.</term> said. And this thing from which the stone is extracted is possessed by both the poor and the rich. It is the "work of women" and "children’s play," and its flower is the stone. 

Therefore, receive in the name of God that thing which is not perfect. For nothing can be made from a finished, perfect thing; because the species of perfect things are not changed by their nature, but rather are corrupted. Nor is that thing from which our stone is extracted, or the matter of the stone, entirely imperfect—since according to the art, nothing could be made from such a truly imperfect thing. The reason for this is that the alchemical art cannot introduce the first dispositions of nature. Instead, it is a "middle thing" between perfect and imperfect bodies; what nature did not finish in it, but only began, can be brought to perfection through the art. 

Therefore, **Fledius the Philosopher** <note>Fledius: Likely a corruption or variant name for an early alchemical author, possibly Khalid ibn Yazid (Calid).</note> says: "Since man is the most worthy of creatures, for whose sake all..."

It emphasizes that the Work must begin with a "middle" substance that is neither fully perfect nor completely raw.</summary>

### *How our stone ought to be known through its circumstances.*

And if you do not understand the stone now, you will never understand it.

### *On the separation of the elements in our stone, to be understood philosophically.*

Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis," referring to the 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi.</note> the Philosopher says: Know for a truth that the Philosophers never intended for our stone to be divided into four elements separately, as the foolish Alchemists do, as clearly appears through what Arnaldus <note>original: "Arnoldus," likely Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a medieval physician and alchemist.</note> says: Know for a truth that the elements are not divided in our stone according to their substance, but indeed according to their <term>virtue|the inherent power, quality, or essential property of a substance</term>: <insert>since any pure and simple element is not found except in its own sphere alone <note>In the medieval cosmos, elements were thought to exist in pure "spheres" (e.g., the sphere of Fire above the Air); on Earth, they were always found in mixed forms.</note></insert>. Nevertheless, it is the case that the active and passive qualities of the elements, according to a certain predominance, can be separated and divided from one another; for instance, while the viscous <note>thick or sticky</note> water and its substance are separated, in which coldness predominates, then it is said that "water is separated." But when the more sunken <note>original: "depressa," likely meaning the more concentrated or dense part</note> substance is separated, in which heat dominates, then it is said that "air and fire," or the "airy and fiery substance," is separated. He who can grasp this, let him grasp it; and he who cannot, let him by no means involve himself in this science and art. Therefore, to speak in conclusion: Our water is extracted from the substance of the hand <note>original: "manus." In alchemical Latin, this may be a cryptic term for the "massa" (the mass of matter) or a metaphor for the work of the practitioner; it is unlikely to mean a literal human hand.</note>, and not from another, because in them is the greater <term>tincture|the concentrated essence or coloring principle that transforms the nature of a metal</term>. As for the earth, truly I do not care what its color or substance may be, so long as it is subtle, clear, and <term>fixed|stable and resistant to evaporation or the effects of fire</term>,

->etc.<-

### *On the true Philosophical Putrefaction of our stone.*

Arnoldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famed medieval physician and alchemist.</note> says in his *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosario," referring to the *Rosarium philosophorum*, a seminal alchemical text.</note>: In our work, <term>putrefaction|the process of breaking down a substance through heat or moisture, often signaled by a black color (nigredo), which alchemists viewed as a necessary "death" before rebirth</term> is necessary, because nothing is ever born, or grows, or is animated, except after putrefaction. For if a substance has not been putrefied, it cannot be melted, nor dissolved. And if it is not dissolved, it will be reduced to nothing. Therefore, our putrefaction is not filthy or unclean, but is the mixing of water with earth, and earth with water, at the smallest possible scale <note>original: "per minima," a philosophical term referring to the most minute particles of matter</note>, until the whole body becomes one. Hence the Philosopher Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: In the putrefaction of our bronze <note>original: "æris," often used in alchemy to refer to the base metal or the starting "body" of the Work.</note>, the spirits are united with the body and are dried out within it. And unless the water were dried with the earth, the colors would not appear. Furthermore, our putrefaction is nothing other than the mortification <term>mortification|the stabilization or "killing" of the volatile qualities of a substance so it can be transformed</term> of the moist with the dry.

<margin>Note Well: Sublimation <note>original: "Sublimatio," the process of heating a substance so it rises as vapor and then solidifies again, used here to explain how the "heavy" and "light" components interact.</note></margin>

And our putrefaction does not occur without the moist and the dry, because the earth is held within dryness, and it cannot rise by itself. The reason is this: heavy things cannot ascend higher, nor can light things remain below with the heavy and be thrust down without their companionship; rather, each is the beginning and the end of the other. Hence King Hali <note>Likely Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Arabic authority in alchemical literature.</note> says: Know that unless you have sublimated the body until it becomes water, the water will not putrefy in its entirety; nor can it be congealed except by fire. For fire congeals the mixture of our stone. And similarly, we dissolve bodies so that the heat may cling to their depths...

<summary>This page explains the alchemical concept of putrefaction as a vital process of uniting "water" (moisture/spirit) and "earth" (dryness/body) to allow for the stone's eventual solidification. It cites authorities like Arnoldus, Morienus, and King Hali to emphasize that this decay is a controlled, philosophical refinement rather than literal rot.</summary>

### *How our water is blackened from its nature; hear what Johannes Auster says.*

Johannes Auster <note>An alchemical authority often cited in medieval anthologies, though his historical identity remains obscure.</note> says: Indeed, the more our <term>bronze|original: "Æs"; in alchemy, this rarely refers to the literal alloy of copper and tin, but rather to the "body" or base matter of the Work</term> is cooked, the more it is dissolved and blackened, and becomes a more subtle and spiritual water.

Secondly, the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened and dried out, and it becomes of a greater whiteness.

Thirdly, the more it is cooked, the more it is colored and reddened, and it becomes a <term>tincture|a potent substance capable of coloring and transforming metals</term> of the intended redness. Because it is necessary that our stone first becomes black. This is proven as follows: Because the generation of one thing does not occur except through the corruption of another. But the corruption of putrefaction does not occur except through heat acting upon moisture.

But heat acting upon moisture first produces blackness: wherefore it is clearly evident that the beginning of our work is blackness and the <term>raven’s head|original: "caput corui"; a traditional alchemical term for the "nigredo" or black stage, symbolizing the death of the old form</term>. Then it is necessary to continue a gentle fire over it, until it has conceived the dark cloud which it has brought forth. The whole intention of all the Philosophers is and was, that the body, now dissolved into a black powder,

### *How our stone ought to be turned red; hear the Rosary.* <note>original: "Rosarium," referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note>

Unless you first whiten our <term>bronze|original: "æs," representing the base material or "body" of the stone</term>, you cannot make it red: because no one can pass from one extreme to the other, except through the middle. This is to say: no one can come from black to yellow <note>original: "citrinum," the citrine or yellow stage sometimes seen between white and red</note>, except through white, because yellow is composed of much white and the purest black. Therefore, whiten the black and redden the white, and you will have the <term>mastery|original: "magisterium," the completed Alchemical Work or the Philosopher's Stone</term>.

For just as the year is divided into four parts, so also is our blessed work. For first is **Winter**, which is cold, moist, and rainy. The second season is **Spring**, which is hot, moist, and flowery. The third season is **Summer**, which is hot and dry: that is, reddish. The fourth season is **Autumn**, which is cold and dry, and the time for gathering fruit. By this arrangement, we tint natural things until they bring forth fruit according to our wishes: because now winter has passed, the rain has gone, the night has receded, and flowers have appeared in our land, and the time of pruning has come. <note>This passage is a direct paraphrase of the Song of Solomon 2:11–12, used here to describe the joy of reaching the white stage of the work.</note>

But when we stand upon the **white rose**, we will only gain this effect by converting metallic and "sick" bodies <note>Alchemists viewed base metals like lead or tin as "diseased" versions of gold; the Stone was the medicine that healed them into perfection.</note> into white by art and operation. And when you see that supereminent whiteness, be joyful and certain, because in that whiteness the **redness** is hidden. And this redness it does not behoove... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the next page begins with "you to extract."</note>

### Again on the natural, reciprocal, and circular
### proximity of the elements to one another.

Albertus Magnus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a famed Dominican scholar and philosopher who was widely believed in the Middle Ages to have discovered the secret of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> says: It must not be kept silent that in all things which relate to each other circularly through generation, their transition is easier, because they share a greater agreement in their properties.

It is for this reason that gold is more easily made from silver than from any other metal. Nature has therefore ordered things well, so that the elements <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> should communicate their qualities to one another in a circle, so that circular transmutations may be made from them, and that they may result from that circular transmutation. For instance, **earth** communicates its dryness to **fire**, **fire** indeed communicates its heat to **air**, **air** communicates its moisture to **water**, **water** indeed communicates its coldness to **earth**, and **earth** again communicates its dryness to **fire**. 

And thus, in a circular fashion, the matter of the earth <term>desires</term> <note>original: "appetit." Medieval science often used "appetite" or "desire" to describe the natural tendency of matter to seek a new "form" or state of being.</note> to exist under the form of fire: because fire, as if naturally thirsty, acts upon the earth and converts the earthy matter into its own form. Again, this same matter of the earth desires to exist under the form of air—for air is, as it were, naturally sensitive to fire. Therefore, it acts upon the fire and the earthy matter. And as for the fire, which had turned the earth into its own form, then that matter naturally desires to exist under the form of water. Water, sensing this, acts upon the air and upon that matter which was once fire, air, and earth, and thus converts it into its own form. Then that matter naturally...

It argues that because elements share qualities (like heat or dryness), they can naturally transform into one another in a circular cycle, which justifies the possibility of turning silver into gold.</summary>

In it I beheld all the forms of the elements, and even their contrarieties in that matter of the stone—by what power I know not, unless it be from appetite <note>The natural "desire" or "inclination" of matter to reach its most perfect state.</note>.
>
> For from the redness I perceived the form of fire; from the transparency, the form of water; and from the brilliance, the form of air.

...or father, <term>Hermes the Philosopher</term> <note>original: "Hermes Philosophus." This refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary, mythical founder of alchemy to whom many foundational texts were attributed.</note> says: That metals consist of the four elements, and each element abounds in its own matter out of the four elements, since a <term>simple element</term> <note>A "simple" element is a pure, theoretical form of Fire, Air, Earth, or Water; in the physical world, they are always found mixed or "compounded."</note> is not available to us for our work. Furthermore, in the matter of metals, it is necessary that the elements possess one common matter of bodies, which is of the common form of the elements, so that through them they can be transmuted.

And let that same matter which belonged to water, be of air, earth, and fire. There are therefore four qualities or virtues proceeding from the being of the elements, and any of these can be spoken of regarding elemental matter: and these virtues are those of heating, cooling, dryness, and humidity. Two of these qualities are active, namely hot and cold; while two are passive, namely moist and dry. There are therefore two elements—in comparison to elemental things—that are active, namely fire and water, and two that are as if passive, such as earth and air. Thus, to the extent that they are active and passive among themselves, they also share in a common nature.

It is for this reason that one element communicates its quality to another, so that by circulating in this way, it can convert the other's quality into itself, and it is transmuted. It must also be known that it is common to all metals that their matter is very close to one another in nature, in virtue, and in potential.

Hence <term>Albertus Magnus</term> <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a prominent Dominican scholar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, widely cited in alchemical literature for his works on minerals and nature.</note> says: Because in nature...

### *A recapitulation of the entire work of Alchemy, and of our stone, according to the intention of all the Philosophers.*

For every thing whose root is earth and water becomes "dying." This is to say, the earth becomes water, and the qualities of water overcome it; thus is the <term>solution</term>...

<header>THE ROSARY OF THE PHILOSOPHERS <note>original: "ROSARIUM PHILOSOPH." One of the most famous alchemical treatises, first printed in 1550, which uses the metaphor of a rose garden to describe the stages of the Great Work.</note></header>

Hear these things, children of the ancient Philosophers, which I desire to proclaim with as loud a voice as I can. For I come to reveal to you the principal state of human affairs, the <term>secret of all secrets</term> <note>original: "secretissimum omnium secretorum." Nor can anyone deservedly strike me with slanders: for since the ancient Philosophers wrote as obscurely as they did confusedly—so much so that not only are they not understood, but they do not even seem to agree—it was in order that they might either deceive those seeking this most precious art, or deter them from their purpose. <header>THE ROSARY</header>

Wherefore first we make it known, that all those operating **outside of nature** are deceivers, and labor in an improper thing. Furthermore, from a human nothing is born but a human, and from a beast nothing but a beast, and every like thing produces nothing but its own like. For this reason, he who does not possess the seed from the thing's own nature cannot have a result from a foreign nature according to his will. We say this, however, so that no one may lose his money. For since some have been deceived by the slowness of their own wit, and led to poverty, they also attempt to seduce others and drive them to misery. 

I advise, moreover, that no one should involve himself in this art for the sake of discovery, unless he recognizes the principle of **true nature** and its <term>regimen</term> <note>original: "regimen." In alchemy, this refers to the controlled method of directing the heat and the stages of the chemical process.</note>; once this is known, he needs no more things than one, nor does it require great expenses, since there is **one stone, one medicine, one vessel, one regimen, and one disposition.** 

And you should know that the art is most true. Furthermore, the Philosophers would never have studied to express so many diversities of colors and their order, unless they had seen and touched them. Wherefore we repeat that: All those laboring outside of nature are deceived and are deceivers. 

Therefore, our exercise and focused obedience take place within nature: because our <term>stone</term> <note>original: "lapis." The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the work.</note> is from an **animal, vegetable, and mineral** thing. Be of one will, therefore, in the work of nature, nor should you presume to attempt now this, now that, because our art is not perfected in a multitude of things. For however much its names are diversified, yet...

<meta>catchword: yet [tamen]</meta>

According to the philosophers, there is a double path in this art: namely, the **universal** and the **particular**. The **universal path** is easy and rare. It is such that it is drawn out from true and natural principles: by which a **seminal** and **restorative power** <note>original: "virtus seminaria & reformatiua." But the second path is called **particular**, and it is difficult and laborious. Note that although Alchemy in the universal path is partly natural and partly artificial, it is nevertheless more natural: because in the path of true Alchemy, nature introduces nothing foreign or external. Nature possesses that upon which it works, because the active agents are joined to the passive subjects through a suitable union or application; for the rest, nature operates by itself.

### PHILOSOPHY

...[radi]cal humidity, purity, clarity, fixing Earth, and Tincture.

The first of these distinct properties is **Oiliness** itself, which, during the <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiectione." The final stage of the alchemical process where the Stone or "medicine" is cast upon molten base metal to effect its transformation.</note>, provides a universal fusion and opening of the medicine. For the very first necessity after the projection of the medicine is its sudden and suitable melting, which is perfected and thoroughly integrated through its natural oiliness.

The second is the **Thinness** of the matter, or its spiritual subtlety, which is so thin or flowing when melted—much like water—that it penetrates into the very depths of the substance to be changed. This is because, secondly, after the melting of the medicine, its immediate entry into the metal is required.

The third is **Affinity** or closeness between the <term>Elixir</term> <note>original: "Elixir." A synonym here for the perfected Stone or medicine.</note> and the substance to be transmuted; this provides a lasting connection when it encounters its own likeness, ensuring it is retained. This is because, thirdly, after the medicine has entered the metal, a proper adherence is both fitting and necessary.

The fourth is the **Radical Humidity** <note>original: "radicalis Humiditas." In medieval science, this was the "essential moisture" or life-force inherent in a substance that allows it to remain flexible and alive; in alchemy, it is the fundamental liquid principle that prevents the Stone from being destroyed by fire.</note> and fire-like quality, which congeals and solidifies the retained parts by clinging to what is similar to it, creating an inseparable union of all like parts forever. For fourthly, after that adherence, the consolidation of the parts is made possible and necessary by its viscous radical humidity.

The fifth is **Purity** and purified **Clarity**, which grants an eminent splendor even in the heat of the fire—

...I conclude <note>original: "dò." Likely the end of "concludo" (I conclude) or "dico" (I say), following from the previous page.</note> that no **dissolution** <note>original: "solutio." The first major stage of the Great Work, symbolizing the chaos or the "death" of the old form.</note>. Seventhly, that it should be coagulated in the dryness of the Sun in moisture: that is, in the **bath of Mary** <note>original: "balneo Mariæ," or bain-marie. A water bath used to provide gentle, even heating.</note>. Eighthly, that the time for the perfection of the **Elixir** is at least one year. However, it is to be noted that it ought to be the time of a human fetus in the mother's womb <note>Alchemists often compared the growth of the Stone to the development of a baby, roughly nine months to a year.</note>. Ninthly, that Mercury is in no way **killed** <note>original: "interficitur." To "kill" mercury means to "fix" it, turning it from a volatile liquid into a stable solid that can withstand fire.</note> except with the scent of a perfect red body for the red work, and a white body for the white work: and that the body can give weight while its own weight remains.

There are four things by which our work is completed: namely weight, fire, body, and spirit. Tenthly, that all common recipes are to be scorned in this art. Eleventhly, that once the things are prepared and placed in the vessel, it will be **child's play** <note>original: "ludus puerorum." A common alchemical phrase suggesting that after the difficult preparation is done, the final transformation requires only steady heat and patience.</note>, and that the **mastery** <note>original: "magisteriũ." The Great Work or the completion of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> can be fulfilled in a single vessel.

Likewise, whoever possesses the true **Mercury**, possesses the **Elixir** <note>The "Elixir" or "Philosopher's Stone" is the goal of the work, capable of perfecting metals and human health.</note>, and that the Elixir is Mercury **mortified** <note>original: "mortificatus." Likewise, note that it is absolutely necessary that **Mercury** be made in the body: that is, that the fixed becomes **volatile** <note>Substances that evaporate or rise when heated.</note> with the volatile: that is, with pure Mercury. And it is necessary that there be more of the volatile than the fixed, from double the amount up to fivefold, or sevenfold, up to tenfold, and no further. And the more volatile parts there are, the more slowly they are fixed, and the fixed becomes volatile in the space of one month. And note that there cannot be an Elixir unless the body and spirit pass through all the elements: that is, through the natures of all the elements, so that they first become **earth**, then **air**—that is, vapor—thirdly **water**, and fourthly **fire**: [so that] the unfixed <note>original: "infixa." Referring to the volatile state that has not yet been stabilized.</note> flees from the fire; for "fire" is the name given to everything that does not flee the fire, and which does not wither or be consumed in the fire.

Whoever wishes to investigate the secret of this art must know the **First Matter** <note>original: "materia prima." The fundamental, undifferentiated substance from which all metals and things are created.</note> of our bodies, otherwise he will be frustrated in his labor.

The First Matter of bodies is not common mercury <note>original: "Mercurius vulgi." Oily or greasy. Alchemists believed metals were composed of a "fatty" sulfur and a "moist" mercury.</note> and moist vapor. For from the moist comes the mineral stone, and from the unctuous comes the metallic body. For it is necessary that bodies be converted into such an unctuous vapor, and in this conversion, the bodies are destroyed <note>original: "interimuntur."</note>.
