### ROSARIVM

[Hermes] <note>original: "dicit" (he says). The catchword from the previous page indicates this is a quote from Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy.</note> says: It is necessary that the **medicine** be of swifter melting <term>fusion|The process of a solid becoming liquid through heat; here, the "medicine" must liquify before the mercury can evaporate.</term> than **Mercury**, so that it flows more quickly before the flight <note>original: "fugam." In alchemy, "flight" refers to the evaporation or sublimation of volatile substances like mercury.</note> of Mercury. And it is necessary that fire can neither consume nor destroy it. And then it is called **fusible salt**, and **incombustible oil**, and the **soap of the wise**. Likewise: Note, the **salt of metals** transmutes Mercury into true **Sun and Moon** <note>original: "Solem & Lunam," the standard alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver.</note>. And thus the **salt of animals** transmutes any animal substance into a true temperance and an optimal constitution. 

The **fire of dung** <term>ignis fimi|A traditional alchemical heat source created by the fermentation of manure, providing a steady, gentle, and moist warmth.</term> is the active cause in the work of the **digestion** of our stone; nor is the fire of the **Bath of Mary** <term>balnei Mariae|A water bath (the ancestor of the bain-marie), which the author argues is less effective for this specific stage than manure.</term> suitable in its place, even though it may be very temperate. 

Whence **Alphidius** <note>An Arab alchemist frequently cited in medieval texts.</note> says: To cook with the fire which I shall show you is to hide the matter in moist **horse dung**, which is the fire of the wise—moist and obscure—and it is hot in the second degree and moist in the first degree. The property of this fire is not to destroy the oil—that is, the **matter**—but it increases it on account of its temperate moisture. For only that heat is equal and temperate, and such is highly necessary in the generation of this thing. 

Whence **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> says: Because these are the most subtle vapors <note>original: "fumi." Refers to the volatile spirits within the alchemical vessel.</note>, they need a temperate boiling <note>original: "decoctione."</note>, so that they may be thickened <note>original: "inspissentur."</note> within themselves according to a state of equality. For only temperate heat is capable of thickening moisture and perfecting the mixture, and it does not exceed the proper limit. For the generations and procreations of natural things are only able to occur through the most temperate and equal heat, such as is found only in moist and hot **horse dung**.

# ROSARIUM

<insert>AB</insert>

->*Geber, in the book of the perfect magistery.* <note>original: "Geber libro perfecti magisterij." Geber refers to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous figure in early Islamic alchemy, though the "Perfect Magistery" is likely a Latin work attributed to him.</note><-

The practitioner of this science must be of the most subtle intellect, and must know and recognize the natures of metals and their births, weaknesses, and imperfections in their ores <note>original: "mineris"</note> before he may arrive at this art. However, a practitioner who is filled with a dull and stubborn wit should not approach this investigation, nor should one who is greedy or stingy regarding costs and expenses. Nor should he be a man of double-mind—lacking resolve <note>original: "sine felle & ceruice," literally "without gall and neck," implying a lack of courage or steadfastness</note>—or changeable in mind, nor too hasty or headstrong. Rather, he should be a **son of the doctrine** <term>doctrinæ filius|A traditional term for an initiate or student of alchemical secrets who follows the established lineage of wisdom.</term>, a man graced with a most subtle intellect, sufficiently wealthy, generous, healthy, firm and constant in purpose, patient, gentle, long-suffering, and temperate. 

Alphidius: Know, my son, that you cannot possess this science until you purify your mind for God, and until God knows that you have a certain and upright soul; then He will make you a master of the world. 

Aristotle: Oh, if God recognized a faithful mind in a man, He would surely reveal the secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> to him.

->*The Corrector of Fools.* <note>original: "Corrector Fatuorum." Likely a reference to the *Correctorium Alchymiae*, a text intended to correct the errors of "false" alchemists.</note><-

In every art it is necessary to follow the refining process <note>original: "scoriam," referring to the dross or slag from which the pure metal is separated</note>, and to recognize the nature of that thing whose nature it is; thus art imitates its own nature. Know, O fool, that nature is distinguished through art, and it cannot be corrected; for it would be impossible for the **secrets of the Philosophers** to reach a perfect end for one who does not follow nature.

# PHILOSOPHERS

->*Hermes & Geber.*<-

He who has once perfected this art, even if he were to live for a thousand thousands of years and were required to feed four thousand men every single day, he would never be in want <note>original: "non egeret." This refers to the belief that the Philosopher's Stone could provide inexhaustible wealth and health.</note>. The Elder <note>original: "Senior," referring to the 10th-century Arabian alchemist Zadith ben Hamuel.</note> confirms this, saying: One who possesses the stone from which the **Elixir** <term>Elixir|From the Arabic 'al-iksir', a substance believed to be capable of changing base metals into gold or prolonging life.</term> is made is just as wealthy as one who possesses fire; for he who has fire can give fire to whomever he wants, whenever he wants, and as much as he wants, without any personal risk or loss to himself. Aristotle, in the twentieth <note>The source cites the 20th book of "De Anima," though Aristotle's "On the Soul" only contains three books; this likely refers to a specific medieval compilation or a misattribution.</note> book *On the Soul*: The most natural and perfect work is to generate something that is exactly like itself.

->*Table of the Greater Science.*<-

In the first stage, the true matter is found in our **Green Lion** <term>Leo viridis|A symbolic term for a potent acidic solvent or the raw mineral state of the matter (often associated with vitriol or antimony) before it is purified.</term>; it is known by what color it is, and it is called **Adrop** <note>original: "Adrop," a term often signifying lead or the "body" of the stone.</note>, **Azoth** <note>original: "Azoth," the essential transformative agent or universal solvent.</note>, or **Green Duenech** <note>original: "Duenech viride," likely a reference to antimony or a specific mineral ore.</note>.

In the second and the thirtieth stages, it is similarly held how bodies are dissolved into the **living silver** <note>original: "argentum vivum," usually meaning mercury.</note> of the Philosophers: that is, into the water of our **Mercury** <term>Mercurius|In alchemy, this is not common quicksilver, but the "philosophical" mercury, the spirit or soul of the matter.</term>, and thus one new body is created. In the fourth, the **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio|The stage of decay or "death" of the material, essential for its subsequent rebirth and purification.</term> of the Philosophers occurs, which has never been seen in our days, and it is called **sulfur**. In the fifth, it is held how the greater part of this water is made into a black and dreggy earth, <insert>AB.</insert> of which all the Philosophers speak. In the sixth, it is held how that black earth stood upon the water in the beginning, and was gradually submerged into the bottom of the vessel. In the seventh, it is held how that earth is dissolved back into water with the color of oil, and it is then called the **Oil of the Philosophers**.

## PHILOSOPHY

...to whiteness <note>original: "albedinem."</note>, and it changes copper from a physical state to a spiritual one <note>original: "à corporalitate ad ſpiritualitatem." In alchemical terms, 'spirituality' refers to a substance being made volatile or "subtle" enough to penetrate other metals.</note>, and through that substance, bodies are calcined. Whence the *Light of Lights* <note>A common title for authoritative alchemical texts, often referring to a work attributed to the Persian polymath Rhazes.</note> says: "If almighty God had not created this salt, the **Elixir** would not be perfected, and the alchemical study would be in vain."

Note, there are four Mercuries: namely, crude Mercury, sublimated Mercury, Mercury of **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia|In early alchemy, this does not refer to magnesium oxide, but to the "mother" or base mineral substance that contains the 'seed' of the metals; here equated with the full Moon or Silver.</term>, and unctuous <note>oily or fatty</note> Mercury. # ROSARIUM

...ours and that of the wise, and it is not found upon the earth except for that which is extracted from those bodies. **Arnoldus** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>: **Sulphur** which is hidden in **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento viuo."</note> is that which gives the golden form to the quicksilver itself, through the power of the color of its external mineral sulphur. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose works were central to the development of alchemy.</note>: Such sulphur is not found upon the earth, except for that which is in the bodies [of metals]. Therefore, let those bodies be subtly prepared, so that we may have sulphur upon the earth. For a perfect body, through our **mastery** <term>Mastery|Latin: magisterium. The technical process or the "Great Work" of the alchemist.</term>, assists and perfects the imperfect body, without the mixing of any foreign thing. Otherwise, sulphur of whatever kind it may be hinders proper melting <note>original: "fuſionem."</note>, as is evident in iron, which does not melt because it is known to have fixed sulphur within itself. If, however, it is not fixed, it anticipates the proper melting and is hindered by the fire, and it is burned and evaporates, as is evident in lead and in other weak bodies. Therefore, common sulphur <note>original: "sulphur vulgare."</note> is not part of the truth of our art, nor of its perfection, since it hinders the perfect substance in all its operations. Whence **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the "Father of Alchemy."</note>: Sulphur can never be fixed unless it is **calcined** <term>Calcined|The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or to oxidize it.</term>; and when it has been calcined, it gives no melting at all. **Senior** <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century Arabic alchemist.</note>: Sulphur and arsenic are not the true medicine of this mastery, because they do not complete nor perfect, as is sufficiently known concerning all the "lesser minerals." **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and influential scholar.</note>: It is the property of sulphur to congeal **Mercury** and to bring it to perfection with Mercury. But the tincture only...

### PHILOSOPHY

...the <term>Philosopher’s Stone|Latin: lapis Philosophorum. The legendary substance sought by alchemists, believed to have the power to transform base metals into gold and provide the Elixir of Life.</term> consists. From that which is perfect, nothing [new] can be made, because it is already perfect; we have an example of this in nature or art in the form of bread. Leavened and baked bread is perfect in its state or being, and it has reached its ultimate end; nothing more can be <term>leavened|Latin: fermentari. In alchemy, "fermentation" is the process where a small amount of a potent substance—the "ferment"—is added to a larger mass to transform it, similar to how yeast transforms dough.</term> from it. It is the same with gold: pure gold has been brought through the trial of fire into a firm and fixed body, and it is entirely impossible for the Philosophers to leaven anything further with it, unless the <term>prime matter|Latin: materia prima. The primal, formless substance that alchemists believed was the foundation of all physical reality.</term> of metals is obtained, in which the gold may be dissolved back into its first matter and into mixable elements. 

Therefore, let us take that matter from which gold originates, and by means of the <term>art|Latin: artificium. A standard term for the practice and skill of alchemy.</term>, let it be led into the true ferment of the Philosophers. And let us skillfully change this into perfect matter, or into the spirit of perfect bodies. For this reason, many among the modern workers—and even some philosophers—are deceived, because they abandon the work at the very point where it ought to have been started. Woe to you, sons of doctrine, who hope to gather fruit before it is ripe, and hope to reap before the harvest!

**Another Philosopher:** Nothing can be made from the perfect, since a species of thing that is perfect in its nature does not change, but is rather corrupted <note>original: "corrumpitur". Nor can anything be made entirely from the imperfect according to the art. The reason is that art cannot provide the primary <term>dispositions|The fundamental natural qualities or arrangements of matter that allow it to become a specific substance.</term>; instead, our stone is a middle thing between perfect and imperfect bodies, and that which nature itself began, this [is completed] through...

### The arrangement of the vessel suitable for our work, according to the tradition of a certain man named Ferrarius <note>Ferrarius, also known as Efferarius the Monk, was a renowned 13th- or 14th-century alchemical author known for his practical laboratory instructions.</note>.

Let there be a round glass basin <note>original: concha vitrea</note>, the bottom of which is of a small size in the manner of a side-dish <note>original: parapsidis; a shallow bowl or plate used in dining.</note>. And in its center, let a spindle-base <note>original: spódilium</note> be formed with a glass ring surrounding it. And above that ring, let a round wall be cast, equally distant from the basin's wall by the thickness of the basin’s lid, so that in this space the wall of the lid may fit loosely without pressure. 

The height of this wall should be equal to the height of the basin's wall, or a little more or a little less. Truly, let two lids be formed to the measure of the concavity of these two walls, which should be equal in length—each being two large hand-spans <note>original: palmarum</note>—and their shape should be identical, namely pyramidal. At their tips, let there be two equal holes, one in each lid, through both of which a single hen's feather might fit. 

The entire purpose of the vessel is so that its lid can be removed at the will of the craftsman, and that the joint be so ingenious that even without any sealing-clay <note>original: lutatione; "lute" was a specialized paste used by alchemists to seal vessel joints airtight to prevent the escape of vapors.</note>, it does not lie open <meta>catchword: to spirits</meta>

...of magnesia <term>magnesia: in alchemy, this is not just magnesium oxide but a term for the "raw material" or the "mother" of the stone</term> to be mixed so that it may be cooked and ground with the water of life <term>aqua vitae: "water of life," usually referring to distilled alcohol or a potent solvent</term>, until it is broken down. And what you do in the white body, do also in the red: because this medicine is one in essence, and similarly one in its manner of operating.

### PHILOSOPHERS

...[it achieves] constriction, whiteness, and redness, and it is called the **great animal**. And the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical symbol for Silver</note> is called a plant, and **alkali salt** is made from it. **Mercury**, however, is called the mineral stone, and common salt is made from it. 

**Likewise:** When the Philosophers saw the matter of this art dissolved, they called it sal ammoniac. And when it was putrefied <term>putrefaction: the stage where the matter decomposes and turns black</term>, then they said "our stone is vile, and is found in a dunghill." And many have dug and worked in dung, and found nothing. 

But when it was turned into water, both the rich and the poor have it, and it is found in every place, at any time, and in everything—though the search for it weighs heavily on the seeker. And when it was whitened, they called it **Arsenic**, and by the name of every white thing, and **virgin’s milk** <term>lac virginis: a symbolic name for a white, milky liquid or precipitate produced during the process</term>. And when it was red, they called it **sulfur**, **hyacinth**, and **blood**, and by the name of any red thing.

**Gratianus:** From every thing ash can be made, and from that ash salt can be made, and from that salt water is made, and from that water Mercury is made, and from that Mercury, through various operations, the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol," the alchemical symbol for Gold</note> is made.

**Arnoldus:** This ash, however, lacks the ability to melt. But so that it may enter into the metal to "tinge" it <term>tinge: to transform or dye a base metal into gold or silver</term>, surely the ability to liquefy is restored to it, or a "sweat," through the method handed down by the Philosophers. What then is that method? Is it by dissolving it into water? Certainly not; because the Philosophers do not care for waters that stick to the touch <note>original: "aquis tangenti adhaerentibus," likely referring to common water that wets the hands, as opposed to "mercurial water"</note>, or such kinds of dampness.

# ROSARY

**The Philosopher:** Whoever wishes to alter bodies and spirits, and change them from their original nature, must first reduce them to the nature of **salts** and **alums** <term>alums: a group of hydrated double sulfates, but used here to refer to a specific class of astringent mineral substances used in fixing dyes or "fixing" the alchemical spirit</term>; otherwise he will accomplish nothing. **The Philosopher:** Salts and alums are those things which are created by our operations. Wherefore **Arnoldus** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says: "Whoever possesses a fusible salt and an incombustible oil would praise God." **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy</note> says: "If you wish to be enriched, prepare the salts until they become pure water; for salts are converted into spirit by the fire. And that coagulated mixture will be the perfect medicine.

**Note:** Every well-prepared salt returns to the nature of **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "salis armoniaci"</note>, and the entire secret lies in the prepared common salt. **Note:** **Roman Vitriol** <term>Roman Vitriol: copper(II) sulfate or iron(II) sulfate, often used as a source of sulfuric acid or for its "sharp" acidic qualities</term> has the nature of the stone of metals, and it is hot and dry. **Likewise:** **Alum** seems to be a coagulated Mercury, but it falls short of its completion; it is hot and moist, and is called "the peer of one"—that is, Mercury. He, therefore, who knows salt and its dissolution, knows the hidden secret of the ancient wise men. Therefore, set your mind upon the salt, and do not think about...

## CONJUNCTION OR
### Union <note>original: "Coitus"</note>

O **Luna** <note>The Moon, representing the feminine principle, cool and moist, often associated with Silver</note>, through my embrace and sweet love,
You shall become beautiful, strong, and powerful as I am.
O **Sol** <note>The Sun, representing the masculine principle, hot and dry, often associated with Gold</note>, you are to be recognized above all lights,
Yet you have need of me, as the rooster needs the hen.

<note>This famous illustration and accompanying verse depict the "Chemical Wedding" or **Conjunction** <term>Conjunction: the stage where the dualities of nature—masculine and feminine, fixed and volatile—are joined into one</term>. The King (Sol) and Queen (Luna) represent the two primary forces of the work. Their union in the water signifies the dissolution of their individual forms into a single, unified substance. The rooster and hen analogy is a classic alchemical metaphor for the biological necessity of both sexes for generation; even the "superior" gold (Sol) cannot reproduce or reach perfection without the "inferior" silver (Luna).</note>

### Arisleus in a vision.

Therefore, join your son Gabricus <note>Gabricus is a symbolic name for the masculine principle, often associated with sulfur or "the spirit." For this reason, you should not take up this nature unless it is pure, clean, raw, pleasant, earthy, and true <note>original: "rectam"</note>. If you do otherwise, it will be of no use. Join, therefore, our servant to his fragrant sister, and they shall beget a son between them who will not resemble the parents. And although Gabricus is dearer to Beya, generation cannot happen without Gabricus. Indeed, the mating <note>original: "concubitus"</note> of Gabricus with Beya is followed immediately by death. For Beya rises over Gabricus and encloses him in her womb so completely that nothing of him can be seen. She embraced Gabricus with such love that she absorbed his whole being into her own nature and dissolved him into indivisible parts. Regarding this, Masculanus <note>An alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval texts like the Rosarium.</note> says in verse:

> *The conception which was like milk changes to blood,*
> *Pale things turn black, and the scattered red things begin to shine,*
> *The white woman, if she be married to a red husband,*
> *They soon embrace, and having embraced, they are joined together.*

The ***Turba*** <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum* — "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note> says: Our grinding <note>original: *contritio* — the process of breaking down or pulverizing matter</note> is not done by hands, but by the strongest decoction <term>decoctio — the process of extracting the essence of a substance by boiling or intense, prolonged heating</term>. **Calidius** <note>referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince traditionally credited as the first Arab alchemist</note>: A lesser fire grinds everything. Note: there is a difference between an element, a thing composed of elements <note>original: *elementatum*</note>, and the fifth essence <term>quinta essentia — the "quintessence," a pure, incorruptible celestial substance distinct from the four terrestrial elements</term>. An element is the first of things capable of being composed; hence neither earth, nor water, nor air, nor fire is a pure and simple element among us, because these things are mixed with one another, and especially in that part where they join together. But the fifth essence is a body subsisting by itself, differing from all elements and things composed of elements, as much in matter as in form, as much in nature as in power; it has no cause of decay within itself, and it is called the "fifth essence" for this reason: because it is extracted from all things composed of elements, and there is no elemental motion within it, as there is in other elemental bodies. Therefore the Stone is called "every thing": because it has within itself and from itself every thing ne- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with "necessary" on the next page.</note>

Our Stone is called "one thing" when the substance of the body and the water are prepared indivisibly, so that one cannot be separated from the other.

If you extract this stone from the thing in which it is found and begin to work upon it toward perfection, starting from the point where nature left it, you will find perfection within it and you will rejoice.

**Parmenides the Philosopher:** <note>A Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher. **Bacchus the Philosopher:** <note>Likely referring to a legendary figure or a corruption of a name like Boccus; in this context, he represents the voice of natural philosophy.</note> When natures are corrupted and decay, then they bring forth life.

**Plato the Philosopher:** We have an example in the egg, which first decays, and then the chick is born, which—after the whole has been corrupted—is a living animal. <note>The "philosophical egg" was a common term for the sealed glass flask used by alchemists, suggesting that life only emerges from the breakdown of the initial contents.</note>

**Plato:** Note that without corruption, generation cannot occur; therefore, you should focus your study on putrefaction.

**The Philosopher:** <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle, whose natural philosophy formed the backbone of medieval alchemy.</note> The corruption of one thing is the generation of another.

**Hermes:** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> The second step is to rot and to grind. **Plato:** The first reign of **Saturn** <note>In alchemy, Saturn is the planetary symbol for lead and the color black; its "reign" signifies the beginning of the decay process.</note> is to rot, and to place it upon the **Sun**. <note>The Sun represents gold or the essential heat needed to facilitate the change.</note> The composition, indeed, is made from four nights.

**Democritus:** <note>A Greek philosopher often associated in alchemy with the secret properties of minerals.</note> Do not be lazy nor too swift in rotting the stones; and when the bodies are arranged and joined together, pay attention to your work, and you shall succeed.

**Morienes:** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> Nothing grows or is born except after putrefaction. But if the rot was not—

**Morienes:** <note>Morienes, or Morienus, was a legendary 7th-century hermit of Jerusalem, said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid. He represents the transmission of "hidden" wisdom from the East to the West.</note> Our Stone is the very composition of the mastery itself, and in its order, it is likened to the creation of a human being. For first is intercourse, second is conception, third is pregnancy, fourth is birth, and fifth, nourishment follows. O most dear friend, understand these words of Morienes, and you shall not stray from the truth. Open your eyes, therefore, and see that the **sperm of the Philosophers** <term>sperma Philosophorum — the active, fluid principle of the work, often associated with "philosophical mercury"</term> is **living water**; <note>original: "aqua viva"</note> but the **earth** is the **imperfect body**, which earth is rightly called the **mother**, because she is the mother of all the elements. Therefore, when the "sperm" is joined with the "earth" of the imperfect body, it is then called "intercourse"; for then the earth of the body is dissolved into the water of the sperm, and they become one water, without any division.

**Whence Hali says:** <note>Likely referring to Haly Abenragel or another Arab alchemist whose works were translated into Latin. Medieval alchemists relied heavily on these "authorities" to validate their chemical theories.</note> The dissolution of the body and the thickening of the spirit are two things, yet they possess a single operation. For the spirit is not thickened <note>original: "coagulatur" — to become solid or fixed</note> except by the dissolution of the body. Nor is the body dissolved except by the thickening of the spirit; and when the body and the soul are joined together, each acts upon its like.

**For example:** When water is joined to the earth, the water—by its own moisture and power—strives to dissolve the earth. It makes the earth more subtle <note>In alchemy, "subtle" means refined, purified, or broken down into its most basic, potent form.</note> than it was before, and renders the earth similar to itself, because water is more subtle than earth. The soul acts in the same way within the body. And in this same manner, the water is thickened by the earth, and becomes similar to the densified earth...

For a pure body, once it has been putrefied <note>original: "putrefactum" — in alchemy, this refers to a stage of decomposition or breaking down of matter to its primal state</note>, immediately grows and multiplies into its own likeness. Conception and the betrothal <note>original: "desponsatio" — the symbolic marriage of the chemical ingredients</note> take place in the putrefaction at the bottom of the vessel, and the generation of the offspring will take place in the "air," namely in the head of the vessel: that is, the <term>alembic — the cap or "still-head" of a distilling apparatus</term>. This is so that nothing rises; for if anything were to ascend, a separation of the parts would occur. This must not happen until the male and female <note>symbolizing the active/sulfuric and passive/mercurial principles</note> are perfectly joined and one receives the other. The sign of this is seen on the surface by the cleverness of a perfect solution. And although <term>azoth — a term for the universal solvent or the essential mercurial spirit</term> appears white in the first mixing or conjunction (because the "female" overcomes with her color), nevertheless, both are turned black in putrefaction through the benefit of the fire. Through the fire increasing the heat within the moisture, the matter putrefies into a blackness, which is the <term>tincture — the concentrated essence capable of transforming metals</term>, and therefore it must be preserved. **A great secret.**

Geber <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> proves in the *Book of Examinations* that if Sol <note>Gold</note> and Luna <note>Silver</note> are incorporated together by art, they are not easily separated. And after one has been joined to the other, they embrace each other with such a strong bond and contain each other in such a way that one cannot easily be torn from the other. This will be much stronger if one of them is spiritual: that is, medicinal: and thus capable of dyeing <note>original: "tingibile" — in alchemy, the power of a substance to penetrate and change the color or nature of another metal</note>, by reason of its spirituality. 

Gold is gold in actuality, and it is the matter itself; but if it is spiritualized, it is transformed from an actual state into a potential one, and from matter into form, and from a passive act into an active agent, and from a female into a male, and from a created thing into a creative thing <note>original: "ex re nata res naturans" — a scholastic concept distinguishing between the final product (res nata) and the creative force that produces it (res naturans)</note>. Therefore, since there is no matter of gold—that is, no gold which was not previously silver—as the Philosopher says: 
> If, then, such a form is joined to its own matter (that is, to Luna), they will certainly embrace each other most greedily; and the greater perfection completes the lesser perfection, and this happens naturally and amicably, because every nature desires to be perfected and naturally abhors being destroyed.

A letter to Hafen <note>Possibly a reference to an alchemical author or a corrupted name common in medieval manuscripts.</note> concerning the hidden matter. The intention of those working in this art, or rather the intention of the art itself, according to the possibility of the nature of things, is to clothe the matter of one thing with the form and nature of another. For example: to clothe copper <note>original: "Cuprum"</note> with the form and nature of silver, or lead <note>original: "plumbum"</note> with that of gold, and so on for the others similarly. For since the "form" is the nature of each individual thing (as is held in the second book of the *Physics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Physics*, the foundational text for medieval science which argues that a thing is defined more by its "form" (its essential nature) than its "matter."</note>), once a thing is stripped of its form and another form is induced upon it, undoubtedly its very nature is transmuted from its species. We say, therefore, that the name Alchemy <note>original: "Alkimia"</note> in Greek signifies Transmutation. And hence we say that Alchemy is the science of the transmutation of things from their forms and species, according to
->how the forms of things<-
->are divided.<-

### *pistle of Hermes <note>original: "Epistolam Hermetis"; referring to the famous Emerald Tablet, a foundation of Hermetic philosophy.</note> says:*

Only he who knows how to make the **Philosopher's Stone** understands their words concerning the Stone. And it is called sublimation, exaltation, and dignification, because the Moon is dignified and [ennobled like] Mercury. For when the union is made in such dignity, the Moon is like the Sun and Mercury. Thus...

...ours, and there to see and possess roses, both white and red, without that **vile thing** <note>original: *re vili*. And in it is contained every secret, and it is called a divine mystery given by God, and in the World there is no thing more sublime after the rational soul.

You ought to note carefully: I told you that our **stone** is adorned with a **triple garment** <note>The "triple garment" refers to the three constituent principles of all matter in alchemy: Body (*Corpus*), Soul (*Anima*), and Spirit (*Spiritus*). O Master, I do not understand.

Son, I will speak to you more clearly: It is **one stone**, or rather, one thing only: because the body is reduced into its own nature, namely, into its own **water**; that is, into its **first matter** <note>original: *primam materiam*. The "First Matter" is the formless, original substance from which all things were created, sought by alchemists as the starting point for the Great Work.</note>. For the first matter of bodies is **unctuous water** <note>original: *aqua unctuosa*. This "oily water" represents a substance that is both fluid (mercurial) and flammable or cohesive (sulfurous), often associated with the "mercury of the philosophers."</note>, and then it is first called "one thing," when the substance of the body and the water of union are indivisibly united through the smallest parts. This is the **Philosophical Stone** from which infinite branches are multiplied. And this is called the "Stone" known in the books of the Philosophers. Therefore, son, from that stone its own proper water is extracted, and it is in the spirit by means of separation.

Our **sublimation** <note>original: *Sublimatio*. In modern chemistry, this is a solid turning to gas. In alchemy, it meant a process of purifying a substance by heating it so that the "pure" spirit rose and the "impure" dross remained at the bottom.</note> is the elevation of the non-fixed parts from the fixed parts. Truly, the non-fixed parts are elevated by smoke and wind.

But we wish that these two be fixed together, and provide for easy **fusion** <note>original: *fusionem*. The ability of the material to melt and flow like wax, indicating it has reached a state of metallic perfection.</note>. And in this way, you may understand our true and certain sublimation, and the stone which no one can touch with his tongue.

# PHILOSOPHY #
->Ss 5<-

Hermes says: **Separate the subtle from the gross**, etc. The **earth** is calcined <term>calcined|A process of heating a solid to high temperatures to remove volatile substances or reduce it to a dry powder (calx)</term>, and the **water** is sublimated <term>sublimated|In alchemy, this refers to heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the purified solid as it cools</term>: the earth remains below, the water ascends above. The earth is purified through calcination, and the water through sublimation: both through **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction|A stage of 'decay' or fermentation where the matter turns black, seen as a necessary death before rebirth into a purified state</term>. 

Water protects the earth so it is not burned, and earth binds the water so it does not flee; once both are sufficiently purified, they become **one thing**, inseparable from then on. This is because one cannot exist without the other. The first part of this substance, when projected <note>The "projection" is the final step of alchemy, where a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone is cast onto molten metal to transform it.</note> upon a hundred parts of quicksilver <note>original: *argenti vivi*, literally "living silver" or mercury.</note>, tinges it into true silver. And if such a **tincture** <note>In this context, a "tincture" is the concentrated transformative power of the Stone itself.</note> is turned into the red, one part tinges just as many parts into true gold—than which no better gold is found—and this occurs through a nature that is both hidden and acquired through the heat of fire, etc.

**Note:** The Spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters before the creation of heaven and earth, Genesis chapter one.

It must therefore be seen that all things were created from **water**. God divided this water when He spoke, and He commanded a part of the water into dryness, and that He called **earth**. The water not converted into earth He preserved for irrigation and moistening, because dry earth does not yield much fruit unless it is moistened frequently by its own rain-water from above, and without water it yields little or nothing at all.

<note>The author is paralleling the "Great Work" of alchemy with the divine Creation in Genesis. Just as God separated the "waters" to create the world, the alchemist separates the "subtle" from the "gross" to create the Stone.</note>

<summary>This page describes the alchemical process of purifying earth and water through calcination and sublimation to create a unified substance capable of transforming mercury into silver or gold. It draws a direct parallel between the alchemist's work and God's creation of the world from water as described in Genesis.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, calcination, sublimation, putrefaction, quicksilver, tincture, Philosopher's Stone, Genesis, Creation, alchemy and religion</keywords>

# ROSARY #

## THE JUBILATION OF THE SOUL, OR
### *The Rising, or Sublimation.*

Here the soul swoops down, 
And revives the purified body once more.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration depicting the "Animae Iubilatio" (Jubilation of the Soul). In the upper register, a naked human figure representing the soul dives downward from stylized clouds. Below, a stone sarcophagus sits on the ground, containing the recumbent body of a man. At the base of the tomb in the foreground, two birds, appearing to be crows or ravens, are perched on the earth; one looks forward while the other looks back toward the tomb.</image-desc>

Now the fourth stage <note>original: *verbum*, literally "word," but referring here to a stage of the process or a dictum of the masters.</note> follows, which is: that the water, which has been thickened and coagulated with the earth, should ascend through **sublimation** <term>sublimation|A process where a substance is heated to become a vapor and then collects again as a solid; in alchemy, this represents the purification and 'spiritualization' of matter</term>. Thus you have **earth**, **water**, and **air**. And this is what the Philosopher <note>In alchemical texts, "The Philosopher" usually refers to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus.</note> says: **Whiten it** <note>original: *dealbate*</note>, and quickly **sublimate it with fire**, until the **spirit** emerges from it, which you will find within it, which is called the **Bird**, or the ash of Her- <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "metis" indicates the full word is "Hermetis" or "The Ash of Hermes," a term for the stabilized metallic seed.</note>

<summary>This page describes the "Jubilation of the Soul," the stage where the purified spirit/soul returns to the body (the "earth") to revivify it. It details the transition from a thickened state to a sublimated one, involving the elements of earth, water, and air.</summary>

...mes. <note>original: *metis*, completing the name *Hermetis* (of Hermes) from the previous page.</note> Whence also Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist and teacher of Prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says:

# THE ROSARY

Rosinus: <note>original: *Rosinus*; a Latinized name usually referring to Zosimos of Panopolis, a Greco-Egyptian alchemist of the 3rd century.</note> For the body rejoices when the soul enters into it. The same author says: The body truly takes hold of the soul, and every body that finds a soul easily takes hold of it. And you should know that the soul is punished with the body, and is imprisoned with it, and by the body it is turned into the body. 

Hermes: <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" founder of the alchemical tradition.</note> The spirit itself is the extractor of the soul, and the one who brings it back, and the reformer of the whole work, and all things that we seek are within it. 

Senior: <note>Senior Zadith, the Latin name for the 10th-century alchemist Ibn Umail.</note> Nothing is more vile in appearance than it, and nothing in nature is more precious than it, and God has not set a price for it to be bought. 

Senior: Our preparation arises by nature through bolts opening the locks.

Hermes: It behoves us to know the knowledge of the beginning of both natural and artificial things. For he who is ignorant of the principles does not come to the end. The same author says: This secret is the life of every thing, and it is water, and water receives the nourishment of humans and others, and in water is the greatest secret. 

But so that you may err less, it is fitting for you to know that our **sublimating** <term>sublimating|In modern chemistry, this is when a solid turns directly into a gas. In alchemy, it refers to "exalting" or refining a substance to its highest, most spiritual state.</term> is nothing other than to **exalt the bodies**: that is, to lead them into the spirit, which is not done except by a gentle fire. For thus we say: "that man has been **sublimated** to the rank of bishop": that is, **exalted**. 

And therefore common sublimation—which is only an effect, namely, that the body to be sublimated has already been made so spiritual that it can be sublimated—contributes nothing to our work, nor is it required further after the preparation of the first stone: because such sublimation does not spiritualize, but only...

...shows the effect of spirituality. Therefore, that royal philosopher Geber <note>original: *Geber*; the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in Arabic and European alchemy.</note> says well: That in the work of our **mastery** <term>mastery|Latin: *magisterium*; the complete process or "Great Work" of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term> we need nothing but a single vessel, a single furnace, and a single disposition—understand this as being after the preparation of the first stone.

Genesis: <note>Referring to Genesis 1:2.</note> From water all things were made, and the spirit of God was carried over the waters, and the beginning of the generation of man is from it.

Aristotle: No tinting poison <note>original: *venenum*; often used in alchemy to mean a potent, transforming substance rather than a toxin.</note> is generated without the Sun and its shadow: that is, the wife. <note>In alchemical allegory, the "Sun" represents the masculine principle (Gold), and the "wife" or shadow represents the feminine principle (Silver or Mercury).</note>

**Sublimation** <term>sublimation|The process of purifying a substance by heating it into vapor and then cooling it back into a solid. Symbolically, it represents the "exaltation" or spiritualization of matter.</term> is twofold: The first is the removal of superfluity, so that the purest parts remain, separated from the elementary dregs, and thus they possess the virtue of the **quintessence** <term>quintessence|The "fifth essence"; the purest, most spiritual state of matter that exists beyond the four physical elements.</term>. And this sublimation is the reduction of bodies into spirit, namely when the density of the body passes into the subtlety of the spirit.

The second Sublimation is the extraction of what is in it of the nature of the quintessence, from the dregs...

...separated from the elemental parts. ->Vincent on the Stone of the Elixir.<-

Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais (c. 1190–1264), a Dominican friar whose "Speculum Naturale" (Mirror of Nature) was a massive encyclopedia often cited by alchemists.</note> in the *Mirror of Nature*, Book I: In mineral bodies, after the fashion of nature's own operation, the Alchemists have attempted to do in a short time what nature does in a thousand years. From this, they have taught how to make a certain thing which transmutes the bodies upon which it is projected. This is called by them the **Elixir**, and it is called the **stone that is not a stone**: it is a stone because it is ground; it is not a stone because it is melted and flows without evaporating, just like gold, nor is there any other thing to which that property belongs.

Avicenna: <note>Latin: *Auicen*; refers to the Persian polymath Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note> The **Elixir** <term>Elixir|The "tincture" or medicine of the metals capable of transforming base matter into gold.</term>, therefore, is a thing which is projected upon a larger body and changes that thing from its own nature into another. It is made when a lesser body, the spirit, the elements, and the ferment are mixed together, and from all of them one composition is made. 

And "Elixir" is a Greek word <note>While medieval authors often claimed a Greek origin, the word actually derives from the Arabic *al-iksīr*.</note> which signifies "great treasure," or "the best of treasures." And indeed, the Elixir that mixes itself with a body is like **tutty** <term>tutty|Latin: *tutia*; zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces, used in the making of brass.</term> with **copper** <term>copper|Latin: *cuprum*.</term>. But the copper is increased or grows from that tutty; the reason for this is because tutty is an earthy thing, while the Elixir is a spiritual thing, and the nature of its genus is returned to another genus.

The Alchemist: The **Elixir** <term>Elixir|A substance believed to be capable of changing base metals into gold or silver and providing a universal medicine.</term> is produced in two ways. One way is from mineral spirits and prepared pure bodies. The other way is from certain things originating from living beings, namely from hair, or eggs, or blood, and so on.

In the first method, it is done like this: certain spirits are **mortified** <term>mortified|Latin: *mortificantur*; in alchemy, this refers to the "death" of a substance, usually by stripping its external form or volatility to reach its inner essence.</term> and **sublimated** <term>sublimated|The process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifying it again to purify it.</term> until they become pure. After this, one of the bodies generated by nature is burned until it can be ground; then it is **calcined** <term>calcined|Latin: *calcinatur*; reduced to a fine powder or "calx" by intense heat, a process meant to purify the substance.</term> until it is made pure in the manner of lime.

Finally, the spirits and bodies prepared in this way are ground and soaked with distilled **sharp waters** <term>sharp waters|Latin: *aquis acutis*; these are typically corrosive or acidic liquids, such as mineral acids or strong vinegars, used to dissolve or "open" a substance.</term>. Afterward, they are moistened for so long until they are converted into clear water; then they are congealed, and at the last, they are placed in the fire for so long until they are made **fixed** <term>fixed|Latin: *fixa*; rendered stable and resistant to evaporation or change when exposed to intense heat.</term>.

->*On the Completion of the Elixir.*<-

**Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational to European alchemy.</note> in his letter to Hasen: The Elixir, therefore, tints with its own **tincture** <term>tincture|The active power or "soul" of the elixir that imparts color and properties to other metals.</term>, and is submerged in its own oil, and is fixed by its own lime. The **white elixir** <note>The "white" stage (albedo) of the work, which transmutes metals into silver.</note> is indeed completed by three things, in which there is no fire. But the **citrine** <note>Yellow or gold-colored (citrinitas), representing the transition to the final "red" stage.</note> is completed by all four. 

<gloss>The Gloss: It is true that the white Elixir needs nothing except three things, namely: oil, tincture, and lime. But the **red elixir** <note>The final stage (rubedo), which transmutes metals into gold.</note> needs four: namely, oil, lime, tincture, and a second tincture, which is called **Fire**. And for this reason, Avicenna adds: In which ->there is no fire.<-</gloss> <note>Avicenna's phrase "in which there is no fire" specifically refers to the white elixir, distinguishing it from the red elixir which requires the fourth element of spiritual fire.</note>

### On the manifold kinds of fire.

Fire is indeed manifold, and its quality is diverse, distinguished through certain degrees. For one kind of fire is hot in the first degree and moist in the second, namely the **heat of a horse’s belly** <term>horse's belly|Latin: *ventris equi*; a common alchemical term for a "dung bath" (fimus equinus). Flasks were buried in warm, fermenting horse manure to provide a gentle, consistent, and moist heat.</term>. Its property is that it does not destroy the **oil** <note>In alchemy, "oil" often refers to the essential, combustible, or "soul" component of a substance being purified.</note>, but rather increases it because of its moisture; for other kinds of fire destroy it because of their dryness. Therefore, no other fire in the world is like this except for the **material fire of a healthy human body** <note>The alchemist suggests that the warmth of fermenting manure is biologically similar to human body heat.</note>.

The fire of the Sun is indeed hot in the same degree, but it is dry. This [moist fire of the horse], however, is what masters the substance; it is produced from an **animated thing** <note>Latin: *re animata*; a living or once-living source, such as manure.</note> and is nourished like a child who is given milk in the beginning. For a child is nourished and grows from heat and moisture; in this same way, the horse’s fire increases the oil by its moisture, yet it **fixes** <term>fixes|Latin: *figit*; the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</term> the stone by tempering it with its heat.

Between these two, there is also another kind of fire, which is hot and dry in the second degree, like the heat of an **oven after the bread has been removed** <note>This refers to the residual, "falling" heat of a baker's kiln, which is dry but lacks the violence of an active flame.</note>. This fire melts things gently and does not burn them, because there is no flame in it, nor a great intensity of heat. For the heat recedes by declining little by little. But if that heat were to remain steady, it would fix the spirit within the body, or outside the body.

The horse’s fire, however, neither melts nor burns; instead, it masters the substance and increases the moisture. There is also a fourth fire, the **fire of the furnace of fixation** <note>Latin: *furni fixionis*; a specialized furnace designed to maintain a steady heat for long periods to stabilize a substance.</note>. This fire melts and fixes, but does not burn, because it is not flaming. It does not differ from the preceding fire except that in this one the heat is continuous, while in the other it is not.

The fifth fire is called **flaming** <term>flaming|Latin: *flammalis*; a direct, active fire with visible flames, representing the highest and most aggressive degree of heat.</term>, and it is hot and—

<meta>catchword: dry [Latin: siccu]</meta>

[The fifth fire is] dry in the third degree: this only **calcines** <term>calcines|Latin: *calcinat*; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures, usually to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</term>, and does not **melt** <term>melt|Latin: *fundit*; also known as fusion, the process of liquefying a solid.</term>, namely, in comparison to gold and silver and other bodies in the same degree or beyond; and it is the fire in the furnace of calcination.

The sixth is hot and dry in the fourth degree: and this melts and **fixes** <term>fixes|Latin: *figit*; the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</term> strongly, softening bodies gently, neither dissipating them nor scattering them. This is the fire of the furnace of fusion in the same degree.

There is also the **fire of the bellows** <term>fire of the bellows|Latin: *ignis follium*; a fire where the temperature is intensified by forced air from bellows.</term>, which dissipates and scatters bodies, and melts them, and this is the seventh.

The eighth is that which melts and calcines, and is **flaming**: because in it only the flame works. The substance of fire is coals and flame, and in this one, only the flame of wood; this also is in the same degree as the preceding ones. In the same degree also is the ninth, namely, that which is the master over all: such as the **fire of officiating** <note>original: *ignis officiationis*</note>: that is, of **examination** <term>examination|Latin: *examinationis*; the process of assaying or testing a metal's purity, often through intense heat like cupellation.</term>; this melts and burns, and dissipates and scatters the evil, but saves and rectifies the good, and is like a judge, discerning the just from the unjust.

->*The fire of junipers.*<-

A continuous artificial fire, lasting in the same degree as you wish, for one, or two, or three months, until you bare the coals <note>The alchemist is describing a "self-feeding" or "slow-burning" heat source where the coals are buried.</note>: therefore you must always keep them covered, and you can increase or decrease the heat at your pleasure, and this according to the addition of more or fewer ignited coals. In the first place, you should have sufficient ashes, and made only from **juniper wood** <note>original: *ligno Iuniperi*. Juniper charcoal was traditionally believed to retain its heat longer than any other wood when buried in its own ashes.</note>. Then you should have a large pot

[...an earthenware] pot, in the middle of which should be another smaller pot or **crucible** <term>crucible|Latin: *crucibulum*; a vessel designed to withstand high temperatures.</term>, and by placing ashes in the large pot, let it stand over the heat of the fire until the ash itself grows hot: and so, all around the smaller pot upon the ashes, you shall place coals also made only from the aforementioned **juniper wood** <note>Juniper wood was highly valued in alchemy for its ability to hold heat for a long duration, allowing for the steady temperatures required in long operations.</note>.

Finally, you should have even more heated ashes of the same wood, which you will sprinkle over the aforementioned coals, and cover them very well with their own hot ash. And in that smaller pot or glass vessel, you should have your **material to be digested** <term>digested|Latin: *digerendam*; the alchemical process of heating a substance slowly over a long period, mimicking biological digestion.</term>, and place a cover over the larger pot, and place it in the **heated room** <note>original: *stubam*; a stove-heated room or chamber.</note> under a bench or above—but upon a stone, lest perhaps damage be caused <note>A safety precaution to prevent the heat from the pot from igniting wooden furniture or floors.</note>. By such a practice, you can prepare several fires of this kind: you can also place hot water in the smaller pot, or a **moist horse's belly** <term>horse's belly|Latin: *ventrem equi humidum*; a method of providing gentle, steady heat by burying a vessel in fermenting horse manure.</term>, and in that, the flask of the material.

You shall make the aforementioned coals in this manner: Cut the juniper wood into small pieces, to the thickness of two fingers or larger; place them in a large pot, well-sealed on all sides and **coated with clay** <note>original: *perlutatam*; "luting" was the practice of sealing a vessel's lid or joints with a paste of clay, sand, and sometimes hair or dung to make it airtight.</note>, and filled: place that pot for a whole day in the strong fire of a **wind furnace** <term>wind furnace|Latin: *furni venti*; a furnace that uses a natural or forced draft of air to reach high temperatures.</term> or a wood flame. Then, allow it to cool by itself: open the pot, and you will have what you desire. The ashes, however, you shall burn in the common way. This fire can be
->a fire of the first or second degree for the fixation<-
->of spirits.<- <term>fixation of spirits|Latin: *fixio spirituum*; the process of transforming a volatile, vaporous substance into a stable solid that no longer evaporates when heated.</term>

I am the unique daughter of the wise, completely unknown to fools <note>original: *Ego sum vnica filia sapientum, stultis penitus ignota.* This is a personification of the Philosophers' Stone or the secret Wisdom itself.</note>. **Hermes**: Just as the Sun is among the stars, so gold is among the metals. Likewise: the **tincture** <term>tincture|In alchemy, a "tincture" is the concentrated essence or power of the Stone, capable of "dyeing" or transforming base metals into gold.</term> must be corporeal, extracted from perfected metallic bodies through the benefit and medium of minerals.

### *General Rules.*

Every thing consists of that into which it is resolved: for ice is converted into water by means of heat; it is therefore necessary that it was water before it was ice. In the same way, all metals were previously **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver|Latin: *argentum vivum*. While we know this as the element mercury, alchemists believed it was the "First Matter" or liquid essence from which all other metals grew in the earth.</term>, which is evident because when they melt in the fire, they are converted into it. Note here that the Philosopher also calls molten metal **Mercury**, or quicksilver; therefore, the reduction of metals into quicksilver in this manner is called "liquation," even though it happens through the violence of fire. However, because it maintains the appearance of quicksilver in that strong melting, he therefore also names it quicksilver. But this is not the **Philosophical solution** <term>Philosophical solution|The "lay" or common solution is simply melting a metal with heat; the "Philosophical" solution is a secret chemical process that reduces a metal to its spiritual, liquid essence without destroying its "seed" or life-force.</term>, but a "lay" one; nevertheless, it corresponds in some way to the sayings of Philosophy regarding the particulars known to you.

### *Second Rule.*

Every nature naturally desires to be perfected,

<header>ROSARY</header>

...and it shrinks from and flees destruction <note>original: *& destrui abhorret & fugit*. This completes the thought from the previous page: substances naturally seek to return to their original, "perfect" state to avoid being destroyed.</note>. Therefore, it eagerly embraces that which improves it and rejects its opposite as much as it can. According to this principle, **Art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers specifically to the art of alchemy.</note> must imitate **Nature**; otherwise, it will always go astray.

### *The Third Rule.*

Every inferior thing at work in any art strives, out of its natural corruption, to destroy the superior thing. Conversely, every superior thing at work in an art tries to perfect the inferior. Therefore, you must first understand the natures of things so that you may know how to distinguish what is "superior" or "inferior" in nature—from what a thing is perfected, and by what it is hindered. You must also ensure that the quantity of the inferior substance does not exceed the quantity of the superior; otherwise, you will fall into great error.

### *The Fourth Rule.*

Every dry thing naturally desires to "drink" its own moisture so that its parts may be unified. Note here what is the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture|Latin: *humidum radicale*. In medieval science, this was the essential, life-sustaining fluid found in all things. In alchemy, it refers to the internal mercury of a metal that allows it to melt and be transformed.</term> of all things that can be melted. Feed the overly dry substance with such moisture, and it will become balanced. In this way, you will achieve your desired goal.

### *common sulfur & the simple sulfur of the Philosophers*
### *which does not burn.*

WHEN the Philosopher <note>original: *Philosophus*. Likely referring to Aristotle, who was the primary authority for medieval science.</note> speaks generally, saying that sulfur coagulates <note>In alchemy, "coagulation" is the process of turning a liquid substance, like mercury, into a solid.</note>, it must be said that it does not. This is because every kind of common sulfur <note>original: *sulphur vulgi*</note> is, according to the Philosopher, foreign and contrary to metals. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose writings on alchemy were highly influential in Europe.</note> says: That which is not born from it does not enter into the **mastery** <term>mastery|Latin: *magisterium*. The alchemical process of transformation, or the Great Work of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term>, because it always stains, blackens, and corrupts, in whatever way it may be prepared by the art. It is, in fact, a tainted fire, and therefore it hinders **fusion** <note>original: *fusionem*. The melting or casting of metal.</note>. If, however, it is **calcined** <term>calcined|Latin: *calcinatur*. The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the air to remove volatile parts or to reduce it to a powder.</term>, it returns to an earthy substance, like a dead powder.

How, then, can it breathe life into others? For it possesses a double superfluity: namely, a flammable substance and an earthy foulness <note>original: *fœculentiam*</note>. Therefore, consider by these things that common sulfurs are not those of the Philosophers, since the sulfur of the Philosophers is a simple living fire, bringing life to other dead bodies <note>In alchemical texts, "dead bodies" usually refers to base metals that have not yet been transformed into "living" gold or silver.</note>, and maturing them, so that it supplies the defect of nature. For this sulfur is of overflowing maturity, insofar as it is made perfect in its own nature, and is purified more and more through the art. Whence Avicenna says: Such sulfur is not found upon the earth, except insofar as...

### How the red sulfur is in the Sun, and the white in the Moon.

Since it has been said that the red sulfur of the Philosophers exists in the **Sun** <note>original: *Sole*. Symbol for gold.</note> through a greater digestion, and the white sulfur exists in the **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*. Symbol for silver.</note> through a lesser digestion. Hence the Philosopher <note>The author likely refers to a classical authority like Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus.</note> says: **Yellowing** <term>Yellowing|Latin: *citrinatio*. An intermediate stage of the alchemical process where the material turns yellow, signaling the transition from the "white" stage to the final "red" stage.</term> is nothing other than complete digestion. For heat acting upon the moist first generates blackness, and acting upon the dry causes whiteness; but if the fire transcends this, its action changes the substance into the purest yellowing. All these things can be observed in the **calcination of lead** <note>The chemical process of heating lead until it oxidizes and turns into a powder.</note>. And the Philosopher says that each of the perfect bodies <note>Gold and silver, the "noble" metals.</note> already actually contains its own good sulfur along with **Mercury**, namely, golden sulfur in gold and silver sulfur in silver; therefore, white sulfur becomes gold through yellowing. For this reason, the sulfur within it is red sulfur, the substance of fire, which has digested this white sulfur more; and thus both white and red sulfur exist from both sides within the Sun. Therefore, fire is its perfection, and it was generated in fire; and so nature amicably rejoices in its own fiery nature.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 299 regarding the relationship between natural processes and the alchemical "Art." It uses a biological analogy to explain how heat "digests" matter, leading to the perfection found in gold.</meta>

<page-num>300</page-num>

...[natural] things <note>The text likely completes a word like "naturalibus" from the previous page.</note> cannot cause these effects, since **Art** is nothing else—with **Nature** acting as the mediator—except the decoction and digestion <term>Decoction and Digestion|In alchemy, these terms refer to the prolonged application of steady heat to "ripen" a substance, mimicking the way the earth ripens metals over centuries or how the stomach processes food.</term> of that nature through simple labor. For example: In the morning when I rise and see my urine is white, I judge that I have slept too little; then I lay myself down to sleep again, and after more sleep, the urine becomes **yellow** <note>original: *citrinatur*. This refers to the "citrine" or yellow stage of the Great Work.</note>; and this happens because of the greater digestion of the **natural heat** existing within me.

Thus you should follow nature, to similarly decoct, digest, ripen, and sublimate through Art, since Nature already actually contains within itself the natural fire by which it is ripened. Other things do not have this fire, and therefore they cannot give it. In the **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*. The alchemical symbol for silver.</note>, however, there is only **white sulfur**, which is simple, yet not "digested" in the same way as the red, nor is it so purged of its blackness by the action of the heat which it naturally contains within itself.

But this species of fire is covered and hidden, acting upon the substance more through Art than through Nature, and vice versa; and therefore it is not impossible for Art to succeed, with Nature mediating. <margin>B</margin>
...purity, nor is there anything in it that is superfluous, nor anything lacking; for this reason the Philosophers have preferred and magnified it. They have said that **gold** <note>original: *aurum*</note> holds the same place among the bodies as the **Sun** <note>original: *Sol*</note> does among the stars by its own light and splendor; for by that light, plants germinate in the earth, and every fruit is perfected by the will of God. Likewise, gold contains and gives life to every body within itself, because the **Elixir** is a **leaven** <term>Leaven|Translated from 'fermentum.' In alchemy, this is a substance (usually gold or silver) added to the "base" of the work to "infect" it with its own noble nature, much like yeast transforms dough.</term>, without which the work is by no means completed. Just as dough is not leavened nor does it rise without leaven, so it is when you whiten, sublime, and cleanse the bodies, and extract from them the dregs and filth: then, wishing to unify, join, and mix them together, place the leaven upon them. Examine carefully how the leaven of the dough is nothing other than leaven. Meditate, therefore, and contemplate whether the leaven of a thing can be anything except that which is of its own nature. This is the **key of all Philosophers**. And it should be noted that the leaven whitens the composition, inhibits burning, and contains the **tincture** <term>Tincture|The concentrated essence or 'soul' of the metal that allows it to transform other substances.</term> so that it does not flee; it softens the bodies and makes them enter into one another and join, which is the goal of the operator. By this knowledge, the bodies are cleansed and their work is completed, God granting His favor. **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a prolific writer to whom many alchemical treatises were attributed.</note> says in *The Apertory*: "Now, through the second part, the stone shall color itself; it is fixed and leavened. The leaven of the stone for the **white** <note>The *Albedo* stage, resulting in silver.</note> is silver, and for the **red** <note>The *Rubedo* stage, resulting in gold.</note> it is gold, as the Philosophers demonstrate: because without leaven, the Sun [Gold] does not come..."

**Calid the Philosopher** <note>original: *Calidius*; referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince credited with introducing alchemy to the Islamic world</note> says: No one has ever been able, nor will they ever be able, to dye the **foliated earth** <note>original: *terram foliatam*; a specific stage in the alchemical process where the material becomes white and flaky like leaves or scales</note>, except with **gold**. Gold is the **ferment** <note>original: *fermentum*; a substance that acts like yeast, "rising" and transforming the larger mass</note> of the work, without which it is by no means completed: because it is like the leaven of dough, the curdling agent of milk in cheese, and like musk in fine spices; and with it is made the composition of the Great <term>Elixir|A potent alchemical substance capable of transforming base metals into gold or granting longevity.</term>: because it illuminates the work and preserves it from **adustion** <note>original: *adustione*; the process of being scorched or burnt, which alchemists believed ruined the substance</note>, which is a sign of perfection. Hence a certain person said: Unless you place gold in gold, you do nothing. **Arisleus** says: Know most firmly that if little gold is placed in the composition, the tincture will come out manifest...

### That it is impossible for lesser minerals to be artificially made into metals

But because it was determined in the preceding chapter that it is impossible for lesser minerals to be artificially turned into metals, it remains here to be proven. First, it is because lesser minerals are not generated from the **primary matter** <term>Primary matter|*Materia prima*; the foundational substance of all things, which in alchemy refers to the most basic, undifferentiated state of matter before it takes a specific form.</term> of metals, which is Mercury. Their generation differs from the generation of Mercury from the very start—in form, in nature, and in composition. Therefore, they cannot become metals, because for things of a single species, there is one primary matter and **seed** <note>original: *sperma*; the vital starting material or reproductive essence from which a substance grows</note> from which they are generated. 

The first part of the previous statement is clear: that lesser minerals are not generated from Mercury. This is the reason: because Mercury always remains the primary matter of metals, and not extraneous sulfurs. Thus **Aristotle** and **Avicenna** <note>Aristotle and Avicenna|Two of the most cited authorities in medieval alchemy. This is because nourishment in a man cannot become a man through generation unless it is first converted into **seed** <note>original: *sperma*</note>, and thus added to its like, a new man is generated. 

But because lesser minerals are of a nature foreign to metals—although they certainly participate in some mineral power—they are of a weaker virtue and are **combustible** <term>Combustible|*Adustibilia*; materials that are easily burned away or consumed by fire. In alchemy, true metals are expected to survive the fire, whereas lesser minerals perish.</term>; therefore the metallic nature does not rejoice in them, but rather dissolves and preserves only those things which are of its own nature. 

For example: if water were mixed with earth, they are separated from one another because the earth seeks the bottom, since it is heavy and dry, while the water seeks the surface. In no way can they be so joined artificially that these contrary natures remain together in a single nature. Water can certainly wash and cleanse the earth, but it should not be believed that the dryness of the earth can be artificially changed into an aqueous humidity, even though the earth may be moistened by the water. In the same way, lesser minerals can indeed be joined with metals to purge them, and in some way introduce a new form; but nature does not permit them to remain with the metals, nor to mature that which is immature.

-># THE ROSARY<-

In the **Astronomy** of the firmament we see that the **Sun** <note>original: *Sol*. ### *in this art.*

For if they were transformed into **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*</note>, and mixed with the Sun and the Moon, then their Mercury would still possess that previously mentioned "bad sulfur" within itself.

But with the natures on both sides being locked away, each would be separated from the other during the examination <note>original: *examine*. Do not believe that these are common elements—for instance, water from a cloud or similar things. Instead, understand them by their qualities:
*   Cold and dry is **earth**
*   Cold and moist is **water**
*   Moist and hot is **air**
*   Hot and dry is **fire**

And thus the elements exist within the natures of things. However, Art can by no means separate the parts connected during their creation so that they are simply **transmuted** <term>transmutentur: to change from one substance into another</term> back into the basic elements they once were. This is because the primary nature has already changed one quality into another. In this manner, Art is well able to separate qualities—such as the moist from the dry, or the cold from the hot—but nevertheless, one quality still possesses the nature of the other in some part, due to their natural mixing...

### PHILOSOPHICAL WORKS 323

Through these methods, they can be joined back together by **Art** <note>The practice of alchemy</note> in a reverse process, just as they were divided. This would be the case if it were not for the fact that one quality shares the nature of another—for instance, **water** shares the nature of **earth** in its coldness, and **air** shares the nature of **water** in its moisture, and so on. If this were not so, the work of nature would be totally destroyed. When the elements were in their simplest state, as they were before the generation of **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurij*; the fundamental metallic principle</note>, Art would have destroyed Nature by starting at the "head"—that is, from **gold** and **silver**—and going back to the beginning. This beginning is **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum viuum*; literal mercury</note>, and to go beyond these principles of the simple elements to the state they were in before Mercury was even generated is impossible for Art to achieve from such a distance.

If it were possible, it would follow that Art could compose elements anew from something outside the **Prime Matter** <term>prima materia: the original, formless "stuff" of the universe from which all things are made</term> of metals. In that case, Art would generate Mercury in the same way it destroyed it, which is impossible to do artificially. Indeed, Art "destroys" from the head down to the feet; that is, it takes Mercury and builds it up from the "foot" to the "head" in a more refined and subtle form, provided that the substance of Nature, which existed before, allows the Art to do so. In this way, the **species** <note>The essential "kind" or identity of a substance</note> of things are divided when they are transformed into a form other than what they were before. 

This is because **Aristotle** <note>This quote is actually from a 12th-century translation of the Persian philosopher Avicenna, though medieval alchemists usually attributed it to Aristotle</note> says: "Let the practitioners of alchemy know that the species of things cannot be truly transmuted." This statement is true unless the substances are first reduced or converted back into their **Prime Matter**—that is, into **quicksilver**. Beyond this, he does not advise proceeding, for to do otherwise is 

->impossible, etc.<-
