### *The purification of the stone follows, before it is*
### *placed in decoction.* CHAPTER II.

This work, which I have demonstrated to your understanding, shows itself to be pure, clean, pleasant, sincere, and upright. Once shaped into thin plates, it reveals that it has been purged of mineral coarseness through melting by fire. By the methods of **elevations** <term>elevations: In alchemical practice, this refers to sublimation—the process of heating a substance until it rises as vapor and then solidifies again, leaving impurities behind.</term>, it becomes subtle, leaving behind certain excesses of the burning, as well as earthy qualities and those things mixed in a thin yet strong union; meanwhile, certain corrupting moistures are exhaled. There are two signs of this refining: one, indeed, is that the substance rising is a **citron-colored spirit** <note>original: "spiritus citrinus." A yellow or golden-hued vapor or substance, often indicating the presence of philosophical sulfur.</note>, which has become a stone of lesser hardness, possessing a degree of transparency. The other sign is that which remained at the bottom of the vessel: a thin and **black earth** <note>original: "terra nigra." This represents the *nigredo* stage, where the "body" of the matter is broken down and purified through metaphorical death or "putrefaction."</note>. 

However, pay close attention to this: in this elevation, if it is performed correctly, a certain permanent thing is found. This must be brought by force over the abundantly volatile part and elevated; then, that which was elevated must be returned to the part that remains, until the whole becomes "fleeing" <term>fleeing: "volatilis" in Latin. A substance that vaporizes easily when heated, often representing the spirit of the matter.</term>. And then, the aforementioned black earth remains from both, now converted into the aforesaid stone—hard and of a deep citron color. Yet, do not be content with this volatility until it is found that the entire mass of the stone, having been elevated by fire and returned to its vessel, continuously ascends through that same vessel; do this so that nothing—neither clean nor dirty—remains in the depths.

...from the mold split through the middle: and it must be a **vessel one cubit** <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> **long**, narrow at the top; and this narrowing should allow nothing of the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritu." In alchemy, the "spirit" refers to the volatile parts of a substance that vaporize when heated.</note> to exhale. The length of the vessel should cause the fumes to precipitate <note>To fall back down as liquid after condensing.</note>, if any happen to be elevated, and it should consume the corrupting humidities within itself. For those seeking the arrangement of the furnace and vessel, it is a **vision of the lily** <note>original: "lilij visio." This likely refers to the symbolic "whiteness" or purity the alchemist must envision, or perhaps a specific lily-shaped glass apparatus.</note>, not a matter of mere writing. The heat must surround the vessel on all sides, so that there is an **equality of heat** everywhere; otherwise, it would be called a **bath** <note>original: "balneum." This refers to the *balneum Mariae* or water bath, used for gentle, even heating.</note> in vain. 

And at the summit of the furnace, there must be a hole through which a single piece of glass, round and long, should emerge, closing the opening of the said vessel. By touching this piece of glass, it can be known if the matter is being **decocted** <term>decoction: a process of long, slow heating in a closed vessel to mature the substance</term> with the appropriate heat. And if by chance any smoke is seen to rise within the aforementioned vessel, the specific arrangement <note>original: "dosis"</note> does not permit it to exhale, no matter how much the vessel might even be held open. 

Regarding this, it is said by **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the influential 8th-century alchemist.</note>: "One is never truly separated from the other, although to the sight they may seem to be segregated or superficially separated. Nor can one exist without the other; for their spirits are tempered through the path of perfect nature to such an extent that they are not separated from one another." 

In this degree of heat, however, the matter is made **black**; for active heat produces **blackness** <note>original: "nigredinem"</note> in that which is moist. For this reason, it is said in the **Assembly of Philosophers** <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: "When you see the blackness looming over it, know that the body has now been liquefied." Likewise, at the beginning of the work, all things are blackened. This result occurs so that one may beware of excessive fire; because...

Excessive heat causes the matter to perish and the composite substance to separate. Therefore, the work must proceed with a tempered fire: it is matured through slow heating <note>original: "decoquitur." This refers to decoction, a process of long-term, gentle simmering in a sealed vessel.</note>, just as a child is nourished by milk. All the masters agree on this point. This is also demonstrated in the Practice regarding the various colors that are contained within the stage of blackness.

### *Concerning the degree of fire when blackness arrives.*
#### CHAPTER IV.

When the whole substance is truly black, let the fire be continued at that same level until the whiteness, which is hidden in its belly, appears; for in this way, the fixed substance <note>The "fixed" part of the matter is that which can endure the fire without vaporizing.</note> draws near. It should be noted, however, that within this blackness many colors appear, which the Philosophers <note>In alchemical texts, "the Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval masters of the art, such as Hermes Trismegistus or Geber.</note> mention. For sometimes the whole becomes green, sometimes lead-colored <note>original: "liuidum." A bluish-gray or bruised hue often associated with the planet Saturn and the initial stages of decay.</note>, and sometimes violet. Sometimes one side of the vessel is green while the other is black, or it appears leaden inside and green on the outside; yet all these colors are classified under the stage of blackness. And since no essential perfection exists within these intermediate colors, the Philosophers primarily name only three among all the others—those which are called the virtues of the soul—namely: black, white, and red. Therefore, it is said in the *Turba* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among ancient sages.</note>: "Venerate the king and his wife <note>Symbolic terms for the primary metallic or chemical principles, often associated with Gold/Sulfur and Silver/Mercury.</note>, and do not burn them, lest you drive them away with excessive fire. For you do not know when you will need those who improve the king and his wife. Cook them so that they become black, then white, then red:"

...then, by dyeing, let it become a poison <note>original: "venenum." In this mortification, the spirits are united—that is, they are dried out—because unless the bodies are dried, the colors of the soul (which are called "blackness" and "clouds") do not appear.

Likewise, when the magnesia <note>original: "magneſies." Likewise, the staining and vivifying spirit is introduced after the corrupting moisture has departed and is no longer nourished, which is the path toward whitening or whiteness. Therefore, when the red color appears, nature reveals its hidden perfection.

For this is not true, as they assert, unless they are [first] reduced to their <term>primary matter</term> <note>original: "primam materiam"; the fundamental substance from which all things in the universe were believed to be created</note>. The reduction of the metal itself to primary matter is easy and possible. 

Therefore, I show you that <term>multiplication</term> <note>The alchemical process of increasing the quantity or the power of the "Medicine" or the gold produced</note> in metals is possible. For everything that grows and is born is multiplied, as is evident in plants and trees: for from a single grain, a thousand grains are procreated; from a single tree, infinite little branches proceed, from which various and infinite trees are made. And thus they increase and multiply their number. Metals, moreover, are born and grow in the earth: therefore, augmentation and multiplication in them is possible even unto infinity.

I have shown you, my dearest son, [the end/beginning] of wisdom: fi...

Thus you have, according to others, the element which is water. <note>The text here mirrors the logic that solids precipitate out of liquids, viewing the residue as a purified elemental "earth."</note>

Concerning this, Pheyrer also said in the book *The Assembly*: "Join the dry with the moist—that is, the earth to the water." Behold, you now have water by itself, and the earth whitened with the water.

# OF BROTHER ROGER
## BACON THE ENGLISHMAN, ON THE
### *Marvelous Power of Art and Na-*
### *ture, a Little Book.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap for the letter 'I' at the beginning of the first paragraph, featuring ornate floral and foliate scrollwork inside a square frame.</image-desc>

I respond to your request: For although nature is powerful and marvelous, yet art, using nature as an instrument <term>instrumentali; Bacon argues that technology (art) is a tool that directs the inherent powers of the natural world</term>, is more so, as we see in many things. Whatever, however, exists beyond the operations of nature or art is either not human, or it is a fiction and fraught with fraud. For there are those who, by quick movement, by the appearance of limbs, by diversity of voices, by the subtlety of instruments, by darkness, or by conspiracy, present many wonders to mortals that have no reality of existence. The world is full of these, as is obvious: for jugglers <note>original: *ioculatores*; in the Middle Ages, this referred to sleight-of-hand performers, acrobats, or minstrels</note> deceive by great speed of hand, and ventriloquists <note>original: *phytonissæ*; historically "pythonesses" or sorceresses, but Bacon here describes the physical mechanics of projecting the voice from the "belly and throat" to debunk "spirits"</note> create human voices with a variety of tones in the belly and throat, and with inventions and the mouth, from far or near, as they wish, as if a spirit were then speaking in human fashion; they even imitate the sounds of animals. Indeed, the causes [of these voices], hidden under the grass or concealed in the sides of the earth, show that it is a human force and not a spirit, which they fashion with a great lie. When, however, in the shadows of twilight or the night

495
->DE MIR. POT. ART. ET NAT.<-
<note>original: *De Mirabili Potestate Artis et Naturae*; "On the Marvelous Power of Art and Nature"</note>

If indeed inanimate things are moved quickly, it is not truth, but fraud and deception: for conspiracy <note>original: *consensus*; here meaning a secret agreement or plot between people</note> feigns all those things that men desire, according to how they are arranged among themselves. In all these matters, neither physical reason considers them, nor art, nor does the power of nature hold sway. For this reason, it is a wicked occupation when a man despises the laws of Philosophy <term>Philosophia; in Bacon's time, this referred to "Natural Philosophy," the study of the physical world and the precursor to modern science</term>, and against all reason invokes nefarious spirits so that through them he may fulfill his will. And in this lies the error: that they believe spirits are subjected to them, and that spirits can be compelled by human will, for this is impossible—because human force is far inferior to that of spirits.

Or they wander even further astray because they believe that through certain natural things which they use, evil spirits are either summoned or given form; and they err still further when, through invocations, prayers, and sacrifices, they strive to appease those spirits and bring them forth for human benefit. For it would be incomparably easier to obtain from God, or from good spirits, whatever a man ought to consider useful. 

But evil spirits do not assist favorably even in these useless matters, except insofar as it is permitted by God because of human sins—God who rules and governs the human race. Therefore, these ways are outside the teachings of wisdom; indeed, they more likely work to the contrary. Those practicing Philosophy <note>original: *Philosophantes*; refers to scholars of natural science</note> have never cared for these six modes <note>Bacon previously categorized different types of false magic and trickery</note>.

What indeed of incantations <note>original: *carminibus*; spells or ritual chants</note> and symbols <note>original: *characteribus*; magical inscriptions or sigils</note>,

<summary>Roger Bacon argues that "magic" is usually either human trickery or a dangerous and futile attempt to control spirits. He asserts that true scientists (philosophers) should rely on the laws of nature and divine favor rather than demonic invocation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 495 regarding the distinction between true natural phenomena and the deceptive practices of magic. While the previous page focused on the error of invoking spirits, this page explains how philosophers intentionally hid scientific truths behind magical-looking symbols to protect them from the unlearned.</meta>

496
->ON THE MARVELOUS POWER<-
<note>original: *DE MIRAB. POTEST.*; short for *De Mirabili Potestate Artis et Naturae* (On the Marvelous Power of Art and Nature)</note>

...and what should be held regarding these matters, I consider in this manner. For without a doubt, all things of this kind in our time are false and doubtful; for some belong to the irrational, which Philosophers <term>Philosophi; in this context, "natural philosophers" or early scientists</term> recorded within the works of nature and art, so that they might hide secrets from the unworthy. It is just as if it were entirely unknown that a magnet <term>magnes; a naturally occurring magnetic rock or lodestone</term> attracts iron; if someone, wishing to perform this feat before the people, were to draw symbols <term>characteres; magical signs, shapes, or inscriptions</term> and recite charms <term>carmina; incantations or ritual songs</term> so that the force of attraction might be completed, this whole performance would be an error <note>original: *error*; here meaning a deception or a fundamental misunderstanding of the cause</note>. 

Thus, many things are hidden in the books of the Philosophers in many ways; in these matters, a wise man ought to have the prudence to disregard the charms and symbols, and instead examine the work of nature and art. And so he will see both animate and inanimate things conform to nature, because of their natural affinity <note>original: *conformitatem*; the idea that things with similar natures naturally act upon one another</note>, and not because of the power of a charm or a symbol. 

In this way, many secrets of nature and art are thought to be magical by the unlearned, and magicians <term>magi; those who claim to use supernatural powers through rituals</term> foolishly trust in charms and symbols, believing they provide power. In their pursuit of these things, they abandon the true work of nature or art because of the error of those charms and symbols. Thus, both types of these men <note>meaning both the unlearned who are deceived and the magicians who believe their own charms</note> are deprived of the utility of wisdom, compelled by their own foolishness. 

There are, however, certain supplications <term>deprecationes; formal prayers or petitions intended to avert evil</term> instituted of old by men of truth, or rather ordained by God and the angels, and these may retain their original power.

<meta>catchword: Sicut (Just as)</meta>

<summary>Roger Bacon argues that many "magical" effects are actually natural phenomena, like magnetism, which have been disguised by philosophers using charms and symbols to keep scientific secrets away from the unlearned. He concludes that relying on such superstitious symbols causes one to lose the true benefits of wisdom and natural science.</summary>

->OF ART AND NATURE<-

Just as in many regions certain prayers are still performed over glowing iron, and over river water, and similarly other things in which the innocent are proven and the guilty are condemned, and these are believed to take place by the authority of the prelates <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops</note>. For even the priests themselves perform exorcisms, as in the blessing of Holy Water, or as is read in the Old Law regarding the Water of Purgation <note>original: *Aqua purgatorij*; a reference to the "bitter water" ordeal for suspected adultery described in the biblical Book of Numbers, chapter 5</note>, by which adultery or a wife’s faithfulness is tested; and there are many things of this kind.

But those things contained in the books of Magicians are all to be shunned, even if they contain some truth: because they abuse so many falsehoods that the truth cannot be discerned from the false. Therefore, whoever claims that Solomon <note>King Solomon was historically—though spuriously—credited with writing many medieval grimoires and magical manuals</note> or other Sages composed them must be refuted: for books of this kind are not accepted by the authority of the Church, nor by wise men, but by deceivers who take only the bare literal meaning <note>original: *nudam accipiunt literam*; implying they lack the deep, symbolic, or scientific understanding of the text</note>. These men compose new books themselves and multiply new inventions, as we know through experience. And so that men might then be more powerfully enticed, they place famous titles upon their works and imprudently attribute them to great Authors. Furthermore, so that their readers suspect nothing, they use a grandiloquent style and forge their lies under the form of a proper text. Their symbols <term>characteres; specifically magical signs, shapes, or inscriptions</term>, however, are either words composed of signs wrapped in letters, containing the sense of a manufactured prayer, or they are made for the worship of the stars at chosen times. Regarding symbols, therefore, first...

Therefore, he who makes them exactly as they are depicted in books, looking at nothing but the shape they fashion after a model, is judged by every wise man to accomplish nothing. 

But those who perform their works under the appropriate <term>constellations</term> <note>astrological alignments of stars and planets</note>, according to the "faces of the heavens," are able to arrange not only their symbols but all their works—whether of art or of nature—according to the power of the sky. Yet, because it is difficult to perceive the certainty of celestial movements, there is much error among many people in these matters; there are few who truly and usefully know how to arrange anything. Because of this, the common crowd of <term>Mathematicians</term> <note>original: *Mathematicorum*; in the Middle Ages, this term frequently referred to astrologers and those who calculated planetary positions for divination</note> who judge and operate by means of "magical" stars do not achieve much. Nevertheless, those who are most expert and possess sufficient skill could produce many benefits, both through their works and their judgments, at carefully chosen times. 

It must be considered, however, that a skilled physician (or anyone else practiced in a craft) can usefully employ incantations and symbols—even if they are fake—according to <term>Constantine the Physician</term> <note>Constantine the African (c. 1020–1087), a scholar whose translations of Arabic medical texts into Latin revolutionized Western medicine</note>. This is not because the symbols and incantations themselves perform any work, but so that the medicine may be received more devoutly and eagerly, and the spirit of the patient may be stirred, and they may trust more fully and rejoice. # OF ART AND NATURE

When Octavian Augustus was asked what he had done to live so long in such a state, he replied in a riddle that he applied oil on the outside and honeyed wine <note>original: *mulsum*. A popular Roman beverage made of wine and honey, often associated with health and longevity.</note> on the inside. But afterward, many things occurred: for a peasant digging in the fields found with his plow a golden vessel containing a noble liquor. Thinking it was "celestial dew," <note>In medieval alchemy, dew was believed to be a pure, primordial substance capable of capturing the "spirit of the world."</note> he washed his face and drank it; he was renewed in spirit, body, and the goodness of wisdom. From a mere plowman, he was made a bearer for the King of Sicily, which happened in the time of King Ostis. <note>likely referring to a legendary or historical figure in the medieval tradition of "wonders."</note> 

It is also proven by the testimony of papal letters that a German man, taken captive among the Saracens, received a medicine by which he prolonged his life for up to five hundred years. For the King who held him captive had received messengers from a Magian King <note>original: *regis Magi*. This likely refers to a king of the "Magi" or wise men from the East, a common trope in medieval longevity legends.</note> with this medicine. But because he held the medicine in suspicion, he wished to test the gift he had been sent on the captive. 

Furthermore, the Lady of Tormery in Great Britain, while searching for a white hind, <note>The "white hind" or white deer is a common motif in medieval folklore, often leading characters to magical discoveries or otherworlds.</note> discovered an ointment with which the keeper of the woods had anointed his entire body, except for the soles of his feet. He lived for three hundred years without any physical decay, except for pains and sufferings in his feet. <note>A parallel to the myth of Achilles, where the unprotected part of the body remains vulnerable to time or injury.</note> 

And we have experienced many cases in our own times where country folk have lived for a hundred and sixty years or thereabouts without the advice of doctors. These things are also confirmed by the actions of animals, such as the stag, the eagle, and the serpent, <note>Medieval bestiaries claimed stags renewed their youth by eating snakes, eagles by flying near the sun and diving into water, and serpents by shedding their skin.</note> and many others, which renew their youth through the power of herbs and stones. And for this reason, the wise have given...

...against the corruption of the parents; not that a man might be restored to the life of Adam or of Artephius <note>original: *Artephirij*. I believe that no matter how much a wise man might achieve in these times—even though it is possible in theory and within the capacity of human nature, as it existed in the first men—this is no surprise, since that capacity extends even to immortality, just as it was before sin and will be after the resurrection.

Having previously discussed how even great thinkers like Aristotle were ignorant of certain truths that later became common knowledge, Bacon now addresses why the "secrets of nature" must be intentionally hidden from the general public.</meta>

->### ON MIRACULOUS POWER ###<-

...that he diminishes the majesty of things who divulges mystical matters, nor do secrets remain secret when the crowd becomes aware of them. For by a probable distinction between the **common people** <note>original: *vulgus*. In this context, Bacon refers to the uneducated or those without philosophical training, regardless of social rank.</note> and the wise, one must state the opposite: for while it is true that what appears to everyone is true, and similarly what appears to the wise and especially the most renowned is true; nevertheless, what appears to the majority—that is, the crowd—insofar as they are the crowd, must be false. I speak here of the "crowd" as it is distinguished from the wise in this discussion. For in common mental concepts, the crowd agrees with the wise, but in the specific principles and conclusions of arts and sciences they disagree, toiling over appearances in **sophisms** <term>sophismatibus: logical fallacies or arguments that seem true but are intentionally misleading.</term>, subtleties, and things for which the wise have no concern. In specific or secret matters, therefore, the common crowd errs, and is thus set apart from the wise; but in common matters, they are held under the law of all and agree with the wise. Truly, common things are of little value, nor are they to be pursued for their own sake, but rather for the sake of particular and specific things. The cause of this **concealment** <note>original: *latētiæ*. This refers to the tradition of "Esotericism," where scholars hid dangerous or powerful knowledge through codes and metaphors.</note> among all wise men was that the common crowd derides and neglects the secrets of wisdom, and does not know how to use the most worthy things. Furthermore, if some magnificent discovery should fall into their notice, they receive it by chance and accident, and abuse it to the manifold harm of individuals and the community. Therefore, he is **insane** who writes any secret unless it be hidden from the common crowd, so that it can only be understood with difficulty by the studious and the wise. Thus the life of the wise runs from the be[ginning] <meta>The catchword "cip" indicates the next word is "principio" (beginning).</meta>

<summary>Bacon argues that scientific and philosophical secrets must be kept from the "common crowd" to prevent their misuse and to preserve the dignity of knowledge. He asserts that while the masses may understand basic truths, they lack the training to handle complex or powerful "secrets of nature."</summary>

beginning, and in many ways they have hidden the secrets of wisdom from the common people. For some have hidden them using characters and spells; many others through riddles and figurative language, as Aristotle says in the *Book of Secrets*: 

> O Alexander, I wish to show you the greatest of secrets, and may divine providence assist you in hiding this mystery, and in perfecting the goal of the art of that **stone** <term>lapis: a reference to the "Philosopher’s Stone," which in alchemical tradition was not a literal rock but a refined substance representing the height of physical and spiritual transformation.</term> which is not a stone, and is found in any human, and in any place, and in any time, and is called the goal of all Philosophers;

Thirdly, they hid things by their manner of writing: namely, by using **consonants only** <note>original: *consonantes tantùm*. ...of the mind: and therefore it will be a part of the **stone**, which is **not a stone** <note>original: *lapidis, qui non est lapis*. This is a classic alchemical paradox. <meta>This page concludes the treatise by Roger Bacon. It follows the cryptic chemical recipes of the previous page by providing a theoretical justification for the "medicine" (the elixir) based on Aristotelian physics and finishing with a solemn benediction and the work's title.</meta>

# OF ART AND NATURE. 525

It is my view that you must reduce everything to that base matter which you will find discussed by Aristotle in well-known and famous passages; for this reason, I remain silent on those details. Once you have obtained those materials, you will then possess several simple and equal substances; you shall achieve this through three contrary and various operations, which I previously referred to as the **Keys of the Art.** Furthermore, Aristotle states that an equality of powers determines the action and the suffering <note>original: *passionem*. In this philosophical context, "passion" refers to the capacity of a body to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> of bodies.

Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd, famous for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> asserts this as well while refuting Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the Greek physician whose theories on the four humors dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>. This is considered to be the simplest and purest medicine that can be found; it is effective against fevers and the ailments of both the soul and the body, yet it is more common <note>original: *vilior*. Literally "viler" or "cheaper." Alchemists often claimed the Great Work began with a substance that was common and overlooked by the ignorant.</note> than anything else. Whoever records these secrets will possess the key that opens and no one shuts, and when it shuts, no one opens <note>A biblical allusion to Revelation 3:7, signifying the absolute power and finality of the alchemical secret.</note>.

---

-> *of the English Order of Friars Minor, regarding the* <-
-> *Marvelous power of art and* <-
-> *nature.* <-

-> THE END OF THE LITTLE WORKS OF THE <-
-> **CHEMICAL ART.** <-

It ends with a formal attribution to Bacon and a biblical metaphor for the secrecy and power of the alchemical art.</summary>
